options / answer: A) heat energy that comes from inside the earth | B) sound energy from music | C) energy from water in the ocean | D) energy from living plants
why correct: geo (earth) + therm (heat) = heat from the earth.
tip: Break long words into roots.

stem: What does “it’s raining cats and dogs” mean?
options / answer: A) Pets are playing in the rain. | B) It is raining very hard. | C) It is a little cloudy. | D) Animals are falling from the sky.
why correct: This idiom describes very heavy rain.
tip: Idioms mean something different from their words.

stem: Kareem was “all ears” when the coach announced the team. What does this mean?
options / answer: A) He covered his ears. | B) He had large ears. | C) He listened very carefully. | D) He could not hear.
why correct: “All ears” means paying close attention.
tip: Use the situation to understand an idiom.

stem: What does the adage “The early bird catches the worm” teach?
options / answer: A) Never wake up early. | B) Birds should eat worms. | C) Worms are hard to find. | D) People who start early often succeed.
why correct: The saying encourages getting a head start.
tip: Adages are short sayings with life lessons.

stem: Match each saying with its meaning.
options / answer: Break the ice = start a friendly conversation | Hit the books = study hard | Actions speak louder than words = what you do matters more than what you say | Practice makes perfect = doing something often makes you better
why correct: The first two are idioms; the last two are adages.
tip: Think about when people use each saying.

stem: In “The bat flew out of the cave,” what does bat mean?
options / answer: A) a flying animal | B) a stick for hitting a ball | C) to hit something | D) to blink your eyes
why correct: Something that flies out of a cave is an animal.
tip: Use the rest of the sentence to pick the meaning.

stem: Which sentence uses “light” to mean NOT HEAVY?
options / answer: A) Please light the candle. | B) The empty box was light enough to carry. | C) Turn on the light. | D) The room was full of light.
why correct: An empty box that is easy to carry is not heavy.
tip: Test each meaning in the sentence.

stem: Read: “The coach told the team to stick together.” What does stick mean here?
options / answer: A) to poke | B) to glue | C) stay | D) a piece of wood
why correct: “Stick together” means stay together as a group.
tip: Notice whether the word is a noun or a verb.

stem: In which TWO sentences does “ring” mean a sound?
options / answer: A) I heard the phone ring. | B) She wore a gold ring. | C) The boxers stepped into the ring. | D) The bells ring at noon.
why correct: Phones and bells make sounds.
tip: Group sentences by the meaning used.

stem: Choose the word that means “not tidy”: “Clothes all over the floor made the room ____.”
options / answer: A) tidy | B) retidy | C) tidier | D) untidy
why correct: un- means not: untidy = not tidy, messy.
tip: un- = not.

stem: Choose the word that means “not agree”: “The two friends ____ about the best game.”
options / answer: A) disagree | B) reagree | C) preagree | D) overagree
why correct: dis- means not or opposite: disagree.
tip: dis- = not, opposite of.

stem: What does “overcooked” mean?
options / answer: A) cooked again | B) cooked before | C) not cooked | D) cooked too much
why correct: over- means too much.
tip: over- = too much.

stem: Which word means “not able to be seen”?
options / answer: A) invisible | B) visible | C) revisible | D) previsible
why correct: in- means not: invisible = not able to be seen.
tip: Some prefixes mean “not”: un-, in-, im-, dis-, non-.

stem: What does “teacher” mean?
options / answer: A) the act of teaching | B) one who teaches | C) full of teaching | D) teaching again
why correct: -er can mean “one who.”
tip: -er/-or = one who.

stem: What does “joyful” mean?
options / answer: A) one who brings joy | B) joy again | C) full of joy | D) without joy
why correct: -ful means full of.
tip: -ful = full of.

stem: Choose the word that means “in a quiet way”: “The baby slept ____.”
options / answer: A) quietness | B) quietly | C) quieter | D) quietful
why correct: -ly means “in a … way.”
tip: -ly often makes an adverb.

stem: How does the suffix change the word in “The movement of the ship made me dizzy”?
options / answer: A) -ment means “one who moves.” | B) -ment makes the word mean “not move.” | C) -ment makes the word plural. | D) -ment turns the verb “move” into a noun.
why correct: move (verb) + -ment = movement (noun).
tip: Suffixes can change a word’s part of speech.

stem: Which word is a synonym for “brave”?
options / answer: A) courageous | B) lazy | C) sleepy | D) timid
why correct: Courageous and brave mean almost the same.
tip: Synonyms have similar meanings.

stem: Which word is an antonym for “ancient”?
options / answer: A) old | B) modern | C) dusty | D) historic
why correct: Ancient means very old; modern means new.
tip: Antonyms have opposite meanings.

stem: Match each word with its ANTONYM.
options / answer: ancient = modern | generous = selfish | timid = bold | rough = smooth
why correct: Each pair has opposite meanings.
tip: Think of the opposite meaning first.

stem: Which word is spelled correctly?
options / answer: A) becuase | B) becaus | C) because | D) beacause
why correct: because: b-e-c-a-u-s-e.
tip: Say each part slowly: be-cause.

stem: Add -ed to the word stop: “The bus ____ at the corner.”
options / answer: (typed)
why correct: Double the final consonant before adding -ed: stopped.
tip: Short vowel + one consonant: double it before -ed.

stem: Which sentence has every word spelled correctly?
options / answer: A) We were surprised by the beatiful weather. | B) We were surprised by the beautiful wether. | C) We were suprised by the beautiful weather. | D) We were surprised by the beautiful weather.
why correct: surprised, beautiful and weather are spelled correctly.
tip: Check tricky words letter by letter.

stem: Add -ing to the word make: “I am ____ a card for my mother.”
options / answer: (typed)
why correct: Drop the silent e before adding -ing: making.
tip: Silent e + -ing: drop the e.

stem: Which word is more precise than “said” in: “‘Help!’ he ____.”
options / answer: A) shouted | B) did | C) talked | D) went
why correct: “Shouted” shows how he spoke.
tip: Precise words give clearer pictures.

stem: Which sentence uses the most precise language?
options / answer: A) The dog ate stuff. | B) The golden retriever chewed the red sneaker. | C) The animal did something to the thing. | D) The dog chewed the shoe.
why correct: Specific nouns and details create a clear picture.
tip: Replace general words with specific ones.

stem: Which sentence is the most precise for a science report?
options / answer: A) The water boiled pretty fast. | B) The water did a cool thing. | C) The water boiled at 100 degrees Celsius after eight minutes. | D) The water got really hot after a while.
why correct: Reports use exact numbers and terms.
tip: Use measurements and specific vocabulary in reports.

stem: Which revision of “The big storm made a lot of damage” is MOST precise?
options / answer: A) Something happened during the storm. | B) The storm was really big and bad. | C) The large storm made much damage. | D) The fierce sandstorm tore three palm trees from the ground.
why correct: Specific words (fierce sandstorm, three palm trees, tore) show exactly what happened.
tip: Precise language names exact things, numbers and actions.

stem: Which word means almost the same as “happy”?
options / answer: A) joyful | B) angry | C) hungry | D) tired
why correct: Happy and joyful both describe feeling good and pleased.
tip: Synonyms feel the same when you read them in a sentence.

stem: Which word is an antonym for “noisy”?
options / answer: A) loud | B) quiet | C) busy | D) messy
why correct: Noisy means full of sound; quiet means little or no sound — opposites.
tip: Test an antonym by putting “not” in front: not noisy = quiet.

stem: Choose the synonym: “The cheetah ran ____ (fast) across the field.”
options / answer: A) slowly | B) loudly | C) swiftly | D) sadly
why correct: Swiftly means moving very fast, the same as the word in parentheses.
tip: Try the word in the blank — a synonym keeps the same meaning.

stem: Which word is an antonym for “careful”?
options / answer: A) neat | B) slow | C) careless | D) cautious
why correct: Careful means paying close attention; careless means not paying attention — opposites.
tip: Many antonyms are formed by adding a prefix or suffix like -less.

stem: Match each word with its SYNONYM.
options / answer: quick = fast | joyful = happy | tiny = small | polite = courteous
why correct: Each pair has almost the same meaning.
tip: Try saying each word in the same sentence to check the meaning stays close.

stem: True or false: when describing a surface, “rough” and “smooth” are synonyms.
options / answer: True | False
why correct: Rough means bumpy or uneven, and smooth means even and flat — these are opposites, not synonyms.
tip: If two words describe opposite feelings when you touch something, they are antonyms.

stem: Which word is a synonym for “gentle” in: “She gave the kitten a gentle pat”?
options / answer: A) fast | B) loud | C) rough | D) soft
why correct: A soft pat and a gentle pat both describe a light, kind touch.
tip: Picture the action in the sentence to check which word fits the same way.

stem: Choose the antonym: “The sky was sunny in the morning but ____ by noon.”
options / answer: A) clear | B) bright | C) warm | D) gloomy
why correct: Gloomy (dark and cloudy) is the opposite of sunny.
tip: Look for a word that paints the opposite picture in the sky.

stem: Which word means almost the same as “scared”?
options / answer: A) frightened | B) curious | C) excited | D) proud
why correct: Scared and frightened both describe feeling afraid.
tip: Picture the feeling each word shows.

stem: Which word is an antonym for “messy”?
options / answer: A) cluttered | B) neat | C) dirty | D) colorful
why correct: Messy means untidy; neat means tidy and organized — opposites.
tip: Picture a messy room, then picture its opposite.

stem: Match each word with its ANTONYM.
options / answer: loud = quiet | strong = weak | wet = dry | bright = dim
why correct: Each pair has opposite meanings.
tip: Think of the exact opposite picture for each word.

stem: Read: “Dana felt upset when her kite got stuck in the tree.” Which word could replace “upset” without changing the meaning?
options / answer: A) thrilled | B) confused | C) unhappy | D) relieved
why correct: Upset and unhappy both describe feeling bad about something.
tip: Replace the word in the sentence and check if the meaning stays the same.

stem: A friendly neighbor smiles and waves, while an unfriendly neighbor looks away without a word. True or false: this contrast shows that “friendly” and “unfriendly” are antonyms.
options / answer: True | False
why correct: Friendly means warm and kind to others; unfriendly means cold or unkind — opposite meanings.
tip: The prefix “un-” often creates an antonym, as in friendly/unfriendly.

stem: Choose the synonym: “The puppy was very ____ (small).”
options / answer: A) tiny | B) heavy | C) loud | D) fast
why correct: Tiny and small both describe something little in size.
tip: Match the word to the meaning given in parentheses.

stem: Which word means almost the same as “repair”?
options / answer: A) replace | B) break | C) ignore | D) fix
why correct: Repair and fix both mean to make something work again.
tip: Think about what you do to something that is broken.

stem: Read: “Elephants flap their large ears to cool down in the heat. The ears are full of blood vessels, and flapping them helps release heat into the air.” Which detail explains HOW elephants’ ears help them cool down?
options / answer: A) “The ears are full of blood vessels, and flapping them helps release heat into the air.” | B) “Elephants live in hot climates.” | C) “Elephants flap their large ears to cool down in the heat.” | D) “Elephants are the largest land animals.”
why correct: The sentence about blood vessels and releasing heat is the actual mechanism, which answers “how.”
tip: Look for the sentence that explains the process, not just the fact.

stem: Read: “Spider silk comes in two kinds. Sticky silk traps insects, while non-sticky silk forms the frame. The spider is careful to walk only on the non-sticky strands.” Which TWO details explain why the spider does not get stuck in its own web?
options / answer: A) “non-sticky silk forms the frame” | B) “Sticky silk traps insects.” | C) “The spider is careful to walk only on the non-sticky strands.”
why correct: The web has two kinds of silk, and the spider only walks on the non-sticky kind.
tip: Choose evidence that explains the SPECIFIC claim, not just related facts.

stem: Read: “Yara practiced her violin every afternoon for a month before the recital. The night before, her hands trembled as she packed her case.” Which detail shows that Yara felt nervous the night before the recital?
options / answer: A) “before the recital” | B) “her hands trembled as she packed her case.” | C) “Yara practiced her violin.” | D) “Yara practiced her violin every afternoon for a month.”
why correct: Trembling hands are a physical sign of nervousness.
tip: Look for descriptions of feelings or body language.

stem: Read: “Bees communicate by dancing. A figure-eight dance tells other bees the direction and distance to flowers.” True or false: the text says bees use sound, not movement, to share information about flowers.
options / answer: True | False
why correct: The text says bees communicate by dancing (movement), not sound.
tip: Check whether the statement matches exactly what the text says.

stem: Read: “Rainforests cover about 6 percent of Earth’s land but are home to more than half of the world’s plant and animal species.” Which detail is evidence that rainforests are extremely important for wildlife?
options / answer: A) “Earth’s land” | B) “cover about 6 percent of Earth’s land” | C) “home to more than half of the world’s plant and animal species” | D) “Rainforests”
why correct: More than half of all species living there shows huge importance for wildlife.
tip: Match evidence to exactly what the claim is about.

stem: Read: “Khalid forgot his lunch at home. At recess, Fatima handed him half of her sandwich without saying a word, and Noor gave him one of her dates.” Which TWO details show that Khalid’s classmates were kind to him?
options / answer: A) “At recess” | B) “Khalid forgot his lunch at home.” | C) “Noor gave him one of her dates” | D) “Fatima handed him half of her sandwich without saying a word”
why correct: Sharing food with Khalid shows kindness from his classmates.
tip: Look for actions that directly help someone.

stem: Read: “Octopuses can change both the color and the texture of their skin in less than a second. This lets them blend in with rocks, sand, or coral to hide from predators.” Which detail explains WHY octopuses change their skin?
options / answer: A) “Octopuses can change both the color and the texture of their skin.” | B) “in less than a second” | C) “with rocks, sand, or coral” | D) “This lets them blend in with rocks, sand, or coral to hide from predators.”
why correct: Hiding from predators is the stated reason for changing color and texture.
tip: The word “why” means you need the reason, not just the action.

stem: Read: “Lina’s hands shook as she stepped onto the stage, but by the time she finished her poem, she was smiling and bowing to loud applause.” Which detail shows Lina’s feelings changed during her performance?
options / answer: A) she was smiling and bowing to loud applause | B) she finished her poem | C) she stepped onto the stage | D) her hands shook as she stepped onto the stage
why correct: Comparing the shaking hands at the start with the smiling at the end shows her feelings changed from nervous to happy.
tip: Compare the beginning and the end of the sentence to find a change.

stem: Read: “Most adult humans have 32 teeth, including four wisdom teeth that often appear in the late teenage years.” True or false: the text states that all 32 teeth appear by the age of five.
options / answer: True | False
why correct: The text says wisdom teeth often appear in the late teenage years, not by age five.
tip: Watch for specific ages or numbers that do not match the text.

stem: Read: “A rainbow forms when sunlight passes through raindrops and separates into different colors.” Which detail tells you WHAT two things are needed to form a rainbow?
options / answer: A) different colors | B) sunlight passes through raindrops | C) A rainbow forms | D) separates into different colors
why correct: The text names sunlight and raindrops as what must come together to form a rainbow.
tip: Find the exact words that answer the question being asked.

stem: Read: “Jamal practiced his multiplication tables every night, even when his friends asked him to play. On test day, he finished early and checked his answers twice.” Which detail shows that Jamal resisted a distraction to keep studying?
options / answer: A) On test day | B) he practiced his multiplication tables every night | C) even when his friends asked him to play | D) he finished early and checked his answers twice
why correct: Despite being asked to play, Jamal kept studying — showing he resisted the distraction.
tip: Look for the exact moment the text shows a choice.

stem: Read: “Volcanoes can be helpful as well as dangerous. The ash from eruptions makes soil rich for farming, but fast-moving lava and toxic gases can destroy everything in their path.” Which TWO details show that volcanoes can be dangerous?
options / answer: A) “ash from eruptions makes soil rich for farming” | B) “fast-moving lava” | C) “toxic gases can destroy everything in their path” | D) “Volcanoes can be helpful as well as dangerous.”
why correct: Lava and toxic gases are named as the dangerous parts of volcanoes.
tip: Separate the helpful details from the dangerous ones before choosing.

stem: Read: “Honey never spoils if it is stored properly, because its low moisture and natural acidity stop bacteria from growing.” Which detail explains WHY honey does not spoil?
options / answer: A) Honey never spoils if it is stored properly. | B) if it is stored properly | C) Honey | D) its low moisture and natural acidity stop bacteria from growing
why correct: Low moisture and acidity stopping bacteria is the scientific reason given.
tip: The word “because” often points straight to the reason.

stem: Read: “Sara’s little brother broke her favorite model airplane. She clenched her fists, took a deep breath, and then helped him find the missing pieces.” Which detail shows that Sara controlled her anger?
options / answer: A) took a deep breath, and then helped him find the missing pieces | B) clenched her fists | C) broke her favorite model airplane | D) her little brother
why correct: Taking a breath and helping, instead of reacting in anger, shows self-control.
tip: Look for what the character does AFTER feeling a strong emotion.

stem: Read: “Reusable water bottles can save a family hundreds of plastic bottles each year, since one bottle can be refilled thousands of times.” True or false: according to the text, a reusable bottle must be thrown away after just a few uses.
options / answer: True | False
why correct: The text says a reusable bottle can be refilled thousands of times, which is the opposite of being thrown away quickly.
tip: Compare the statement word-for-word with what the text actually says.

stem: Read: “Even though Omar’s team lost the match, he shook hands with every player on the other team and congratulated them.” Which word best describes Omar?
options / answer: A) shy | B) sportsmanlike | C) jealous | D) careless
why correct: Congratulating the winning team after losing shows good sportsmanship.
tip: A character’s actions after disappointment reveal a trait.

stem: Read: “Noor noticed a new student standing alone at lunch. She walked over, sat beside him, and asked about his favorite games.” Which word best describes Noor?
options / answer: A) careless | B) nervous | C) welcoming | D) bossy
why correct: Noor notices someone left out and includes him, showing she is welcoming.
tip: Watch how a character treats people who are left out.

stem: Read: “Hassan checked his backpack three times before school to make sure he had every book and pencil he needed.” True or false: this detail shows that Hassan is careless about his schoolwork.
options / answer: True | False
why correct: Checking three times shows Hassan is careful, the opposite of careless.
tip: Match the character’s actions to the trait, not the opposite.

stem: Read: “During the group project, Maya let her teammates choose the topic, then quietly did most of the research herself without complaining.” Which word best describes Maya?
options / answer: A) selfish | B) lazy | C) rude | D) hardworking
why correct: Doing the hard work quietly and without complaint shows Maya is hardworking.
tip: Look at what a character actually does, not just what they say.

stem: Read: “When the power went out during the storm, Yusuf calmly lit a candle, found the flashlight, and told his little sister it would be okay.” Which word best describes Yusuf?
options / answer: A) calm | B) confused | C) angry | D) panicked
why correct: Yusuf’s steady, helpful actions during a stressful moment show he stays calm.
tip: A character’s behavior in a difficult moment often reveals a trait.

stem: Read: “Everyone else cheered when the school trip was canceled because of rain, but Huda sighed and looked down at her new hiking boots.” What is Huda’s perspective on the cancellation?
options / answer: A) She is angry at her classmates. | B) She is disappointed because she was looking forward to the trip. | C) She is relieved like everyone else. | D) She did not care about the trip.
why correct: Sighing and looking at the boots she wanted to wear shows she is upset about missing the trip.
tip: Notice when a character’s reaction is different from everyone else’s — it shows their own perspective.

stem: Read: “Mona thought the broken vase was ruined, but her brother Khalid saw the pieces and said, ‘We can glue this back together — it will look even more interesting.’” How is Khalid’s point of view different from Mona’s?
options / answer: A) Mona wants to fix it, and Khalid wants to throw it away. | B) Both are excited about the broken vase. | C) Mona sees the vase as ruined, while Khalid sees a chance to fix and improve it. | D) Both think the vase cannot be fixed.
why correct: Mona focuses on the damage, while Khalid focuses on the possibility of repair.
tip: Compare what each character says about the same event.

stem: Read: “The coach said the team played well despite losing, but Tariq kicked the ground and refused to look at the scoreboard.” True or false: Tariq shares the coach’s positive view of the game.
options / answer: True | False
why correct: Tariq’s actions show frustration and disappointment, not agreement with the coach’s positive view.
tip: A character’s actions can show a different perspective from what another character says.

stem: Read: “Sami’s grandmother smiled at the old photograph and said, ‘Those were simple, happy days.’ Sami looked at the black-and-white photo and thought it looked dull and plain.” How do Sami and his grandmother see the old photograph differently?
options / answer: A) They both see the same happy memories. | B) Sami remembers the days in the photo better than his grandmother. | C) They both see the photo as boring. | D) His grandmother sees happy memories, while Sami sees only a dull, old picture.
why correct: The grandmother’s words show she values the memory, while Sami’s thought shows he only judges the photo’s look.
tip: A character’s own experience shapes how they see the same thing.

stem: A story is told from Layla’s point of view only. How would readers’ understanding change if her little brother told the same story?
options / answer: A) Readers would learn the brother’s own thoughts and feelings instead of Layla’s. | B) The events in the story would be different. | C) The setting of the story would change. | D) Layla would disappear from the story.
why correct: The narrator decides whose inner thoughts and feelings the reader gets to know.
tip: Point of view controls whose feelings the reader can directly hear.

stem: Read: “Fatima watered the small seed every single day and made sure it got plenty of sunlight by the window.” What will most likely happen to the seed?
options / answer: A) It will dry out and die. | B) It will probably grow into a healthy plant. | C) It will be eaten by a bird. | D) Nothing will happen to it.
why correct: Regular water and sunlight are what a seed needs to grow, so it will most likely grow into a plant.
tip: Think about what usually happens when you combine the clues in the text.

stem: Read: “Khalid forgot his umbrella, and dark clouds were gathering quickly in the sky.” Based on this, it makes sense to predict that Khalid will probably get wet on his way home.
options / answer: True | False
why correct: Dark clouds usually mean rain is coming, and Khalid has no umbrella, so he will likely get wet.
tip: Good predictions connect text clues to what usually happens in real life.

stem: Read: “Noor had forgotten to study for her spelling test, but during recess she quickly asked her friend to quiz her on all the words.” What is the BEST prediction about Noor’s test?
options / answer: A) She will fail the test no matter what. | B) Her friend will take the test for her. | C) She may do better than if she had not reviewed the words at all. | D) She will refuse to take the test.
why correct: A quick review before a test usually helps, even if it is not as good as studying earlier.
tip: Use the clue about her action right before the test to judge the likely outcome.

stem: Read: “The hikers noticed the trail markers becoming fewer and the sky growing darker, but they kept walking deeper into the unfamiliar forest without checking their map.” Which detail BEST supports the prediction that the hikers might get lost?
options / answer: A) “The hikers noticed the trail markers becoming fewer.” | B) “the sky growing darker.” | C) “trail markers.” | D) “they kept walking deeper into the unfamiliar forest without checking their map.”
why correct: Continuing without checking a map, after noticing fewer markers, strongly suggests they will lose their way.
tip: Choose the detail that connects most directly to the exact prediction.

stem: Read: “Every afternoon, Yusuf fed the stray cat behind his building and slowly it began following him to the bus stop.” What will the cat most likely do next?
options / answer: A) It will probably keep following Yusuf and may even trust him more. | B) It will run away and never return. | C) It will stop eating altogether. | D) It will attack Yusuf.
why correct: Since the cat already follows Yusuf after being fed daily, it will likely continue trusting and following him.
tip: A pattern of behavior usually continues unless the text gives a reason for it to change.

stem: Which word is an adverb? “The fox crept silently through the grass.”
options / answer: A) fox | B) silently | C) grass | D) crept
why correct: “Silently” tells how the fox crept.
tip: Adverbs tell how, when, where or how often.

stem: Choose the adverb that tells HOW OFTEN: “Our family ____ eats dinner together.”
options / answer: A) delicious | B) always | C) hungry | D) kitchen
why correct: “Always” tells how often.
tip: Frequency adverbs: always, usually, often, sometimes, never.

stem: Which word does the adverb “almost” describe in “The jar was almost empty”?
options / answer: A) was | B) The | C) empty | D) jar
why correct: “Almost” tells to what extent the jar was empty.
tip: Adverbs can describe adjectives.

stem: Choose the correct form: “Of everyone in the choir, Reem sings ____.”
options / answer: A) clearliest | B) clearest | C) most clearly | D) more clearly
why correct: Comparing many people uses “most” + adverb.
tip: Two → more; three or more → most.

stem: Tap the part of the sentence that has an error.
options / answer: The team played |  real well |  in the |  final match.
why correct: “Really” is the adverb that describes “well”; “real” is an adjective.
tip: Use an adverb to describe another adverb.

stem: Which group of words is a dependent clause?
options / answer: A) We played outside. | B) the heavy rain | C) The rain stopped. | D) until the rain stops
why correct: It has a subject and verb but begins with “until,” so it cannot stand alone.
tip: Subordinating conjunctions make clauses dependent.

stem: What is the independent clause? “Although the test was long, Salma finished early.”
options / answer: A) Salma finished early | B) the test was long | C) Although the test was long | D) finished early
why correct: “Salma finished early” can stand alone.
tip: Remove the clause that starts with although/because/when.

stem: Choose the subordinating conjunction: “Please wait here ____ I get the tickets.”
options / answer: A) and | B) but | C) so | D) while
why correct: “While” makes a dependent clause about time.
tip: Subordinating: while, because, although, unless, until.

stem: Which revision turns two choppy sentences into ONE complex sentence with the clearest meaning? “The museum was closed. We visited the park.”
options / answer: A) The museum was closed and we visited the park. | B) Because the museum was closed, we visited the park. | C) Although we visited the park, the museum was closed. | D) The museum was closed, we visited the park.
why correct: “Because” shows that the closed museum caused the change of plan.
tip: Choose the conjunction that matches the relationship.

stem: Combine: “Hala likes chess. Hala likes painting.”
options / answer: A) Hala likes chess, likes painting. | B) Hala likes chess Hala likes painting. | C) Hala likes chess and painting. | D) Chess and painting likes Hala.
why correct: Join the two objects with “and” and remove repeated words.
tip: Combine words that repeat.

stem: Combine using an appositive: “Dr. Noor is a dentist. Dr. Noor lives next door.”
options / answer: A) Dr. Noor lives next door a dentist. | B) Dr. Noor a dentist lives next door. | C) A dentist lives next door Dr. Noor. | D) Dr. Noor, a dentist, lives next door.
why correct: The appositive “a dentist” renames Dr. Noor and is set off by commas.
tip: Place the appositive right after the noun.

stem: Which is the BEST combined sentence? “The cat jumped. The cat landed on the table. The table was wooden.”
options / answer: A) The cat jumped onto the wooden table. | B) The cat jumped and the cat landed and the table was wooden. | C) Jumping, landing, wooden, the cat. | D) The cat jumped, it landed, the table was wooden.
why correct: One clear sentence keeps all the information without repeating.
tip: Cut repeated words and combine actions.

stem: Combine with a participial phrase: “Ali opened the box. He found a letter.”
options / answer: A) Opening the box, a letter was found by Ali. | B) Opening the box, Ali found a letter. | C) Ali opened the box, found a letter. | D) Ali opening the box found a letter.
why correct: The -ing phrase describes Ali, the subject that follows it.
tip: An introductory phrase must describe the subject right after the comma.

stem: Tap the part of the sentence that has an error.
options / answer: Walking to school, |  the rain soaked |  my backpack |  and my shoes.
correct: segment 2 →  I got soaked by the rain, including
why correct: The phrase “Walking to school” must describe the person walking, not the rain (dangling modifier).
tip: Check who is doing the action in an introductory phrase.

stem: Choose: “A cheetah is ____ than a horse.”
options / answer: A) faster | B) more fast | C) fastest | D) fast
why correct: Two animals → -er: faster.
tip: Two things: -er; many: -est.

stem: Choose: “Mount Everest is the ____ mountain in the world.”
options / answer: A) most high | B) highest | C) higher | D) high
why correct: Comparing with all mountains → highest.
tip: “In the world” signals a superlative.

stem: Which sentence uses “less” or “fewer” correctly?
options / answer: A) This bag has lesser apples. | B) This bag has fewer sugar than that one. | C) This bag has fewer apples than that one. | D) This bag has less apples than that one.
why correct: Apples can be counted, so “fewer.”
tip: fewer = countable; less = not countable.

stem: Tap the part of the sentence that has an error.
options / answer: My new bike |  is |  more lighter |  than my old one.
why correct: Use -er OR more, never both.
tip: Do not double comparatives.

stem: Which sentence is correct?
options / answer: A) Of the two essays, Hadi’s is the strongest. | B) Of the two essays, Hadi’s is the more stronger. | C) Of the two essays, Hadi’s is the most strong. | D) Of the two essays, Hadi’s is the stronger.
why correct: When comparing exactly two, use the comparative form.
tip: Two items → comparative, even with “the.”

stem: Which coordinating conjunction can mean “because”? “We hurried home, ____ a storm was coming.”
options / answer: A) for | B) but | C) so | D) or
why correct: “For” gives a reason, like “because.”
tip: FANBOYS: for = reason; so = result.

stem: Which compound sentence is punctuated correctly?
options / answer: A) The phone rang so, Majed answered it. | B) The phone rang, so Majed answered it. | C) The phone rang, Majed answered it. | D) The phone, rang so Majed answered it.
why correct: Comma + coordinating conjunction joins two independent clauses.
tip: Comma before FANBOYS.

stem: Which sentence correctly uses “not only … but also”?
options / answer: A) Hessa not only won the race also broke the record. | B) Hessa not only won the race but broke also the record. | C) Hessa not only won the race but also broke the record. | D) Not only Hessa won the race but also broke the record.
why correct: “Not only won … but also broke” joins two parallel verb phrases.
tip: Correlative pairs join matching parts.

skill: Nouns: Common, Proper, Concrete, Abstract, Collective
stem: Which TWO words are common nouns? “The scientist studied the volcano near Naples.”
options / answer: A) scientist | B) volcano | C) Naples | D) studied
why correct: Common nouns name general people, places or things.
tip: Proper nouns are capitalized; common nouns are not.

skill: Nouns: Common, Proper, Concrete, Abstract, Collective
stem: Which word is a concrete noun?
options / answer: A) honesty | B) curiosity | C) freedom | D) telescope
why correct: You can see and touch a telescope.
tip: Concrete nouns can be sensed.

skill: Nouns: Common, Proper, Concrete, Abstract, Collective
stem: In “My parents walked the dog around the park,” how is “dog” used?
options / answer: A) as a direct object | B) as the subject | C) as a verb | D) as the object of a preposition
why correct: The dog receives the action of “walked.”
tip: A direct object answers “what?” or “whom?” after the verb.

skill: Nouns: Common, Proper, Concrete, Abstract, Collective
stem: Which word is the object of a preposition? “The kite drifted over the hills.”
options / answer: A) drifted | B) hills | C) kite | D) over
why correct: “Hills” comes after the preposition “over.”
tip: Preposition + noun = object of the preposition.

skill: Nouns: Common, Proper, Concrete, Abstract, Collective
stem: Which sentence uses a collective noun with a singular verb correctly?
options / answer: A) The committee meet every Monday. | B) The committees meets every Monday. | C) The committee meets every Monday. | D) The committee are meeting every Monday.
why correct: A committee acting together is one unit, so the verb is singular.
tip: Collective nouns usually take singular verbs.

stem: Which word is a preposition? “The cat hid behind the sofa.”
options / answer: A) hid | B) cat | C) sofa | D) behind
why correct: “Behind” shows where the cat hid.
tip: Prepositions show position, direction or time.

stem: Choose the preposition of time: “The shop closes ____ midnight.”
options / answer: A) on | B) in | C) at | D) over
why correct: Use “at” with clock times.
tip: at + time; on + day; in + month/year.

stem: What is the prepositional phrase? “Students from every grade joined the parade.”
options / answer: A) from every grade | B) every grade joined | C) Students from | D) joined the parade
why correct: The phrase begins with “from” and ends with the noun “grade.”
tip: Preposition → … → noun.

stem: Which TWO prepositional phrases tell WHERE? “During the trip, we camped beside a lake under the stars.”
options / answer: A) under the stars | B) we camped | C) beside a lake | D) During the trip
why correct: “Beside” and “under” show location.
tip: Ask what each phrase answers: when or where?

stem: Tap the part of the sentence that has an error.
options / answer: The letter |  was addressed |  to my brother and I |  by mistake.
correct: segment 3 →  to my brother and me
why correct: After the preposition “to,” use the object pronoun “me.”
tip: Objects of prepositions use me, him, her, us, them.

stem: Choose: “The dog wagged ____ tail.”
options / answer: A) its’ | B) it is | C) it’s | D) its
why correct: “Its” shows the tail belongs to the dog.
tip: its = belonging to it.

stem: Choose: “Please put your shoes over ____.”
options / answer: A) there | B) they’re | C) their | D) thier
why correct: “There” names a place.
tip: there contains “here”: it is about place.

stem: Choose: “____ been to the new science museum?”
options / answer: A) Who | B) Who’s | C) Whos | D) Whose
why correct: Who’s = who has.
tip: who’s = who is / who has.

stem: Match each word with its meaning.
options / answer: its = belonging to it | it’s = it is | their = belonging to them | they’re = they are
why correct: Contractions have apostrophes; possessive pronouns do not.
tip: Expand each word to test it.

stem: Which sentence is correct?
options / answer: A) You’re welcome to borrow you’re cousin’s bike. | B) You’re welcome to borrow your cousin’s bike. | C) Your welcome to borrow your cousin’s bike. | D) Your welcome to borrow you’re cousin’s bike.
why correct: You’re = you are; your = belonging to you.
tip: Check each one by expanding it.

stem: Which word is a pronoun? “They planted three trees.”
options / answer: A) trees | B) planted | C) They | D) three
why correct: “They” replaces the names of people.
tip: Pronouns replace nouns.

stem: Choose the possessive pronoun: “The blue umbrella is ____.”
options / answer: A) she | B) herself | C) hers | D) her’s
why correct: “Hers” shows ownership.
tip: mine, yours, his, hers, ours, theirs.

stem: Choose the reflexive pronoun: “I taught ____ to juggle.”
options / answer: A) me | B) meself | C) mine | D) myself
why correct: Reflexive pronouns refer back to the subject.
tip: -self / -selves.

stem: Tap the part of the sentence that has an error.
options / answer: Each of the boys |  brought |  their own |  lunch.
why correct: “Each” is singular, so the pronoun should be singular: his.
tip: Pronouns agree in number with their antecedents.

stem: Which sentence has a clear pronoun reference?
options / answer: A) Lina told Sara that she won. | B) They gave them a gift. | C) When Lina met Sara, she gave her a gift. | D) When Lina met Sara, Lina gave her a gift.
why correct: Naming Lina again removes the confusion.
tip: Make sure each pronoun clearly points to one noun.

stem: Choose the past progressive: “At eight o’clock, we ____ dinner.”
options / answer: A) were eating | B) will eat | C) have eaten | D) eat
why correct: Past progressive = was/were + -ing.
tip: Progressive tenses show ongoing action.

stem: Which sentence uses the future perfect tense?
options / answer: A) By June, I will have finished the book. | B) I have finished the book. | C) I am finishing the book. | D) I finished the book in June.
why correct: will have + past participle = future perfect.
tip: Perfect tenses use has/have/had/will have.

skill: Action, Main, Helping and Linking Verbs
stem: Choose the LINKING verb: “After the long race, Omar ____ exhausted.”
options / answer: A) jumped | B) felt | C) ran | D) quickly
why correct: “Felt” links Omar to the word that describes him, “exhausted.”
tip: Linking verbs: is, seem, feel, become, look, appear.

skill: Action, Main, Helping and Linking Verbs
stem: Choose the helping verb: “The guests ____ arriving soon.”
options / answer: A) was | B) is | C) will be | D) has
why correct: “Will be arriving” is a verb phrase showing the future.
tip: Helping verb + main verb = verb phrase.

skill: Action, Main, Helping and Linking Verbs
stem: Which sentence has a transitive verb (an action done TO something)?
options / answer: A) Huda arrived early. | B) Huda painted a mural. | C) Huda laughed. | D) Huda seemed tired.
why correct: “Painted” acts on the object “a mural.”
tip: Transitive verbs have a direct object.

skill: Action, Main, Helping and Linking Verbs
stem: Choose the modal that shows ability: “I ____ swim across the pool now.”
options / answer: A) should | B) must | C) may | D) can
why correct: “Can” shows ability.
tip: can = able; must = required; should = advised.

skill: Action, Main, Helping and Linking Verbs
stem: Which TWO sentences use a verb phrase with a helping verb?
options / answer: A) We are reading a mystery. | B) We read a mystery. | C) The team has practiced every day. | D) The team practiced yesterday.
why correct: has practiced and are reading each contain a helping verb.
tip: Look for has/have/is/are/will before the main verb.

stem: Tap the part of the sentence that has an error.
options / answer: Yes |  Mr. Salem, |  the report |  is ready.
why correct: A comma follows the introductory word “Yes.” (The comma after the name is already correct.)
tip: Introductory words and direct address both need commas.

stem: Which is the abbreviation for “Street”?
options / answer: A) st | B) Str | C) St. | D) ST
why correct: Street → St.
tip: Address abbreviations: St., Ave., Rd.

stem: How should a song title be written?
options / answer: A) underlined | B) in all capital letters | C) with no marks | D) in quotation marks
why correct: Short works (songs, poems, articles) use quotation marks.
tip: Short works → quotation marks.

stem: Which sentence writes a magazine title and an article title correctly?
options / answer: A) I read “Saving the Reefs” in Ocean World. | B) I read Saving the Reefs in “Ocean World.” | C) I read Saving The Reefs in ocean world. | D) I read “saving the reefs” in Ocean World.
why correct: Article titles take quotation marks; magazine titles are italicized.
tip: Part → quotes; whole → italics.

stem: Which date uses abbreviations correctly?
options / answer: A) MON., SEPT. 7 | B) Mon., Sept. 7 | C) mon., sept. 7 | D) Mon Sept 7
why correct: Abbreviated days and months keep a capital letter and take a period.
tip: Mon., Tues., Jan., Feb.

stem: Which sentence is correct?
options / answer: A) Dr Hamid’s book, “The Desert Garden,” won an award. | B) Dr. Hamid’s book, the Desert Garden, won an award. | C) Dr. Hamid’s book, The Desert Garden, won an award. | D) dr. Hamid’s book, The desert garden, won an award.
why correct: Title abbreviation with a period; book title italicized with capitals.
tip: Check abbreviation, marks and capitals.

stem: What is the main purpose of “Why the Moon Changes Shape”?
options / answer: A) to tell a story about astronauts | B) to describe how calendars are printed | C) to persuade readers to visit space | D) to explain why the Moon looks different during the month
why correct: The article explains moon phases.
tip: Ask: inform, persuade or entertain?

stem: Why does the author of “Catching Water in the Desert” begin by describing rare rain?
options / answer: A) to show the problem that the solutions address | B) to describe a holiday | C) to explain how clouds form | D) to complain about the weather
why correct: The opening sets up the problem of saving water.
tip: Openings often introduce the problem or topic.

stem: How is the purpose of the news report different from Rania’s journal in “The Storm: Two Accounts”?
options / answer: A) The journal gives exact rainfall. | B) The report informs with facts; the journal shares personal feelings. | C) Both mainly share feelings. | D) The report is fiction.
why correct: The report lists wind speeds and outages; the journal says “I was scared.”
tip: Compare purpose through the details each writer chooses.

passage: Sea Turtles of the Red Sea
stem: Why does the turtle article include a glossary?
options / answer: A) to list every turtle species | B) to tell a story | C) to help readers understand a key word | D) to persuade readers to protect turtles
why correct: The glossary defines “hatchling.”
tip: Text features support the author’s purpose.

stem: The author of “Catching Water in the Desert” ends with engineers combining ancient ideas and modern materials. What point of view does this ending suggest?
options / answer: A) Modern materials make ancient ideas useless. | B) Engineers should stop using cisterns. | C) Desert farming is impossible. | D) Old solutions are still valuable and can be improved, not replaced.
why correct: The final sentence shows respect for ancient methods and hope for improvement.
tip: Endings often reveal the author’s attitude.

stem: In “Catching Water in the Desert,” what causes rainwater to disappear quickly?
options / answer: A) It rushes over hard, dry ground. | B) Cisterns leak. | C) Check dams block it. | D) People drink it immediately.
why correct: The text says water “rushes over the hard, dry ground and disappears.”
tip: Find what makes something happen.

stem: What is an effect of check dams?
options / answer: A) Rain falls more often. | B) Water soaks into the soil instead of running away. | C) The ground becomes harder. | D) Cisterns become larger.
why correct: The walls slow the water, “giving it time to soak into the soil.”
tip: Signal words like “giving” can show effects.

stem: In “The Storm: Two Accounts,” what was an effect of the 120 millimeters of rain?
options / answer: A) Winds of 90 kilometers per hour | B) Power restored by noon | C) Flooding on six streets | D) Lightning at 3 a.m.
why correct: Heavy rain in six hours flooded streets.
tip: Connect each cause with its direct result.

passage: Sea Turtles of the Red Sea
stem: Match each cause from the turtle article with its effect.
options / answer: Warmer sand in the nest = More hatchlings become females | Bright lights from buildings = Hatchlings crawl the wrong way | Eggs stay warm for about two months = Hatchlings dig their way out
why correct: Each effect in the article follows from a condition on the beach.
tip: Use “because” to test each pair.

stem: What is the central idea of “Why the Moon Changes Shape”?
options / answer: A) Calendars were invented by farmers. | B) Full moons happen every week. | C) The Moon makes its own light. | D) The Moon’s shape seems to change because we see different amounts of its lit half.
why correct: Every paragraph explains our changing view of the lit half.
tip: The central idea connects all paragraphs.

passage: Sea Turtles of the Red Sea
stem: Which detail BEST supports the central idea of the turtle article?
options / answer: A) Females lay about one hundred eggs on sandy beaches. | B) Hatchling is defined in the glossary. | C) The Red Sea is warm. | D) A caption describes a photo.
why correct: The article is about how Red Sea turtles nest and the dangers hatchlings face.
tip: Supporting details develop the main idea.

stem: Which sentence best states the central idea of “The Last Repair”?
options / answer: A) Captains need pocket watches. | B) Under pressure, Khalid succeeds by remembering to slow down. | C) Jeddah smells of sea salt and cardamom. | D) Uncle Faris has a fever.
why correct: The story turns on Khalid calming himself and finding the spring.
tip: Ask what the whole story is mostly about.

stem: Which word BEST describes Dana in “The Second Try”?
options / answer: A) jealous | B) bored | C) supportive | D) rude
why correct: She whispers encouragement and gives advice.
tip: Use dialogue to describe a character.

stem: How does Salma solve the problem in “The Two Wells”?
options / answer: A) She buys water from Hamdan. | B) She leaves the village. | C) She asks the king for help. | D) She observes carefully and leads the children to dig a new well.
why correct: She notices the green grove and digs there.
tip: Characters’ actions show their traits.

passage: The Volcano That Would Not Erupt
stem: What does Yusuf’s question about the baking soda show about him?
options / answer: A) He thinks logically when something goes wrong. | B) He forgot the vinegar. | C) He wants to blame Layla. | D) He has given up.
why correct: Instead of panicking, he checks the steps.
tip: Problem-solving shows character.

stem: How does Khalid change between the moment the spring disappears and the end of “The Last Repair”?
options / answer: A) He gives up and asks the captain for help. | B) He moves from panic to calm, careful action. | C) He stays panicked until the end. | D) He moves from calm to anger.
why correct: He knocks screws over in panic, then counts to ten and searches slowly.
tip: Track how a character’s behavior changes.

stem: What topic do both accounts in “The Storm: Two Accounts” describe?
options / answer: A) a school play | B) a car accident | C) the same storm on March 12 | D) two different storms
why correct: Both are dated March 12 and describe the storm.
tip: Find the shared topic first.

stem: Which detail appears in BOTH accounts?
options / answer: A) Rania hid in her sister’s bed. | B) Electricity returned by noon. | C) Winds reached 90 kilometers per hour. | D) There was flooding in the streets.
why correct: Rania says the street was a river; the report says six streets flooded.
tip: Look for facts both writers mention.

passage: Two Articles: A School Garden and Red Sea Turtles
stem: Using BOTH articles in the paired passage, which statement is true?
options / answer: A) One argues for gardens with reasons; the other explains facts about turtles with headings. | B) Both are stories. | C) Both argue for protecting turtles. | D) Both use headings.
why correct: The texts differ in purpose and structure.
tip: Compare purpose and structure across texts.

stem: A student writes a report about the storm’s effect on families. Why is using BOTH accounts better than using one?
options / answer: A) The report describes Rania’s fear. | B) The report gives exact facts, and the journal shows how it felt to live through it. | C) Both say the same thing. | D) The journal has more numbers.
why correct: Combining facts and personal experience gives a fuller picture.
tip: Different sources add different kinds of information.

stem: Why does the narrator of “The Second Try” leave the note cards in the desk?
options / answer: A) Because the teacher took them | B) Because they were wet | C) To speak naturally instead of reading | D) Because the cards were lost
why correct: Dana advised, “Just talk like you’re telling me.”
tip: Link actions to earlier advice.

stem: What can you infer about Hamdan at the start of “The Two Wells”?
options / answer: A) He is generous. | B) He dislikes water. | C) He is poor. | D) He cares more about money than about his neighbors.
why correct: He charges a silver coin even as poor families go thirsty.
tip: Actions reveal values.

stem: In “The Last Repair,” the captain is pleased with Khalid’s work.
options / answer: True | False
why correct: “The captain’s smile told him everything.”
tip: Facial expressions support inferences.

stem: Why did the news report most likely include “No injuries were reported”?
options / answer: A) To reassure readers that no one was hurt | B) To show the storm was weak | C) To describe Rania’s family | D) To blame the city
why correct: Reports often include safety information readers want.
tip: Think about what readers need to know.

stem: In “City Morning,” why does the speaker say “That minute, friend, is mine”?
options / answer: A) The speaker is late for work. | B) The speaker treasures a quiet moment before the busy day. | C) The speaker owns the city. | D) The speaker dislikes friends.
why correct: The last stanza contrasts the quiet golden sky with the loud day.
tip: Read the final lines in context.

skill: Poetry: Structure, Rhyme, Meter and Form
stem: How many stanzas are in “Harbor at Dawn”?
options / answer: A) one | B) eight | C) two | D) three
why correct: There are two groups of four lines.
tip: Stanzas are separated by blank lines.

skill: Poetry: Structure, Rhyme, Meter and Form
stem: Which pair of words rhymes in “Harbor at Dawn”?
options / answer: A) boats / wet | B) ropes / breeze | C) gulls / thread | D) light / night
why correct: “Light” and “night” end lines 1 and 2 and rhyme.
tip: Check line endings.

skill: Poetry: Structure, Rhyme, Meter and Form
stem: What is the rhyme pattern of “Harbor at Dawn”?
options / answer: A) rhyming pairs (couplets) | B) only the last line | C) no rhyme at all | D) every other line
why correct: light/night, thread/red, knees/breeze, wet/net.
tip: Couplets: two rhyming lines in a row.

skill: Poetry: Structure, Rhyme, Meter and Form
stem: In “City Morning,” how does the sentence run from stanza 2 into stanza 3?
options / answer: A) Stanza 3 repeats stanza 2. | B) The question continues across the stanza break. | C) The poem has no punctuation. | D) Each stanza is a separate sentence.
why correct: “don’t you miss / The quiet way…” carries the thought into stanza 3 (enjambment).
tip: Lines and stanzas can continue a sentence.

skill: Poetry: Structure, Rhyme, Meter and Form
stem: How does the structure of “Harbor at Dawn” support its meaning?
options / answer: A) The stanzas are numbered steps in a process. | B) Each stanza tells a different character’s story. | C) Two short rhyming stanzas move from the sky to the boats, like a scene slowly waking. | D) It has no stanzas.
why correct: Stanza 1 shows sky and town; stanza 2 the harbor sounds and boats waking.
tip: Ask how form and meaning work together.

stem: From what point of view is “The Two Wells” told?
options / answer: A) Salma’s first person | B) second person | C) first person | D) third person
why correct: The narrator uses she, he and they.
tip: Pronouns reveal point of view.

stem: How does Rania’s first-person journal affect what readers learn?
options / answer: A) Readers learn her personal feelings, like fear and amazement. | B) Readers learn the officials’ plans. | C) Readers learn exact wind speeds. | D) Readers learn every family’s story.
why correct: First person shares the narrator’s inner thoughts.
tip: Narrator choice shapes information.

passage: The Volcano That Would Not Erupt
stem: If “The Volcano That Would Not Erupt” were told by Ms. Dawood, what might change?
options / answer: A) The science fair would be canceled. | B) We would see the scene from the teacher’s view, perhaps without knowing about the missing baking soda. | C) Layla would disappear. | D) The volcano would be made of metal.
why correct: A different narrator knows and notices different things.
tip: Imagine the story through another character.

stem: What is the solution in “The Two Wells”?
options / answer: A) Hamdan builds a wall. | B) The village moves. | C) The children dig a new well. | D) Families go thirsty.
why correct: The new well gives free water.
tip: Solution = what fixes the problem.

passage: Sea Turtles of the Red Sea
stem: In the turtle article, the author gives a full solution for the problem of bright lights.
options / answer: True | False
why correct: The section explains the danger but does not describe a solution.
tip: Not every problem in a text is solved.

stem: How do cisterns and check dams solve the SAME problem in different ways?
options / answer: A) Both pump water from wells. | B) Cisterns are for animals only. | C) Both make it rain more. | D) Cisterns store water in tanks; check dams help water soak into the ground.
why correct: Both save scarce rainwater, using storage or soil.
tip: Compare how two solutions work.

stem: Why does the author of the garden letter offer starting small with containers?
options / answer: A) To solve the problem that gardens may cost too much | B) To show gardens are useless | C) To make gardens larger | D) To save time on reading
why correct: This answers the cost objection with a practical solution.
tip: Persuasive texts can include solutions to objections.

stem: In “The Last Repair,” what happens right after the spring disappears?
options / answer: A) He closes the case. | B) Khalid knocks a box of screws to the floor. | C) He finds the spring. | D) The captain leaves the watch.
why correct: His panic follows immediately.
tip: Track time order.

stem: Put the steps of collecting rainwater in a cistern in order.
options / answer: Rain falls on the rooftop. → Gutters guide the water into pipes. → Pipes lead the water to the cistern. → The covered tank keeps the water cool.
why correct: The article describes the path from roof to tank.
tip: Follow the path of the water.

stem: Put the events in the news report in time order.
options / answer: The storm strikes early Thursday morning. → Streets flood and power goes out. → City crews begin clearing drains at 7 a.m. → Electricity is restored by noon.
why correct: The report moves from the storm to the recovery.
tip: Use times as clues.

stem: After a full moon, what happens next in the cycle described in the article?
options / answer: A) The Moon stops reflecting light. | B) A full moon happens again the next night. | C) The pattern reverses until the next new moon. | D) The Moon becomes a crescent immediately.
why correct: The article says, “Then the pattern reverses until the next new moon.”
tip: Cycles return to their starting point.

stem: Which line from “City Morning” uses onomatopoeia?
options / answer: A) “The city yawns and stretches wide,” | B) “Above the rooftop line?” | C) “That minute, friend, is mine.” | D) “The coffee kettles hiss;”
why correct: “Hiss” imitates a sound.
tip: Onomatopoeia = sound words.

stem: Which words in “Harbor at Dawn” show alliteration?
options / answer: A) “salt and diesel… stitch the sky with silver” | B) “fishing boats, still beaded wet” | C) “the last stars folding up the night” | D) “the bread oven breathes”
why correct: Many words repeat the s sound: stitch, sky, silver, salt.
tip: Listen for repeated beginning sounds.

stem: Which sound device appears in “Ropes creak”?
options / answer: A) repetition | B) onomatopoeia | C) alliteration | D) rhyme
why correct: “Creak” imitates the sound of ropes.
tip: Sound words imitate real sounds.

stem: Match each example from “City Morning” with its sound device.
options / answer: hiss = Onomatopoeia | busy, bustling, buzzing = Alliteration | wide / side = Rhyme
why correct: Each example uses sound in a different way.
tip: Say each aloud.

stem: Why does the poet use the alliteration “busy, bustling, buzzing throng”?
options / answer: A) To make the poem rhyme | B) To describe silence | C) The repeated b sounds create a noisy, rushing feeling like a crowd. | D) To slow the poem down
why correct: The fast repeated b sounds echo the energy of the crowd.
tip: Sound devices support meaning.

stem: Which sentence shows that the narrator of “The Second Try” was nervous at first?
options / answer: A) “Dana leaned over.” | B) “Heads lifted.” | C) “I was smiling.” | D) “My hands shook.”
why correct: Shaking hands show nervousness.
tip: Choose evidence that directly shows the idea.

stem: Which sentence supports the idea that cisterns are an old invention?
options / answer: A) “Archaeologists have found cisterns that are more than two thousand years old.” | B) “Farmers build low walls of earth.” | C) “Rain falls only a few times each year.” | D) “Gutters on rooftops guide rainwater.”
why correct: Two-thousand-year-old cisterns prove they are ancient.
tip: Match evidence to the claim.

stem: Which evidence shows that the villagers valued sharing?
options / answer: A) “every bucket costs a silver coin.” | B) “they shared it freely, as they always had.” | C) “Hamdan’s gate stayed locked.” | D) “Their hands blistered.”
why correct: The villagers choose to share the new well freely.
tip: Quote words that prove the point.

stem: Which TWO quotations support the idea that the storm was serious?
options / answer: A) “No injuries were reported.” | B) “winds of up to 90 kilometers per hour” | C) “power outages affecting about 4,000 homes” | D) “electricity was restored to most homes by noon.”
why correct: High winds and many outages show a serious storm.
tip: Choose evidence that fits the claim.

passage: The Volcano That Would Not Erupt
stem: A student claims, “Layla learned from her mistake.” Which quotation is the STRONGEST evidence?
options / answer: A) “The judges come at ten o’clock.” | B) “Everything is ruined!” | C) “You check every step, and you never panic.” | D) “The baking soda… is still in my backpack.”
why correct: Her final line states what she learned.
tip: The best evidence directly proves the claim.

stem: What is a theme of “The Two Wells”?
options / answer: A) Deserts are hot. | B) Children should not dig. | C) Merchants are always kind. | D) Sharing is worth more than profit.
why correct: Hamdan admits shared water is worth more than sold water.
tip: Theme = message about life.

stem: Which detail BEST supports the theme of “The Last Repair”?
options / answer: A) “A watchmaker’s hands must be slower than the sand.” | B) “Uncle Faris had a fever.” | C) “The ship’s horn sounded.” | D) “The narrow lanes smelled of sea salt.”
why correct: The uncle’s lesson about patience is the message of the story.
tip: Find the line that states the lesson.

passage: The Volcano That Would Not Erupt
stem: What theme does “The Volcano That Would Not Erupt” express?
options / answer: A) Partners always cause problems. | B) Staying calm and checking your work helps you solve problems. | C) Science fairs are unfair. | D) Volcanoes are dangerous.
why correct: Layla’s last line states the lesson: check every step and never panic.
tip: A theme is a message about life.

stem: How does the turtle memory in “The Second Try” help develop the theme?
options / answer: A) It explains how to give a speech. | B) It shows turtles are dangerous. | C) The turtles keep going after being knocked back, just as the narrator does. | D) It distracts from the story.
why correct: “Being knocked back… isn’t the same as being beaten.”
tip: Symbols and memories can carry themes.

stem: Read: “The puppy was so lethargic after the long walk that it slept all afternoon.” What does lethargic mean?
options / answer: A) very excited | B) very loud | C) very hungry | D) very tired and slow
why correct: The clue “slept all afternoon” shows tiredness.
tip: Use the effect described in the sentence.

stem: Read: “Unlike his loquacious cousin, who chatted for hours, Tamer rarely spoke more than a few words.” What does loquacious mean?
options / answer: A) very talkative | B) very quiet | C) very rude | D) very tall
why correct: The contrast word “Unlike” and “chatted for hours” show the meaning.
tip: Contrast clues show the opposite of a nearby word.

stem: “The baker sings a sugared song.” What kind of figurative language describes the song as “sugared”?
options / answer: A) a simile using “like” | B) a metaphor suggesting the song is sweet | C) a literal description | D) onomatopoeia
why correct: The song is described as if it were sweet like sugar.
tip: Metaphors compare without like or as.

stem: In “Harbor at Dawn,” what does “The harbor yawns” suggest?
options / answer: A) The harbor is bored. | B) The harbor is wide open and empty forever. | C) The harbor is just waking up, like a sleepy person. | D) The harbor makes a loud noise.
why correct: Personification gives the harbor a human action at dawn.
tip: Personification gives human traits to things.

stem: The Latin root “aqua” means water. Which word names a tank for fish?
options / answer: A) terrarium | B) auditorium | C) planetarium | D) aquarium
why correct: aqua (water) + -arium (place) = aquarium.
tip: Roots carry the core meaning.

stem: The Greek root “chron” means time. What is a chronological list?
options / answer: A) a list in time order | B) a list of colors | C) a list in alphabetical order | D) a list in size order
why correct: chron (time) → in the order things happened.
tip: Think of chronicle, chronometer.

stem: Using roots, what does “benevolent” most likely mean?
options / answer: A) wishing harm on others | B) wishing to do good for others | C) able to fly | D) very strong
why correct: bene (good) + vol (wish) = wishing good.
tip: Combine root meanings to define new words.

stem: Choose the correct word: “The hikers walked for an ____.”
options / answer: A) hour | B) ower | C) are | D) our
why correct: “Hour” means sixty minutes.
tip: Homophones sound alike but differ in meaning.

stem: In which sentence does “lead” rhyme with “bed”?
options / answer: A) Please lead the line to lunch. | B) Who will lead the team? | C) The pencil’s lead broke during the test. | D) The guide will lead us up the trail.
why correct: Lead (the metal or pencil core) rhymes with bed.
tip: Homographs can have different pronunciations.

stem: “The farm was used to produce produce.” How do the two words differ?
options / answer: A) They are spelled differently. | B) Both are nouns. | C) They mean the same thing. | D) The first is a verb (make); the second is a noun (fruits and vegetables), with different stress.
why correct: pro-DUCE (verb) vs. PRO-duce (noun).
tip: Stress can change with part of speech.

stem: Tap the part of the sentence that has an error.
options / answer: The principle |  announced that |  the school |  would close early.
why correct: A principal is the head of a school; a principle is a rule or belief.
tip: Principal = a pal who leads the school.

stem: What does “under the weather” mean?
options / answer: A) feeling sick | B) checking the forecast | C) very happy | D) standing in the rain
why correct: “Under the weather” means feeling unwell.
tip: Idioms are not literal.

stem: Maryam “spilled the beans” about the surprise party. What did she do?
options / answer: A) She hid the gifts. | B) She told the secret. | C) She cooked dinner. | D) She dropped food.
why correct: To spill the beans is to reveal a secret.
tip: Use context to understand idioms.

stem: Match each proverb with its meaning.
options / answer: Look before you leap = think carefully before acting | Many hands make light work = working together makes jobs easier | Don’t judge a book by its cover = don’t judge by appearances | Better late than never = doing something late is better than not doing it
why correct: Proverbs share advice about life.
tip: Think of a situation where each applies.

stem: Choose the word that means “not possible”: “Climbing that cliff without ropes is ____.”
options / answer: A) repossible | B) impossible | C) possibly | D) unpossible
why correct: im- means not: impossible = not possible.
tip: Before p, b or m, “not” is often spelled im-.

stem: Choose the word that means “to spell wrongly”: “Be careful not to ____ the new words.”
options / answer: A) unspell | B) prespell | C) misspell | D) respell
why correct: mis- means wrongly.
tip: mis- = wrongly.

stem: What does “nonfiction” mean?
options / answer: A) writing about the future | B) writing that is made up | C) writing that is not made up | D) poems
why correct: non- means not: not fiction.
tip: non- = not.

stem: Match each prefix with its meaning.
options / answer: pre- = before | dis- = opposite of | over- = too much | non- = not
why correct: Prefixes change the meaning of base words.
tip: Use example words: preview, disagree, overflow, nonstop.

stem: Which word means “to judge someone before knowing them”?
options / answer: A) misjudge | B) rejudge | C) unjudge | D) prejudge
why correct: pre- (before) + judge = judge beforehand.
tip: Choose the prefix that matches the meaning.

stem: Which word is a synonym for “shout”?
options / answer: A) yell | B) listen | C) sing | D) whisper
why correct: Shout and yell both mean to speak very loudly.
tip: Synonyms = similar meanings.

stem: Which word is an antonym for “visible”?
options / answer: A) clear | B) hidden | C) seen | D) bright
why correct: Visible means able to be seen; hidden means not seen.
tip: Antonyms = opposites.

stem: Which word is the BEST synonym for “furious”?
options / answer: A) calm | B) tired | C) enraged | D) annoyed
why correct: Furious and enraged both mean extremely angry.
tip: Match the strength of the feeling.

stem: Match each word with its SYNONYM.
options / answer: swift = fast | ancient = old | courageous = brave | gigantic = huge
why correct: Each pair has a similar meaning.
tip: Synonyms can replace each other in a sentence.

stem: Which pair shows antonyms with the strongest contrast?
options / answer: A) cold / chilly | B) warm / cool | C) hot / warm | D) scorching / freezing
why correct: Scorching and freezing are extreme opposites.
tip: Antonyms can show degrees of contrast.

stem: Which word is spelled correctly?
options / answer: A) neighbor | B) naybor | C) nieghbor | D) neighbour
why correct: neighbor: n-e-i-g-h-b-o-r.
tip: Weigh and neighbor: ei says long a.

stem: Add -ly to happy: “The children played ____.”
options / answer: (typed)
why correct: Change y to i before adding -ly: happily.
tip: Consonant + y → i before a suffix.

stem: Which sentence has every word spelled correctly?
options / answer: A) Our comittee will definitely receive the separate reports. | B) Our committee will definitely receive the separate reports. | C) Our committee will definitely recieve the seperate reports. | D) Our committee will definately receive the separate reports.
why correct: committee, definitely, receive, separate are tricky words spelled correctly.
tip: Check commonly misspelled words carefully.

stem: Which word is more precise than “walked” in: “The tired hiker ____ up the hill”?
options / answer: A) did | B) moved | C) trudged | D) went
why correct: “Trudged” shows slow, heavy walking.
tip: Choose verbs that show how.

stem: Which sentence uses the most precise language?
options / answer: A) The bird did a thing. | B) The bird moved fast. | C) The bird went down and got something. | D) The hawk swooped down and snatched a lizard from the rock.
why correct: Specific nouns (hawk, lizard) and verbs (swooped, snatched) create a clear picture.
tip: Replace general words with exact ones.

stem: Which domain-specific word fits a science report? “The water turned into vapor through ____.”
options / answer: A) evaporation | B) disappearing | C) going away | D) magic
why correct: Evaporation is the scientific term.
tip: Use subject-specific vocabulary in reports.

stem: Which revision is MOST precise for a report? “A lot of people came to the event.”
options / answer: A) Many people came. | B) About 1,200 visitors attended the science fair. | C) People came to the thing. | D) Tons of people came to the event.
why correct: Exact numbers and specific nouns make writing precise.
tip: Replace “a lot” with a number.

stem: Which sentence uses precise language to create a formal tone?
options / answer: A) They put off the meeting ’cause of the storm thing. | B) The meeting got moved, like, later. | C) The committee postponed the meeting because of the sandstorm warning. | D) Stuff happened, so no meeting.
why correct: Precise verbs (postponed) and nouns (sandstorm warning) suit formal writing.
tip: Formal writing avoids slang.

stem: Which word is a synonym for “anxious”?
options / answer: A) joyful | B) confident | C) tired | D) nervous
why correct: Anxious and nervous both describe feeling worried or uneasy.
tip: Synonyms describe the same feeling or idea in different words.

stem: Which word is an antonym for “humble”?
options / answer: A) arrogant | B) shy | C) quiet | D) modest
why correct: Humble means not boastful; arrogant means overly proud — opposites.
tip: Think of someone who brags constantly — that is the opposite of humble.

stem: Choose the synonym: “The lion crept ____ (quietly) toward its prey.”
options / answer: A) quickly | B) loudly | C) clumsily | D) stealthily
why correct: Stealthily means moving in a quiet, sneaky way, matching “quietly.”
tip: Replace the word in parentheses and see which choice keeps the same meaning.

stem: Match each word with its SYNONYM.
options / answer: vast = enormous | fragile = delicate | eager = enthusiastic | reluctant = unwilling
why correct: Each pair describes almost the same idea.
tip: Try substituting one word for the other in a sentence to test if they match.

stem: A generous classmate shares her lunch without being asked, while a stingy classmate refuses to lend even a pencil. True or false: this contrast means “generous” and “stingy” are synonyms.
options / answer: True | False
why correct: Generous means willing to give; stingy means unwilling to share — these are opposites.
tip: If two words describe opposite behavior with money or gifts, they are antonyms.

stem: Which word is a synonym for “stubborn”?
options / answer: A) agreeable | B) obstinate | C) cheerful | D) curious
why correct: Stubborn and obstinate both describe refusing to change one’s mind.
tip: Some synonyms sound more formal than the original word, like obstinate for stubborn.

stem: Which word is an antonym for “cautious”?
options / answer: A) calm | B) careful | C) reckless | D) curious
why correct: Cautious means careful to avoid danger; reckless means acting without thinking of danger — opposites.
tip: Picture someone driving carefully versus someone driving without any caution.

stem: Choose the antonym: “The desert was scorching at noon but ____ at midnight.”
options / answer: A) frigid | B) warm | C) damp | D) bright
why correct: Scorching means extremely hot; frigid means extremely cold — a strong contrast.
tip: Antonyms can show strong, dramatic opposites, like scorching and frigid.

stem: Which word is a synonym for “exhausted”?
options / answer: A) confused | B) energetic | C) curious | D) drained
why correct: Exhausted and drained both describe having no energy left.
tip: Look for words that both describe the same level of tiredness.

stem: Match each word with its ANTONYM.
options / answer: vast = tiny | cautious = reckless | humble = arrogant | generous = stingy
why correct: Each pair has opposite meanings.
tip: Check that the meanings are true opposites, not just different.

stem: Read: “Compared to her shy younger brother, Dana was remarkably outgoing at the family gathering.” Which word is closest in meaning to “outgoing” as used here?
options / answer: A) sociable | B) quiet | C) tired | D) nervous
why correct: Outgoing and sociable both describe someone who enjoys talking with others.
tip: Use the contrast with “shy” in the sentence as a clue to the opposite meaning.

stem: Which word is an antonym for “transparent” (as in see-through)?
options / answer: A) colorful | B) opaque | C) shiny | D) clear
why correct: Transparent means light passes through; opaque means light cannot pass through — opposites.
tip: Picture glass (transparent) compared to a brick wall (opaque).

stem: A volunteer who is “eager” races to sign up first, but a volunteer who is “reluctant” drags their feet and hopes nobody notices. True or false: these two behaviors show the words are antonyms.
options / answer: True | False
why correct: Eager means wanting to do something very much; reluctant means not wanting to do it — opposite feelings.
tip: Antonyms often describe opposite levels of willingness.

stem: Which word is a synonym for “vast”?
options / answer: A) narrow | B) bright | C) immense | D) short
why correct: Vast and immense both describe something extremely large.
tip: Synonyms for size describe the same scale, whether big or small.

stem: Choose the synonym: “The detective made a ____ (correct) guess about the thief.”
options / answer: A) funny | B) accurate | C) careless | D) quick
why correct: Accurate and correct both describe being right or exact.
tip: Match the meaning given in parentheses, not just a similar-sounding word.

stem: Read: “Coral reefs cover less than 1 percent of the ocean floor, yet they support about 25 percent of all known marine species.” Which detail is evidence that coral reefs are vital to ocean life?
options / answer: A) “marine species.” | B) “Coral reefs cover less than 1 percent of the ocean floor.” | C) “the ocean floor.” | D) “they support about 25 percent of all known marine species.”
why correct: Supporting a quarter of all marine species despite their tiny size shows how vital reefs are.
tip: Compare the small space with the large effect to see the real evidence.

stem: Read: “Microplastics have been found in Arctic sea ice and in rainwater collected far from any city. Scientists are still studying their effects on human health, and some researchers use special microscopes to detect the tiny particles.” Which TWO details show that microplastic pollution has spread very widely?
options / answer: A) “found in Arctic sea ice” | B) “some researchers use special microscopes to detect the tiny particles.” | C) “Scientists are still studying their effects on human health.” | D) “rainwater collected far from any city”
why correct: Finding microplastics in the Arctic and in rainwater far from cities shows pollution has reached remote places.
tip: Choose evidence that matches the exact claim — here, how far pollution has spread.

stem: Read: “Dana’s heart pounded as she walked toward the microphone, but when she saw her best friend give her a thumbs-up from the front row, her shoulders relaxed.” Which detail shows that Dana’s friend helped calm her nerves?
options / answer: A) “when she saw her best friend give her a thumbs-up... her shoulders relaxed.” | B) “she walked toward the microphone.” | C) “Dana’s heart pounded as she walked toward the microphone.” | D) “the front row.”
why correct: Her shoulders relaxing right after seeing the thumbs-up shows the support helped calm her.
tip: Find the detail that happens right after the cause you are checking.

stem: Read: “Ancient cisterns carved from rock could hold over two million liters of rainwater. Archaeologists have found some still partly filled after thousands of years.” Which detail supports the idea that these cisterns were built extremely well?
options / answer: A) “rainwater.” | B) “Archaeologists have found some still partly filled after thousands of years.” | C) “Ancient cisterns carved from rock could hold over two million liters of rainwater.” | D) “thousands of years.”
why correct: Still holding water after thousands of years proves the cisterns were extremely well built.
tip: Evidence of lasting quality usually mentions how something performs over time.

stem: Read: “Khalid double-checked the rope, tested each knot twice, and only then let his younger cousin begin the climb.” True or false: this detail shows that Khalid was careless about his cousin’s safety.
options / answer: True | False
why correct: Double-checking the rope and testing each knot shows Khalid was extremely careful, not careless.
tip: Compare the statement to what the text actually describes.
