stem: Read: “A single beehive can produce more than 25 kilograms of honey in one season, and the bees travel the equivalent of several times around the world to collect enough nectar.” Which detail shows how much effort bees put into making honey?
options / answer: A) “one season.” | B) “A single beehive can produce more than 25 kilograms of honey in one season.” | C) “the bees travel the equivalent of several times around the world to collect enough nectar.” | D) “nectar.”
why correct: Traveling the distance of several trips around the world shows an enormous amount of effort.
tip: Separate the result (honey) from the evidence about the process (travel).

stem: Read: “During the group hike, Omar carried extra water for anyone who ran low, counted the trail markers out loud for fun, and gave up his own seat on the final bus ride.” Which TWO details show that Omar was thoughtful of others during the trip?
options / answer: A) “carried extra water for anyone who ran low” | B) “gave up his own seat on the final bus ride” | C) “During the group hike.” | D) “counted the trail markers out loud for fun.”
why correct: Sharing water and giving up his seat are both actions that put others’ needs first.
tip: Look for actions that directly benefit someone else, not just personal habits.

stem: Read: “Villagers built small stone walls across dry streambeds to slow rushing rainwater, giving it time to soak into the ground instead of running off.” Which detail explains the PURPOSE of the stone walls?
options / answer: A) “Villagers built small stone walls across dry streambeds.” | B) “rushing rainwater.” | C) “dry streambeds.” | D) “giving it time to soak into the ground instead of running off.”
why correct: Letting water soak in instead of running off is the stated purpose of the walls.
tip: A purpose explains WHY something was done, not just what was done.

stem: Read: “Layla read the instructions three times and laid out every tool in order before she finally picked up the screwdriver.” Which detail BEST shows that Layla was being methodical?
options / answer: A) “read the instructions three times and laid out every tool in order” | B) Layla | C) “picked up the screwdriver.” | D) “only then.”
why correct: Reading instructions multiple times and organizing tools before starting shows careful, methodical behavior.
tip: Look for repeated or extra careful actions before the main task begins.

stem: Read: “Urban gardens can lower a neighborhood’s summer temperature by several degrees because plants release moisture that cools the surrounding air.” True or false: the text explains a reason why urban gardens cool their neighborhoods.
options / answer: True | False
why correct: The text gives the reason — plants releasing moisture — which explains how gardens cool the air.
tip: A ‘because’ clause usually signals the reason the text is giving.

stem: Read: “After the new traffic light was installed, the number of accidents at the intersection dropped from twelve per year to only two.” Which detail is the strongest evidence that the traffic light improved safety?
options / answer: A) “twelve per year.” | B) “the number of accidents at the intersection dropped from twelve per year to only two.” | C) “After the new traffic light was installed.” | D) “the intersection.”
why correct: The sharp drop in accidents, compared before and after, is the clearest evidence of improved safety.
tip: Look for numbers that are compared before and after a change.

stem: Read: “Hamdan insisted the new well belonged to everyone, even though he had paid for most of the digging himself.” Which detail shows that Hamdan valued the community over his own gain?
options / answer: A) “the new well.” | B) “himself.” | C) “he insisted the new well belonged to everyone, even though he had paid for most of the digging himself.” | D) “the digging.”
why correct: Sharing something he paid for shows he values the community more than personal profit.
tip: Look for a contrast between what a character could have kept and what they chose to do.

stem: Read: “Solar panels need very little maintenance, but they produce far less electricity on cloudy days, and the panels themselves are expensive to install at first.” Which TWO details describe a DRAWBACK of solar panels?
options / answer: A) “they produce far less electricity on cloudy days” | B) “Solar panels need very little maintenance.” | C) “the panels themselves are expensive to install at first”
why correct: Less electricity on cloudy days and high installation cost are both disadvantages mentioned in the text.
tip: Separate the advantages from the disadvantages before choosing.

stem: Read: “Noor’s drawing won no ribbon at the fair, but she pinned it above her desk anyway and started sketching a new one that same evening.” Which detail shows that Noor did not let disappointment stop her?
options / answer: A) “the fair.” | B) “Noor’s drawing won no ribbon at the fair.” | C) “a new one.” | D) “she pinned it above her desk anyway and started sketching a new one that same evening.”
why correct: Starting a new drawing right away, instead of giving up, shows she kept going despite disappointment.
tip: Look for what a character does immediately AFTER a setback.

stem: Read: “Public libraries lend more than just books; many now lend tools, musical instruments, and even seeds for home gardens.” Which detail supports the idea that libraries offer more than books?
options / answer: A) “many now lend tools, musical instruments, and even seeds for home gardens.” | B) “home gardens.” | C) “books.” | D) “Public libraries lend more than just books.”
why correct: Naming specific items beyond books — tools, instruments, seeds — proves libraries offer more.
tip: The supporting evidence gives specific examples, not just a repeated claim.

stem: Read: “When the team captain was injured, Rania quietly took over organizing practices without ever mentioning it to the coach, letting him think he had planned it himself.” Which word best describes Rania?
options / answer: A) boastful | B) modest | C) careless | D) jealous
why correct: Rania does important work without taking credit, showing she is modest.
tip: Notice whether a character seeks credit for their actions or avoids it.

stem: Read: “Faisal spent his Saturday rebuilding the neighbor’s fence that his dog had knocked down, refusing any payment for his time.” Which word best describes Faisal?
options / answer: A) lazy | B) stingy | C) responsible | D) proud
why correct: Taking responsibility for his dog’s damage and fixing it himself shows Faisal is responsible.
tip: A character’s response to a mistake — theirs or someone else’s — often reveals a trait.

stem: Read: “Yara read the entire instruction manual twice before assembling the bookshelf, even though her brother said it was a waste of time.” True or false: this detail shows Yara is impulsive.
options / answer: True | False
why correct: Reading instructions carefully twice shows she is careful and thorough, not impulsive.
tip: Impulsive means acting quickly without thinking; look for the opposite behavior here.

stem: Read: “Even after losing the chess match for the third time, Khalid asked his opponent to explain the winning move so he could learn from it.” Which word best describes Khalid?
options / answer: A) arrogant | B) careless | C) sore | D) determined
why correct: Wanting to learn from repeated losses instead of giving up shows determination.
tip: Look at how a character handles failure to find a trait.

stem: Read: “Dalia noticed her little cousin struggling with his shoelaces at the party, so she knelt down and showed him the trick slowly, twice, without anyone asking her to.” Which word best describes Dalia?
options / answer: A) caring | B) shy | C) bossy | D) impatient
why correct: Noticing someone’s struggle and helping patiently, without being asked, shows caring.
tip: An unprompted act of kindness is strong evidence of a caring trait.

stem: Read: “The whole class groaned when the teacher announced a surprise quiz, but Amira pulled out a pencil calmly, since she had reviewed her notes every night that week.” What is Amira’s perspective on the surprise quiz?
options / answer: A) She thinks the quiz is unfair. | B) She is not worried, because she feels prepared. | C) She is upset like the rest of the class. | D) She is confused about what a quiz is.
why correct: Her calm reaction, explained by her nightly review, shows she feels prepared rather than worried.
tip: When a character reacts differently from the group, look for a reason given in the text.

stem: Read: “Tariq thought the old clock tower should be torn down because it no longer worked, but his grandfather believed it should stay because it reminded the town of its history.” How do Tariq and his grandfather see the clock tower differently?
options / answer: A) Both think it should be torn down. | B) Both value its history equally. | C) Tariq values its usefulness, while his grandfather values its connection to history. | D) Tariq wants to keep it, and the grandfather wants it removed.
why correct: Tariq judges the tower by whether it works; his grandfather judges it by its meaning to the town.
tip: Compare the REASON each character gives for their opinion.

stem: Read: “The coach called the scrimmage a success, but Sara kicked the grass and would not meet anyone’s eyes afterward.” True or false: Sara agrees with the coach’s view of the scrimmage.
options / answer: True | False
why correct: Sara’s frustrated body language shows she does not share the coach’s positive view.
tip: A character’s actions can reveal a perspective that contradicts what another character says.

stem: Read: “Grandma Zainab called the crowded, noisy souk ‘wonderfully alive,’ while her grandson Omar found it exhausting and could not wait to leave.” How is Omar’s perspective different from his grandmother’s?
options / answer: A) Neither of them likes the souk. | B) Both enjoy the souk equally. | C) Omar loves the noise, and Grandma Zainab hates it. | D) Grandma Zainab enjoys the souk’s energy, while Omar finds it tiring.
why correct: The same experience feels exciting to one character and exhausting to the other.
tip: The same event can feel different depending on who is experiencing it.

stem: A story about a school trip is told only through the diary entries of one student, Huda. How would the story change if it also included her teacher’s diary entries?
options / answer: A) Readers would also learn the teacher’s private thoughts and concerns about the trip. | B) The trip’s location would change. | C) Huda’s diary entries would disappear. | D) The events of the trip would change.
why correct: Adding a second point of view lets readers hear another character’s private thoughts, not just events.
tip: More than one perspective means readers hear more than one character’s inner thoughts.

stem: Read: “Sami had ignored every warning about the incoming sandstorm and left his bike outside the shed, uncovered, right next to the open gate.” What will most likely happen?
options / answer: A) The sandstorm will not affect the bike at all. | B) The bike will likely be damaged or blown around by the sandstorm. | C) The bike will stay perfectly clean. | D) The gate will close itself.
why correct: Leaving a bike uncovered and exposed during a storm makes damage likely.
tip: Think about what usually happens when something is left exposed to a danger that was already warned about.

stem: Read: “Lina had saved exactly half of the money for the bicycle and had three more months of allowance before the sale ended.” Based on this, it makes sense to predict that Lina will probably be able to afford the bicycle in time.
options / answer: True | False
why correct: If she already has half the money and has enough time left to save more, she will likely reach her goal.
tip: Predictions about money often depend on comparing what is saved with what is still needed and how much time is left.

stem: Read: “Scientists noticed a volcano’s steam vents releasing gas more quickly than usual and recorded several small tremors over the past week.” What is the BEST prediction based on these clues?
options / answer: A) The volcano will stop all activity permanently. | B) The tremors are unrelated to the volcano. | C) The volcano may be building toward a larger eruption soon. | D) The volcano has become completely safe.
why correct: Increasing gas release and small tremors are warning signs scientists use to predict a possible eruption.
tip: Combine several related clues, not just one, to make a stronger prediction.

stem: Read: “Despite being told the bridge was closed for repairs, two hikers decided to climb over the barrier and cross it anyway.” Which detail BEST supports the prediction that the hikers are taking a serious risk?
options / answer: A) “the bridge.” | B) “and cross it anyway.” | C) “two hikers decided to climb over the barrier.” | D) “despite being told the bridge was closed for repairs”
why correct: Ignoring a warning about repairs, specifically, is what signals real danger ahead.
tip: Look for the exact detail that names the danger, not just the action taken.

stem: Read: “After weeks of drought, dark clouds finally gathered over the dry farmland, and the wind carried the smell of rain for the first time in a month.” What will most likely happen next?
options / answer: A) It will probably rain soon, bringing relief to the farmland. | B) The drought will continue with no change. | C) The farmland will flood immediately. | D) A sandstorm will begin instead.
why correct: Dark clouds and the smell of rain are classic signs that rain is about to fall.
tip: Weather predictions often rely on recognizing familiar signs described in the text.

skill: Adjectives, Articles and Order of Adjectives
stem: Which word describes the noun “camel” in “The patient camel waited in the shade”?
options / answer: A) shade | B) patient | C) waited | D) The
why correct: “Patient” tells what kind of camel.
tip: Adjectives describe nouns.

skill: Adjectives, Articles and Order of Adjectives
stem: Which sentence uses a predicate adjective?
options / answer: A) The cool air arrived after sunset. | B) We watched the sunset. | C) The desert air felt cool after sunset. | D) Sunset came quickly.
why correct: “Cool” follows the linking verb “felt” and describes the subject.
tip: Predicate adjectives follow linking verbs.

skill: Adjectives, Articles and Order of Adjectives
stem: Choose the correct form: “Of the two routes, the coastal road is ____.”
options / answer: A) scenicer | B) most scenic | C) more scenic | D) more scenicer
why correct: Comparing exactly two routes: more scenic.
tip: Two → comparative; three+ → superlative.

skill: Adjectives, Articles and Order of Adjectives
stem: Tap the part of the sentence that has an error.
options / answer: She bought |  a new, wooden, |  jewelry box |  in the souq.
why correct: No comma between adjectives that are not coordinate (you would not say “new and wooden jewelry box” naturally), and never a comma before the noun.
tip: Use commas only between coordinate adjectives, and never before the noun.

stem: Which clause is dependent? “Unless the bus arrives soon, we will be late.”
options / answer: A) the bus arrives | B) we will be late | C) we will | D) Unless the bus arrives soon
why correct: “Unless” makes the clause dependent.
tip: Dependent clauses begin with subordinating conjunctions or relative pronouns.

stem: Which sentence contains a relative clause?
options / answer: A) The coach who trained us retired this year. | B) The coach retired, and we were sad. | C) The coach retired this year. | D) Because the coach retired, we were sad.
why correct: “who trained us” describes the coach.
tip: Relative clauses begin with who, which, that, whose.

stem: Choose the relative pronoun: “The book ____ cover is torn belongs to the library.”
options / answer: A) which | B) that | C) who’s | D) whose
why correct: “Whose” shows the cover belongs to the book.
tip: whose = possession.

stem: Which sentence is compound-complex?
options / answer: A) We lit candles. | B) When the power failed, we lit candles, and Mariam told stories. | C) We lit candles, and Mariam told stories. | D) When the power failed, we lit candles.
why correct: It has two independent clauses and one dependent clause.
tip: Compound-complex = 2+ independent + 1+ dependent.

stem: Which revision places the relative clause correctly to avoid confusion?
options / answer: A) That my aunt made, the vase sat on the shelf. | B) The vase sat that my aunt made on the shelf. | C) The vase that my aunt made sat on the shelf. | D) The vase sat on the shelf that my aunt made.
why correct: A relative clause should sit right after the noun it describes.
tip: Place modifiers next to what they modify.

stem: Which is a fragment?
options / answer: A) Yusuf missed the bus. | B) The robotics club stayed late. | C) He walked home. | D) Because the robotics club stayed late.
why correct: A dependent clause alone is a fragment.
tip: Ask: Because… what happened?

stem: Which is a comma splice?
options / answer: A) The reef is fragile, it needs protection. | B) The reef is fragile, so it needs protection. | C) The reef is fragile. | D) The reef is fragile; it needs protection.
why correct: Two independent clauses joined only by a comma form a comma splice.
tip: Comma alone ≠ enough to join sentences.

stem: Which revision fixes the run-on? “Scientists grow corals in nurseries they transplant them to reefs.”
options / answer: A) Scientists grow corals in nurseries, they transplant them to reefs. | B) Scientists grow corals in nurseries; then they transplant them to reefs. | C) Scientists grow corals. In nurseries they transplant them to reefs. | D) Scientists grow corals in nurseries they, transplant them.
why correct: A semicolon correctly joins the two clauses.
tip: Use a period, semicolon, or comma + conjunction.

stem: “Hoping to finish the model before the deadline and working late every night” is a complete sentence.
options / answer: True | False
why correct: It contains only participial phrases; there is no subject and main verb.
tip: Long word groups can still be fragments.

stem: Which paragraph revision contains NO fragments or run-ons?
options / answer: A) The souq is old. Its arches carved. Shops sell spices. | B) The souq is old, its arches are carved, its shops sell spices. | C) The souq is old. Its arches are carved, and its shops sell spices. | D) The souq is old its arches are carved.
why correct: Each sentence is complete and correctly joined.
tip: Check every sentence in a paragraph.

stem: Choose the past tense: “The bell ____ at noon.”
options / answer: A) rang | B) rings | C) rung | D) ringed
why correct: ring → rang → rung.
tip: Past participle needs has/have/had.

stem: Match each verb with its past participle.
options / answer: freeze = frozen | steal = stolen | forgive = forgiven | shake = shaken
why correct: These verbs form the past participle with -en.
tip: Test with “I have ___.”

stem: Choose: “By the time we arrived, the guests had already ____.”
options / answer: A) went | B) gone | C) goed | D) go
why correct: had + gone (past participle of go).
tip: go → went → gone.

stem: Tap the part of the sentence that has an error.
options / answer: The coral |  had |  sank |  to the bottom.
why correct: After “had,” use the past participle “sunk.”
tip: sink → sank → (had) sunk.

stem: Which sentence uses lie/lay correctly?
options / answer: A) Yesterday the tired dog lied in the shade. | B) Yesterday the tired dog layed in the shade. | C) Yesterday the tired dog laid in the shade. | D) Yesterday the tired dog lay in the shade.
why correct: lie (rest) → lay (past). lay (put) → laid (past).
tip: Lie = recline; lay = put something down.

skill: Nouns: Common, Proper, Concrete, Abstract, Collective
stem: Which word is an abstract noun? “Mariam’s loyalty surprised her brother.”
options / answer: A) loyalty | B) surprised | C) Mariam’s | D) brother
why correct: Loyalty is a quality, not something you touch.
tip: Abstract nouns name ideas and feelings.

skill: Nouns: Common, Proper, Concrete, Abstract, Collective
stem: In “Mrs. Qadri gave Yusuf a cup,” what is “Yusuf”?
options / answer: A) the subject | B) the indirect object | C) the direct object | D) the verb
why correct: Yusuf receives the cup: indirect object.
tip: Gave WHAT? (direct) To WHOM? (indirect).

skill: Nouns: Common, Proper, Concrete, Abstract, Collective
stem: Which noun is used as a predicate noun? “The ladder was a gift.”
options / answer: A) a | B) was | C) gift | D) ladder
why correct: “Gift” follows the linking verb and renames the subject.
tip: Predicate nouns rename the subject.

skill: Nouns: Common, Proper, Concrete, Abstract, Collective
stem: Which TWO words are nouns used as appositives? “My sister, a talented artist, painted the mural with Huda, her best friend.”
options / answer: A) friend | B) sister | C) artist | D) mural
why correct: “A talented artist” renames sister; “her best friend” renames Huda.
tip: Appositives rename nearby nouns.

skill: Singular, Plural and Irregular Plural Nouns
stem: Choose the plural of “ox”: “Two strong ____ pulled the heavy cart.”
options / answer: A) oxes | B) oxs | C) oxen | D) ox’s
why correct: ox → oxen, an irregular plural from Old English.
tip: Irregular plurals: ox/oxen, child/children.

skill: Singular, Plural and Irregular Plural Nouns
stem: What is the plural of “analysis”?
options / answer: A) analysises | B) analysis | C) analysi | D) analyses
why correct: Greek -is plurals change to -es: analysis → analyses.
tip: crisis → crises; thesis → theses.

skill: Singular, Plural and Irregular Plural Nouns
stem: Match each singular noun with its plural.
options / answer: cactus = cacti | phenomenon = phenomena | criterion = criteria | larva = larvae
why correct: These plurals come from Latin and Greek.
tip: Learn academic plurals.

skill: Singular, Plural and Irregular Plural Nouns
stem: Tap the part of the sentence that has an error.
options / answer: Both |  of my brother-in-laws |  work |  at the port.
why correct: In compound nouns, pluralize the main word: brothers-in-law.
tip: Pluralize the important word in a compound noun.

skill: Singular, Plural and Irregular Plural Nouns
stem: Which sentence uses plurals and possessives correctly?
options / answer: A) The scientists’ data show that the reefs’ health is declining. | B) The scientists’ datas show that the reefs’ health is declining. | C) The scientist’s data shows that the reef’s health are declining. | D) The scientists data show that the reefs health is declining.
why correct: Plural possessives (scientists’, reefs’) and the plural “data … show.”
tip: Check plurals, possessives and agreement together.

stem: Which sentence is an exclamation?
options / answer: A) Can you see the dunes? | B) What an incredible view from the dunes! | C) The view from the dunes is wide. | D) Look at the dunes.
why correct: It expresses strong feeling and ends with “!”.
tip: Exclamations show strong emotion.

stem: Which sentence is a simple sentence with a compound predicate?
options / answer: A) Mariam waved, and Yusuf smiled. | B) Mariam and Yusuf smiled. | C) Mariam waved and smiled. | D) When Mariam waved, Yusuf smiled.
why correct: One subject, two verbs, one clause.
tip: Simple sentences can have compound parts.

stem: Which sentence begins with an introductory prepositional phrase?
options / answer: A) Bright lanterns lit the market. | B) The market, bright and busy, came alive. | C) The market came alive under the lanterns. | D) Under the bright lanterns, the market came alive.
why correct: “Under the bright lanterns” opens the sentence.
tip: Varying sentence openings improves style.

stem: Which revision best combines these sentences with varied structure? “The tide rose. The boats lifted. The fishermen cheered.”
options / answer: A) As the tide rose and the boats lifted, the fishermen cheered. | B) Rising tide, lifting boats, cheering fishermen. | C) The tide rose and the boats lifted and the fishermen cheered. | D) The tide rose, the boats lifted, the fishermen cheered.
why correct: A dependent clause with a compound subject-verb pair creates variety.
tip: Combine choppy sentences for flow.

stem: Choose the present perfect: “Mariam ____ in the choir for two years.”
options / answer: A) sings | B) will sing | C) sang | D) has sung
why correct: has/have + past participle = present perfect.
tip: Present perfect connects past to now.

stem: Which sentence is in the future progressive tense?
options / answer: A) We sailed at noon. | B) At noon tomorrow, we will be sailing. | C) We are sailing. | D) We have sailed.
why correct: will be + -ing = future progressive.
tip: Progressive = ongoing action.

stem: Which sentence has a correct sequence of tenses?
options / answer: A) After Yusuf misses the bus, he walked home. | B) After Yusuf will miss the bus, he walked home. | C) After Yusuf had missed the bus, he walked home. | D) After Yusuf had missed the bus, he walks home.
why correct: Past perfect (had missed) shows the earlier past action.
tip: Use past perfect for the earlier of two past events.

stem: Tap the part of the sentence that has an error.
options / answer: Every morning, Mariam |  walked |  to the bakery and |  buys bread.
why correct: Keep tenses consistent: walked … bought.
tip: Avoid unnecessary tense shifts.

stem: Which sentence uses verb mood correctly (subjunctive)?
options / answer: A) If I was the principal, I would keep the five-day week. | B) If I be the principal, I would keep the five-day week. | C) If I am the principal, I would keep the five-day week. | D) If I were the principal, I would keep the five-day week.
why correct: Unreal conditions use the subjunctive “were.”
tip: If I were… = imagining something not true.

stem: Which sentence correctly uses commas around an appositive?
options / answer: A) Mrs. Qadri, the baker, opened the door. | B) Mrs. Qadri the baker opened, the door. | C) Mrs. Qadri the baker, opened the door. | D) Mrs. Qadri, the baker opened the door.
why correct: Nonessential appositives are set off by commas on both sides.
tip: Two commas around extra information.

stem: Tap the part of the sentence that has an error.
options / answer: My grandfather |  who planted the orchard |  built |  a ladder.
why correct: A nonrestrictive clause about a specific person needs commas on both sides.
tip: Extra information about a specific noun is set off by commas.

stem: Which sentence punctuates the quotation correctly?
options / answer: A) Mariam said “I knew you’d walk the bakery way.” | B) Mariam said, “I knew you’d walk the bakery way.” | C) Mariam said, I knew you’d walk the bakery way. | D) Mariam said, “i knew you’d walk the bakery way.”
why correct: Comma after the tag; capitalized quotation inside quotation marks.
tip: Tag, comma, “Quotation.”

stem: Which sentence correctly punctuates a question in dialogue?
options / answer: A) “Does that radio still work,” Sara asked. | B) Does that radio still work? Sara asked. | C) “Does that radio still work?” Sara asked. | D) “Does that radio still work”? Sara asked.
why correct: The question mark belongs to the quotation and goes inside.
tip: End marks stay with the spoken words.

stem: Which sentence correctly uses a quotation within a quotation?
options / answer: A) ‘My grandfather always said, “Some things last…”’ Sara explained. | B) “My grandfather always said, “Some things last…,”” Sara explained. | C) “My grandfather always said, Some things last…,” Sara explained. | D) “My grandfather always said, ‘Some things last if you look after them,’” Sara explained.
why correct: Use single quotation marks for a quotation inside a quotation.
tip: Double outside, single inside.

stem: Tap the part of the sentence that has an error.
options / answer: “I came for a short article,” |  Sara said. |  “I’m leaving with a book” | .
why correct: The period belongs inside the closing quotation mark.
tip: Periods and commas go inside quotation marks.

stem: Which sentence correctly integrates a short quotation from a text?
options / answer: A) Huda argues that visitors come for “what is special about a place.” | B) Huda argues that visitors come for “what is special about a place”. | C) Huda argues that visitors come for “What is special about a place.” | D) Huda argues that visitors come for, “what is special about a place.”
why correct: A quoted fragment blends into your sentence without a comma or capital.
tip: Integrate quotations smoothly.

stem: Which word has the most NEGATIVE connotation for a crowded market?
options / answer: A) busy | B) chaotic | C) lively | D) bustling
why correct: “Chaotic” suggests disorder.
tip: Connotation = feeling a word carries.

stem: In “Desert Night,” why does the poet say the sand gives back heat “in slow, warm breaths”?
options / answer: A) To show it is cold | B) To describe a storm | C) To make the desert feel alive and comforting | D) To make the desert seem dangerous
why correct: “Breaths” and “warm” carry gentle, living connotations.
tip: Word choice shapes feeling.

stem: In “The Last Bus Home,” the battery is at “four percent” before the screen goes black. What does this suggest the screen did?
options / answer: A) grew brighter | B) broke into pieces | C) showed a picture | D) turned off because the battery ran out
why correct: Low battery + black screen = it shut off.
tip: Use cause clues nearby.

stem: Which word is a synonym for “ambiguous”?

stem: Choose the synonym: “The volunteers showed ____ (plentiful) kindness toward the flood victims.”

stem: Read: “Renewable energy sources like wind and solar now generate over 12 percent of global electricity, a figure that has tripled in the past decade.” Which detail is evidence that renewable energy use is growing rapidly?

tip: Evidence of growth usually compares a past amount with a present one.

stem: Read: “The city’s new bike-sharing program cut traffic near downtown by 8 percent in its first year, though some residents complained that stations were often empty during rush hour.” Which TWO details give a balanced view of the program’s first year?

tip: A balanced summary uses evidence from both sides of an issue.

stem: Read: “Mr. Aziz ran his thumb along the cracked door frame he had repaired decades earlier and said nothing for a long moment before speaking again.” Which detail suggests that the repair held a deep personal meaning for Mr. Aziz?

tip: A long pause or silence in dialogue often signals strong, unspoken feeling.

stem: Read: “Deep-sea anglerfish produce their own light through a chemical reaction in a special organ, which attracts prey in the pitch-black water.” Which detail explains the PURPOSE of the anglerfish’s light?
options / answer: A) “which attracts prey in the pitch-black water.” | B) “a special organ.” | C) “produce their own light through a chemical reaction.” | D) “pitch-black water.”
why correct: Attracting prey is the stated reason the anglerfish produces light.
tip: Separate the explanation of HOW something happens from the explanation of WHY.

stem: Read: “Although four-day school weeks can save districts money on transportation and utilities, researchers found that younger students’ reading scores dropped slightly compared to five-day schools.” True or false: the text claims four-day school weeks have no drawbacks.
options / answer: True | False
why correct: The text names a specific drawback — a drop in younger students’ reading scores — so it does not claim there are no drawbacks.
tip: Watch for absolute claims like ‘no drawbacks’ when the text actually lists a cost.

stem: Read: “Huda crossed out her first three drafts of the letter, each one angrier than the last, before finally writing one that calmly explained her concerns.” Which detail shows that Huda chose to communicate respectfully rather than react in anger?
options / answer: A) “each one angrier than the last.” | B) “crossed out her first three drafts... before finally writing one that calmly explained her concerns.” | C) “the letter.” | D) “her concerns.”
why correct: Rewriting until she found a calm tone shows she deliberately chose respect over anger.
tip: Look at the FINAL version of a character’s words or actions, not just the early drafts.

stem: Read: “A single mature oak tree can absorb roughly 22 kilograms of carbon dioxide each year, which is why city planners increasingly favor planting them along busy streets.” Which detail supports the claim that oak trees help with pollution from traffic?
options / answer: A) “city planners increasingly favor planting them along busy streets.” | B) “busy streets.” | C) “can absorb roughly 22 kilograms of carbon dioxide each year” | D) “A single mature oak tree.”
why correct: Absorbing carbon dioxide — a pollutant released by traffic — is the direct evidence for the claim.
tip: Trace the claim back to the specific number or fact that supports it.

stem: Read: “Yasmin woke at five every morning to practice before school, enjoyed listening to music on the bus, and kept a log of every mistake she made in rehearsal.” Which TWO details show Yasmin’s strong discipline?

why correct: A strict daily routine and tracking her own mistakes both show serious self-discipline.
tip: Look for repeated habits and self-monitoring as strong evidence of discipline.

stem: Read: “Lightning can heat the surrounding air to temperatures hotter than the surface of the sun, causing the air to expand explosively and produce the sound we hear as thunder.” Which detail explains WHY thunder happens?
options / answer: A) “we hear as thunder.” | B) “Lightning can heat the surrounding air to temperatures hotter than the surface of the sun.” | C) “the surface of the sun.” | D) “causing the air to expand explosively”
why correct: The explosive expansion of superheated air is the direct cause of the sound of thunder.
tip: Find the exact phrase describing the physical cause, not just a related fact.

stem: Read: “Huda signed her letter to the city council ‘Respectfully,’ even after writing three paragraphs disagreeing firmly with their plan.” Which detail shows that Huda disagreed without being disrespectful?

tip: Compare the content of an argument with the TONE used to express it.

stem: Read: “Though bats are often feared, a single bat can eat more than a thousand insects in one night, making them valuable for controlling pests naturally.” True or false: the text presents bats as only dangerous to humans.

why correct: The text actually presents bats as valuable pest controllers, not as dangerous.
tip: Check whether a statement matches the text’s actual claim, especially after a word like ‘though.’

stem: Read: “Switching a school’s lighting to LED bulbs cost the district $40,000 upfront, but the resulting savings on electricity paid back that cost within just three years.” Which detail shows that the LED switch was a good long-term investment?
options / answer: A) “a school’s lighting.” | B) “the resulting savings on electricity paid back that cost within just three years.” | C) “LED bulbs.” | D) “cost the district $40,000 upfront.”
why correct: Paying back the cost in just three years, with savings continuing after, shows a strong long-term benefit.
tip: Compare the initial cost with the eventual payoff to judge whether something is a good investment.

stem: Read: “Sara flipped through her notes one last time, closed the folder, and walked into the interview room without checking her phone even once.” Which detail shows that Sara stayed focused on the interview?
options / answer: A) “the interview room.” | B) “flipped through her notes one last time.” | C) “walked into the interview room without checking her phone even once.” | D) “closed the folder.”
why correct: Not checking her phone, a common distraction, shows she stayed mentally focused.
tip: Look for what a character avoids doing as evidence of focus or self-control.

stem: Read: “Coastal mangrove forests can reduce the height of incoming storm waves by up to 66 percent, protecting the villages behind them from the worst flooding.” Which detail is the strongest evidence that mangroves protect coastal communities?

why correct: The specific percentage reduction in wave height is the measurable evidence behind the claim.
tip: A number or statistic is often the strongest kind of evidence for a claim.

stem: Read: “The region’s new desalination plant provides clean drinking water to 50,000 residents, but it also uses large amounts of electricity and releases concentrated salt water back into the sea.” Which TWO details describe a cost of the desalination plant?

why correct: High electricity use and releasing concentrated salt water are both environmental costs of the plant.
tip: Separate the stated benefit from the stated costs before choosing.

stem: Read: “When the team’s presentation software crashed minutes before judging, Layla calmly grabbed a marker and sketched the diagrams by hand while her teammates panicked.” Which word best describes Layla?

tip: A character’s response to an unexpected problem often reveals a trait.

stem: Read: “Despite knowing the answer, Khalid let his quieter teammate present the group’s findings, coaching her through the key points beforehand instead of taking the spotlight himself.” Which word best describes Khalid?

why correct: Giving up the spotlight to help a teammate shine shows generosity.
tip: Notice when a character gives up personal credit to help someone else.

stem: Read: “Mariam re-checked the lab results three times before reporting them, even though her partner insisted the first result was obviously correct.” True or false: this detail shows Mariam is easily influenced by others’ opinions.

tip: Look for whether a character sticks to their own standards despite pressure from others.

stem: Read: “Omar admitted to the whole class that he had copied the homework answer, even though no one had noticed and he could easily have stayed silent.” Which word best describes Omar?

stem: Read: “Sami offered to carry the heaviest box up three flights of stairs without being asked, then went back down for a second trip while his friends rested.” Which word best describes Sami?

stem: Read: “Noura’s essay argued strongly against her own first opinion once new evidence changed her mind, and she rewrote the entire conclusion the night before it was due.” Which word best describes Noura?

tip: A willingness to change one’s mind based on evidence often reveals open-mindedness.

stem: Read: “Tariq always double-checked the exits and the fire extinguisher locations whenever he entered an unfamiliar building, a habit his friends often teased him about.” Which word best describes Tariq?

tip: A repeated habit, even one that invites teasing, can reveal a consistent trait.

stem: Read: “Rather than arguing when the referee made a clearly wrong call against her team, Amal shook the referee’s hand after the match and thanked him for officiating.” Which word best describes Amal?

why correct: Responding to an unfair call with respect, rather than anger, shows graciousness.
tip: How a character responds to being treated unfairly often reveals their true character.

stem: Read: “Khalid volunteered to tutor the younger students every Tuesday for free, enjoyed drawing comics in his free time, kept a careful record of each student’s progress, and stayed late twice to help a struggling student catch up before an exam.” Which TWO details show that Khalid takes his tutoring role seriously?

tip: A character’s reaction to someone else’s mistake often reveals a trait.

stem: Read: “The coach decided to bench the injured player for the rest of the match.” What does bench mean in this sentence?

stem: What is the setting of “The Interview”?

tip: Combine a character's later words with an earlier action to make an inference.

stem: Which TWO details show that Nour and Sami's problem was caused by unclear communication, not laziness? Choose two.
options / answer: A) Sami says, “We split the work, but we never really talked about what ‘our half’ meant.” | B) Sami says he already finished the volcano diagram. | C) Mr. Farid enters carrying graded tests. | D) Nour says, “I said I'd START it. Not finish the whole thing alone.”
why correct: Both lines show the two partners had different understandings of the plan, not that either one refused to work.
tip: Choose evidence that explains the CAUSE of the conflict, not just any true detail.

stem: Put the events of “The Group Project” in order.
options / answer: Nour complains that the poster and report are still unfinished. → Mr. Farid asks how the project is going. → Sami admits that they never agreed on what “their half” meant. → Nour and Sami make a clear plan and agree to check in the next morning.
why correct: The play moves from the conflict, to the teacher's question, to the honest admission, to the resolution.
tip: Look for the moment each character's attitude or understanding changes.

stem: Unlike a story with a narrator, how does the audience learn how Nour feels during the play?
options / answer: A) through a written letter Nour reads aloud | B) through Sami's opinion of her feelings | C) through her own dialogue and the stage directions describing her tone and actions | D) through a narrator who explains her thoughts directly
why correct: Plays reveal feelings only through dialogue and stage directions, since there is no narrator.
tip: In drama, point of view is shown through what characters say and do, not through narration.

stem: What does hesitating mean in “NOUR: (hesitating) It's... coming along”?
options / answer: A) leaving the room quickly | B) laughing at a joke | C) speaking loudly and clearly | D) pausing because of uncertainty or doubt
why correct: The pause shown by “...” and the stage direction together suggest Nour is unsure how honest to be.
tip: Stage directions and punctuation like “...” can both hint at a word's meaning.

stem: In this play, Sami says they are “stuck.” What does stuck mean in this sentence?
options / answer: A) unable to make progress on a problem | B) finished with all their work | C) glued to an object | D) physically unable to move
why correct: Sami explains right after that they never agreed on the plan, which is why their progress has stopped.
tip: Read the sentence right after a tricky word—it often explains what is really happening.

stem: How do Nour's and Sami's understandings of “our half” differ at the start of the play?
options / answer: A) Both of them thought Sami would write the entire report. | B) Nour thought she only had to start the report, while Sami thought she would finish it alone. | C) Nour thought Sami would do the writing, and Sami agreed. | D) Both of them thought the diagram still needed to be finished.
why correct: Nour says she agreed only to START the report, while Sami believed she would finish the whole thing herself.
tip: Comparing two characters' expectations often reveals the true cause of a conflict.

stem: What is the central idea of “Why Do We Get Goosebumps?”
options / answer: A) Animals with fur never get goosebumps. | B) Scientists do not understand why goosebumps happen. | C) Goosebumps are a leftover reflex from furrier ancestors that no longer serves the same purpose in humans. | D) Goosebumps only happen when people are cold.
why correct: Every section builds on the idea that goosebumps are an old, now mostly useless, inherited reflex.
tip: A central idea is supported across the whole text, not just one paragraph.

stem: Under which heading would you find out that fur makes animals look bigger to predators?
options / answer: A) More Than Just Cold | B) Why Do We Get Goosebumps? | C) Why Humans Still Have Them | D) A Useful Trick for Hairier Ancestors
why correct: The first section explains that raised fur traps warm air and makes an animal look larger to a threat.
tip: Headings organize an article's ideas into clearly labeled sections.

stem: According to the article, what is an EFFECT of fur rising on a cold animal?
options / answer: A) A layer of warm air becomes trapped near the animal's skin. | B) The animal loses its sense of touch. | C) The animal's temperature drops even lower. | D) The tiny muscles under the skin disappear.
why correct: “Raised fur traps a layer of warm air next to the skin,” which is the direct effect described.
tip: Look for the result that follows directly after a described cause.

stem: Why do humans still get goosebumps even though they no longer have thick fur?
options / answer: A) Doctors have not found a way to stop the reflex. | B) The tiny muscles under the skin still react the same old way, even though the reaction is no longer useful. | C) Goosebumps now help humans see better in the cold. | D) Human skin grows fur quickly when cold.
why correct: The article explains that the ancient reflex stayed in our bodies even after it stopped being very useful.
tip: Look for words like “however” that signal why something continues despite no longer being useful.

stem: How is the goosebump reflex different in humans compared to furry animals?
options / answer: A) In furry animals it is only caused by fear, never cold. | B) In humans it keeps them warmer than furry animals. | C) In furry animals it provides warmth and protection, but in humans it no longer serves either purpose. | D) Humans and furry animals get goosebumps for exactly the same practical reason today.
why correct: The article contrasts a useful ancient purpose in furry animals with an outdated, less useful reflex in humans today.
tip: Look for a paragraph that directly compares two groups' experience of the same feature.

stem: What does reflex mean in “Our bodies kept this old reflex even after it stopped being very useful”?
options / answer: A) a muscle used only for walking | B) a type of fur found on animals | C) a decision someone makes carefully | D) an automatic reaction the body makes without thinking about it
why correct: Goosebumps rising automatically, without anyone deciding to make them happen, is the clue that reflex means an automatic reaction.
tip: Think about whether the body's action happens on purpose or automatically.

stem: What does trigger mean in “can trigger the same nervous system signal that cold does”?
options / answer: A) to cause or set off | B) to measure or record | C) to weaken or slow down | D) to prevent or stop
why correct: Since both cold and strong emotion lead to the exact same nervous system signal, trigger must mean to cause or set off.
tip: Compare the word to something else in the sentence that causes the same result.

stem: Which TWO details show that emotions, not just cold, can cause goosebumps? Choose two.
options / answer: A) Emotional reactions and temperature reactions share some of the same nerve pathways. | B) Fear, awe, or moving music can trigger the same nervous system signal that cold does. | C) Underneath each hair on your skin is a tiny muscle. | D) Humans no longer have thick fur.
why correct: Both details directly explain how emotional reactions can produce the very same goosebump response as cold.
tip: Choose evidence that matches the exact claim—here, that emotions ALSO cause goosebumps.

stem: True or false: According to the article, goosebumps are caused only by cold temperatures.
options / answer: True | False
why correct: The article states that strong emotions, such as fear or awe, can trigger the same reaction as cold.
tip: Watch for words like “only” in true/false statements; informational texts often show more than one cause.

stem: What is the author's main purpose in explaining that fur made goosebumps useful for animals?
options / answer: A) to convince readers that humans should grow more body hair | B) to help readers understand why humans still have a reflex that no longer fully makes sense for them | C) to list every animal that has fur | D) to argue that animals are smarter than humans
why correct: Explaining the old purpose of the reflex helps readers understand why it survives in humans even without a clear use today.
tip: Ask why an author includes background information before explaining a modern mystery.

stem: Which is the best summary of the “More Than Just Cold” section?
options / answer: A) Fear is the only emotion that can cause goosebumps. | B) Scientists do not know what causes goosebumps. | C) Strong emotions can cause goosebumps because they trigger some of the same nerve pathways as cold does. | D) Music always feels better when you have goosebumps.
why correct: A good summary keeps only the key, factual point of the section without adding opinions.
tip: A summary should state the main scientific point in your own words.

stem: Which sentence best expresses the theme of “The Spelling Bee”?
options / answer: A) Practicing is a waste of time if you don't win. | B) Judges are usually too strict during competitions. | C) Spelling bees are only fun for people who never make mistakes. | D) Working through panic calmly, one small step at a time, is its own kind of success.
why correct: The final paragraph states directly that finding a way through panic “felt like its own kind of victory.”
tip: Look at the character's final realization to find the theme.

stem: How does Yasmin feel just before the spelling bee begins?
options / answer: A) nervous | B) bored | C) confident and relaxed | D) angry
why correct: “Yasmin's palms were sweating” and her memorized words “seemed to have evaporated,” both showing nervousness.
tip: Physical reactions, like sweating, are strong clues to a character's feelings.

stem: What is the central conflict Yasmin faces on stage?
options / answer: A) Another speller cheats during the competition. | B) Panic makes her forget a word she had already memorized. | C) She forgets to study for the spelling bee. | D) The judge asks her an unfair question.
why correct: Despite weeks of practice, panic makes the word's letters seem to disappear from her memory.
tip: The central conflict is the specific obstacle the character must overcome in the moment.

stem: The story is told in third person, but whose thoughts does the reader follow most closely?
options / answer: A) the audience's | B) the judge's | C) Yasmin's | D) Ms. Adel's
why correct: The narration stays close to Yasmin's thoughts and feelings throughout the passage.
tip: A third-person narrator can still focus closely on one character's inner thoughts.

stem: Why does Yasmin feel a sense of victory even though she does not win the spelling bee?
options / answer: A) She believes the word 'conscience' was unfair. | B) She is happy the competition is finally over. | C) She secretly did not want to win the competition. | D) She successfully managed her panic instead of letting it defeat her completely.
why correct: The last paragraph explains that overcoming the panic, not winning the whole event, is what felt like a victory to her.
tip: An inference about feelings should match the character's own stated realization.

stem: “Every word she had memorized seemed to have evaporated from her mind.” What does this figurative language suggest?
options / answer: A) Her memorized words suddenly felt completely gone, as if they had vanished into thin air. | B) Her memory turned into water. | C) She decided to stop studying. | D) She forgot how to spell forever.
why correct: Comparing memorized words to evaporating water emphasizes how suddenly and completely they seemed to disappear.
tip: Picture the literal action in the figurative phrase, then apply that feeling to the character's situation.

stem: Which TWO details show that Yasmin manages her panic instead of being completely controlled by it? Choose two.
options / answer: A) Her palms were sweating before she reached the stage. | B) Sixty parents were watching the competition. | C) She remembers Ms. Adel's advice to break the word down. | D) She spells the easy part, “con,” first and then continues.
why correct: Both chosen details show Yasmin taking a deliberate, calm step to work through her panic rather than freezing completely.
tip: Choose evidence that shows an ACTION the character takes, not just a feeling she has.

stem: Put the events of “The Spelling Bee” in order.
options / answer: Yasmin practices her spelling words for three weeks. → Her mind goes blank when the judge gives her the word 'conscience.' → She remembers her tutor's advice to break the word into smaller parts. → She spells the word correctly and hears applause.
why correct: The story moves in time order from practice, to panic, to remembered advice, to success.
tip: Look for time clues such as “for three weeks,” “now,” and “she opened her mouth.”

stem: What does evaporated mean in “every word she had memorized seemed to have evaporated from her mind”?
options / answer: A) was written down on paper | B) disappeared completely, as if turned into vapor and gone | C) became easier to remember | D) grew much larger
why correct: Comparing memorized words to evaporating water suggests they felt like they had completely vanished.
tip: Think about what evaporating water actually does: it disappears into the air.

stem: What does ripple mean in “a small ripple of applause moved through the audience”?
options / answer: A) a loud explosion | B) complete silence | C) a gradual spreading motion, like a small wave | D) a single loud clap from one person
why correct: Comparing the applause to a ripple suggests it spread gently and gradually through the crowd, like a ripple on water.
tip: Picture the literal meaning of a word (a ripple on water) to understand its figurative use.

stem: True or false: Yasmin wins the spelling bee at the end of the story.
options / answer: True | False
why correct: The text clearly states she “didn't win the spelling bee” and was eliminated two rounds later.
tip: Check the text carefully; a character can feel successful without actually winning a competition.

stem: How does Yasmin's idea of “winning” change from the beginning to the end of the story?
options / answer: A) Her idea of winning never changes in the story. | B) She believes only the judge's opinion matters. | C) She decides winning does not matter to her at all. | D) At first winning probably meant finishing first; by the end, she sees overcoming her panic as its own kind of win.
why correct: The final paragraph shows she has redefined success to include overcoming panic, not just placing first.
tip: Look for a shift in a character's thinking between the start and the end of a story.

stem: Which sentence best expresses the theme of “The Lighthouse Keeper's Apprentice”?
options / answer: A) Careful patience in a difficult moment can matter more than speed. | B) Lighthouses are difficult machines to build. | C) Sailors always trust what lighthouses tell them. | D) Fevers can be dangerous for lighthouse keepers.
why correct: Yusra's choice to stop and work carefully, rather than force the mechanism, is what saves the night's light—exactly the theme the final paragraph emphasizes.
tip: Look at the character's key decision and its result to find the theme.

stem: How does Yusra feel as she climbs the stairs at the beginning of the story?
options / answer: A) excited to finally be rid of her uncle's rules | B) nervous, since this is her first time tending the lamp completely alone | C) bored, because she has done this job too many times to count | D) confused about how the lamp mechanism works
why correct: Her “damp” palms against the railing are a physical clue to her nervousness about this new responsibility.
tip: Physical details, like sweaty palms, often reveal a character's inner feelings.

stem: What is the setting of the story?
options / answer: A) a classroom where Yusra studies mechanics | B) a modern lighthouse run by machines | C) a harbor lighthouse in Alexandria in 1887 | D) a merchant ship at sea in the present day
why correct: The story opens by naming the place and year, and the lamp room's details confirm a historical, hand-operated lighthouse.
tip: Specific dates and location names at the start of a story usually establish its setting.

stem: The story is told in third person. Whose thoughts and feelings does the narration follow most closely?
options / answer: A) her uncle's | B) the reader's | C) the sailor's | D) Yusra's
why correct: The narration describes Yusra's memories, instincts, and physical sensations throughout the climb and repair.
tip: A third-person narrator can still stay close to a single character's experience.

stem: Order these events from “The Lighthouse Keeper's Apprentice.”
options / answer: Yusra climbs the stairs alone because her uncle is sick with a fever. → She remembers her uncle's warning about the old, fragile clockwork. → She feels the mechanism catch and stops instead of forcing the crank. → A sailor sights the harbor light flashing correctly from three miles out.
why correct: The plot unfolds in a clear sequence from the problem, to the warning, to the careful fix, to the result far out at sea.
tip: Look for details that show cause and effect between each event.

stem: Why does Yusra stop turning the crank instead of forcing it when she feels it catch?
options / answer: A) She remembers her uncle's warning and infers that forcing it could break the gear completely. | B) She decides the lamp does not need to be lit tonight. | C) She wants to let her uncle finish the job instead. | D) She is too tired to keep turning the crank.
why correct: Her uncle's exact warning about forcing a binding gear directly explains why she chooses to stop and investigate instead.
tip: Connect a character's earlier advice to a decision made later in the story.

stem: “The great lens loomed over her.” What does the word loomed suggest about the lens?
options / answer: A) It was small and easy for her to overlook. | B) It appeared large and almost overwhelming, adding to the pressure Yusra feels. | C) It was actually moving toward her on its own. | D) It was glowing brightly with colored light.
why correct: Loomed is often used for something large that feels imposing, which fits Yusra's nervousness at facing this responsibility alone.
tip: A word like loomed adds feeling to a description beyond its literal meaning.

stem: Which TWO details show that Yusra chooses patience over speed while fixing the mechanism? Choose two.
options / answer: A) The lens could bend a flame into a beam seen for twenty miles. | B) She stops and takes a slow breath instead of continuing to force the crank. | C) She works the metal sliver free carefully with the tip of a thin file. | D) She had watched her uncle tend the lamp a hundred times.
why correct: Both details describe a deliberate, careful choice Yusra makes instead of rushing through the repair.
tip: Choose evidence that describes an action taken in the key moment the question asks about.

stem: What does reservoir mean in “check the oil reservoir”?
options / answer: A) a tool used to wind machinery | B) a small flame used for light | C) a container that holds a supply of liquid | D) a window that lets light escape
why correct: Checking the oil reservoir makes sense only if it is a container that holds the oil supply for the lamp.
tip: Think about what object would logically need to be “checked” before lighting a lamp.

stem: What does wedged mean in “a sliver of displaced metal... wedged between two teeth of the largest gear”?
options / answer: A) painted a bright color | B) thrown far away from the gear | C) completely melted away | D) tightly stuck in a narrow space
why correct: The sliver is causing a grinding problem by being caught tightly between the gear's teeth.
tip: Picture the small object causing a mechanical problem to understand what wedged means.

stem: What was the effect of removing the sliver of metal from the gear?
options / answer: A) The mechanism turned smoothly again, and the lens resumed its steady rotation. | B) The lamp went out completely for the rest of the night. | C) The uncle's fever immediately got better. | D) The sailor's ship changed its course toward the harbor.
why correct: Once Yusra removes the metal sliver, “it turned smoothly, and the great lens began its slow, steady rotation.”
tip: Find the sentence describing what happens immediately after the obstacle is removed.

stem: The author describes the sound as “a faint grinding where smooth motion should have been.” What feeling does the word grinding create?
options / answer: A) a sense of excitement and joy | B) a sense that something is wrong or damaged | C) a sense of calm and safety | D) a sense of boredom
why correct: Grinding connotes friction and malfunction, warning the reader—and Yusra—that something needs attention.
tip: Connotation is the feeling a word creates beyond its literal dictionary definition.

stem: How does the author's description in the final paragraph affect the story's tone?
options / answer: A) It creates a comic tone by making fun of the sailor's confusion. | B) It creates a frightening tone by describing a shipwreck. | C) It creates a quietly powerful tone by showing how little the sailor knows about the danger that was just avoided. | D) It creates a confusing tone that leaves the ending unclear.
why correct: Describing what the sailor doesn't know creates quiet dramatic irony that highlights the importance of Yusra's careful choice.
tip: Notice when an author reveals something a character in the story does not know.

stem: What is the author's central claim in this article?
options / answer: A) Students should spend more hours on homework each night. | B) Only high school students should ever receive homework. | C) Homework should be eliminated completely for all students. | D) Homework should be optional, guided by what individual students actually need, rather than mandatory for everyone.
why correct: The introduction and conclusion both state that optional, individualized homework is the author's main position.
tip: The central claim is the position the entire article is built to support.

stem: Which evidence best supports the claim that mandatory homework may not improve achievement?
options / answer: A) A review of multiple studies found a weak connection between homework and achievement in elementary and middle school. | B) Teachers could assign practice problems selectively. | C) Students spend seven hours in class already. | D) Surveys link heavy homework to stress and reduced sleep.
why correct: A review of multiple research studies is strong, direct evidence connected specifically to the claim about achievement.
tip: Match evidence to the EXACT claim it is meant to support.

stem: How does the author respond to the concern that optional homework would let struggling students fall behind?
options / answer: A) The author says struggling students should repeat the grade. | B) The author argues that a flexible system could actually help teachers target support more precisely. | C) The author ignores the concern completely. | D) The author agrees and abandons the main claim.
why correct: This is a concession-and-rebuttal structure: the author acknowledges the worry, then explains why the opposite may be true.
tip: Strong arguments respond directly to objections instead of ignoring them.

stem: Which piece of evidence in the article is the MOST credible support for the author's claim?
options / answer: A) a claim that every teacher agrees homework should be optional | B) a general statement that students are often tired after school | C) a review of multiple research studies comparing homework loads and test scores | D) the idea that students would probably prefer less homework
why correct: A review of multiple studies is a stronger, more reliable form of evidence than a general observation or an assumed preference.
tip: Credible evidence usually comes from research, not from assumptions about what people want.

stem: According to the article, what is one effect of requiring the same homework for every student regardless of need?
options / answer: A) Schools save money on classroom supplies. | B) Parents are required to help with every assignment. | C) Students automatically get better grades. | D) Teachers have less time to notice which specific students actually need extra practice.
why correct: The article explains that uniform assignments make it harder for teachers to identify who truly needs more help.
tip: Look for the sentence describing what happens BECAUSE every assignment blends together.

stem: What does mandatory mean in “Should Homework Be Optional?” when the article discusses “mandatory homework”?
options / answer: A) required for everyone, with no choice | B) assigned only to advanced students | C) graded very strictly | D) suggested but not required
why correct: The article contrasts mandatory homework with optional homework throughout, showing that mandatory means required for all.
tip: Look at the word the author contrasts it with to understand its meaning.

stem: What does documented mean in “excessive mandatory homework has a documented cost”?
options / answer: A) imaginary and not actually true | B) recorded and supported by evidence, such as surveys or studies | C) illegal in most schools | D) kept completely secret
why correct: The sentence immediately mentions “multiple surveys,” showing that documented means backed by recorded evidence.
tip: Check the words right after a tricky term for the proof or evidence being referenced.

stem: Which TWO details support the claim that heavy mandatory homework can be harmful? Choose two.
options / answer: A) Several studies found no meaningful difference in test scores between heavy and light homework loads. | B) Students already spend seven hours in class each day. | C) Surveys link heavy homework loads to higher stress and reduced sleep. | D) Teachers could use quick in-class checks to see what students already know.
why correct: Both chosen details are direct evidence the article uses to argue that heavy, required homework can cause harm without clear benefit.
tip: Select evidence that directly supports the specific harm the question describes.

stem: True or false: The author wants homework eliminated completely for every student.
options / answer: True | False
why correct: The article clearly states that making homework optional “does not mean eliminating it altogether.”
tip: Watch for extreme words like “completely” or “always” that may not match a nuanced argument.

stem: What feeling does the phrase “one-size-fits-all approach” create in the final paragraph?
options / answer: A) a sense that the current system is carefully personalized | B) a sense that the current system is extremely expensive | C) a sense that the current system ignores individual students' different needs | D) a sense that the current system changes too often
why correct: “One-size-fits-all” connotes a rigid system that treats everyone the same, regardless of their actual needs.
tip: Some phrases carry a built-in judgment beyond their literal words.

stem: How would you best describe the author's tone toward critics who disagree with optional homework?
options / answer: A) uninterested, ignoring critics' concerns entirely | B) fully persuaded, agreeing that critics are right | C) dismissive, mocking critics for disagreeing | D) respectful but unconvinced, directly addressing their concern with a counterargument
why correct: The author states the critics' worry fairly, then offers reasoning for a different conclusion—a respectful but firm tone.
tip: Look at how directly and fairly an author restates an opposing view before responding to it.

skill: Poetry: Structure, Rhyme, Meter and Form
stem: How many stanzas does “The Old Olive Tree” have?
options / answer: A) four stanzas | B) sixteen stanzas | C) three stanzas | D) two stanzas
why correct: A stanza is a group of lines set apart from others; this poem has four such groups.
tip: Count the blocks of text separated by blank lines to find the number of stanzas.

skill: Poetry: Structure, Rhyme, Meter and Form
stem: Which pair of words from the poem rhyme?
options / answer: A) gate / birth | B) soil / toil | C) harvest / tends | D) there / elder
why correct: Soil and toil both end with the same “-oil” sound, making them a rhyming pair.
tip: Rhyming words share the same ending sound, even if spelled a little differently.

stem: In the last stanza, the speaker calls the tree “a kind of elder.” What type of figurative language is this, and what does it suggest?
options / answer: A) a simile that compares the tree to a child | B) an example of alliteration | C) a metaphor that compares the tree to a wise, respected older person | D) a literal statement that the tree is an actual person
why correct: Calling the tree “a kind of elder” directly states it IS an elder, which is a metaphor suggesting wisdom and respect earned through age.
tip: A metaphor says one thing IS another, without using like or as.

stem: What does the image “small fists of green and deepening black” most likely describe?
options / answer: A) the tree's roots pushing into the ground | B) storm clouds gathering above the tree | C) the shadows the tree casts at sunset | D) unripe and ripening olives on the tree
why correct: Olives often appear green when unripe and turn dark, almost black, as they ripen—matching this vivid image.
tip: Use sensory details (shape and color) to picture what the poet is actually describing.

stem: What feeling does the phrase “bent low by time” create about the tree, rather than a purely negative idea of weakness?
options / answer: A) a sense of dignity and endurance despite age | B) a sense of confusion about its age | C) a sense of complete failure | D) a sense of danger to people nearby
why correct: Paired with “but never disappears,” the phrase suggests the tree bends under time's weight yet endures with quiet dignity.
tip: Read the words right after a phrase to see whether they soften or change its connotation.

stem: Which statement best expresses the theme of “The Old Olive Tree”?
options / answer: A) Grandparents know more about nature than anyone else. | B) Living things that quietly endure across generations deserve a new kind of respect and attention. | C) Olives are the most valuable crop a family can grow. | D) Trees need regular watering to survive drought.
why correct: The final stanza's shift from seeing the tree as “simply there” to seeing it as an elder reveals this central idea about respect for endurance.
tip: A theme in poetry often appears as a shift in how the speaker understands something by the end.

stem: From what point of view is this poem written?
options / answer: A) third person — a narrator describes the speaker from outside | B) second person — the poem speaks directly to “you” | C) first person — the speaker uses “I” and “my grandfather” | D) third person — the tree narrates its own life
why correct: Pronouns like “I,” “my mother's,” and “my grandfather” show this poem is told from a first-person point of view.
tip: Look for I/me/my to identify first-person point of view.

stem: Why does the speaker's view of the tree change by the end of the poem?
options / answer: A) The tree suddenly grows taller than before. | B) The grandfather tells the speaker to stop visiting the tree. | C) The speaker plants a brand-new tree nearby. | D) Learning the tree's long history from the grandfather helps the speaker see it as something wise and enduring, not just an object.
why correct: The middle stanzas about the tree's long memory and quiet labor explain why the speaker comes to see it differently by the final stanza.
tip: Trace how new information earlier in a poem can explain a change in the speaker's thinking later.

stem: What does toil mean in “the quiet decades of patient toil”?
options / answer: A) hard, steady work | B) a short rest | C) a type of fruit | D) a kind of storm
why correct: Pairing toil with “patient” and “decades” suggests a long, steady kind of hard work.
tip: Look at the words describing HOW LONG and HOW something is done to find a word's meaning.

stem: Which TWO details from the poem show that the olive tree endures hardship? Choose two.
options / answer: A) its trunk grown wide with seasons of drought | B) the wars that passed like weather overhead | C) small fists of green and deepening black | D) the hands that first pressed seed to soil
why correct: Both details describe difficult conditions—drought and war—that the tree has lived through over time.
tip: Choose details that describe a difficulty, not simply a feature or a memory.

stem: How does describing the tree as “a kind of elder” affect the overall tone of the final stanza?
options / answer: A) It creates a frightening tone, as if the tree were haunted. | B) It creates a respectful, almost reverent tone toward the tree. | C) It creates a neutral, purely factual tone with no feeling. | D) It creates a humorous tone that makes fun of old age.
why correct: Comparing the tree to a respected elder elevates it beyond a plant, creating a tone of quiet admiration.
tip: Notice how a single figurative comparison can shift the emotional tone of an entire stanza.

stem: What is the best first step before researching a report on volcanoes?
options / answer: A) Copy a paragraph from a website. | B) Write the conclusion first. | C) List questions you want to answer. | D) Pick the shortest book you can find.
why correct: Good research starts with clear questions that guide what you look for.
tip: Before you search, write down what you want to find out.

stem: Choose the word: 'A ____ source is written by someone who saw or experienced the event.'
options / answer: A) primary | B) fictional | C) secondary
why correct: A primary source comes directly from a witness or participant.
tip: Primary = present at the event; secondary = written about it later.

stem: Which source counts as a secondary source about ancient Egypt?
options / answer: A) a recording of an eyewitness | B) a diary written by a pharaoh's scribe | C) a photograph of a tomb wall | D) a textbook chapter written by a historian today
why correct: The historian did not witness ancient Egypt; they wrote about it afterward using other sources.
tip: Secondary sources are written after the fact, often using primary sources.

stem: You can use any website you find without checking who wrote it.
options / answer: True | False
why correct: Checking the author helps you judge whether the information is trustworthy.
tip: Always ask: who wrote this, and why?

stem: Mariam is researching sea turtles. Which keyword search will give the most useful results?
options / answer: A) sea turtle nesting habits | B) animals | C) sea turtle sea turtle | D) turtle
why correct: Specific keywords help a search engine find exactly the information you need.
tip: Use several specific words, not one broad word.

stem: Which note-taking method helps you avoid copying a source word-for-word?
options / answer: A) Typing the article into your notes. | B) Writing the main idea in your own words on a card | C) Highlighting the whole page. | D) Copying the first sentence of each paragraph.
why correct: Restating the main idea in your own words is called paraphrasing, and it prevents plagiarism.
tip: Read, cover the text, then write what you remember.

stem: Put the steps of a research project in the correct order.
options / answer: Choose a topic and write research questions. → Find and read several reliable sources. → Take notes in your own words. → Organize notes under topic headings. → Write a draft using the notes.
why correct: Research moves from asking questions, to gathering and sorting information, to writing.
tip: Plan before you search, and sort before you write.

stem: A list of all the sources you used at the end of a report is called a ____.
options / answer: (typed)
why correct: This list lets readers see exactly where your facts and ideas came from.
tip: Keep a running list of sources as you research, not just at the end.

stem: Which source is most reliable for facts about climate change?
options / answer: A) a blog post with no author listed | B) a forum comment from a stranger | C) a report published by a national weather agency | D) a cartoon about weather
why correct: A national agency has scientists and reviews its own data before publishing it.
tip: Look for sources backed by experts and institutions.

stem: Tamer found two sources that disagree about when a bridge was built. What should he do?
options / answer: A) Guess which one sounds more official. | B) Use both dates in the same sentence without checking. | C) Pick the date he likes better. | D) Check a third reliable source to see which date is supported
why correct: A third source can help confirm which date most evidence supports.
tip: When sources disagree, look for a tie-breaking source.

stem: When you take exact words from a source and use quotation marks, you are ____ the text.
options / answer: A) skimming | B) quoting | C) paraphrasing
why correct: Quoting means copying someone's exact words and marking them with quotation marks.
tip: Quotation marks always signal someone's exact words.

stem: Which is an example of plagiarism?
options / answer: A) Copying a paragraph from a website without quoting or crediting it | B) Summarizing an article in your own words. | C) Quoting a sentence and naming the source. | D) Listing the website in your bibliography.
why correct: Using someone's exact words as if they were your own, with no credit, is plagiarism.
tip: Always quote or paraphrase, and always give credit.

stem: Which question is too broad to research in one short report?
options / answer: A) Why do coral reefs need sunlight? | B) What is the ocean? | C) How do clownfish protect themselves from predators? | D) How deep can a sea turtle dive?
why correct: A topic as large as 'the ocean' cannot be fully answered in a short report.
tip: Narrow a broad topic into a specific question.

stem: Yusuf wants facts about a local museum's history. Which source should he trust most?
options / answer: A) an advertisement for museum tickets | B) a rumor he heard from a classmate | C) an article from the museum's official history page | D) a tourist's one-star review
why correct: The museum's own history page is written by people with direct knowledge of its history.
tip: Go to the organization itself for facts about itself.

stem: Which sentence correctly paraphrases the source sentence 'Bees communicate through a dance called the waggle dance' without copying it word-for-word?
options / answer: A) Bees communicate through a dance called the waggle dance. | B) Bees dance. | C) The waggle dance is danced by bees who communicate. | D) Bees use a special dance, called the waggle dance, to share information.
why correct: A good paraphrase keeps the meaning but uses different wording and sentence structure.
tip: Say the idea aloud in your own words before writing it down.

stem: Match each type of source to its example.
options / answer: primary source = a letter written by a soldier | secondary source = a history book written years later | reliable website = a university research page | unreliable website = a page with no author and many ads
why correct: Knowing these categories helps you judge how much to trust a source.
tip: Ask who wrote it, when, and why before trusting a source.

stem: Reading only the title of an article is enough to know if it answers your research question.
options / answer: True | False
why correct: A title only hints at the topic; you must read enough of the article to check it truly answers your question.
