stem: Read: “Coral reefs are home to colorful fish, sea turtles, and tiny shrimp. The coral itself looks like branching rock but is actually built by millions of tiny living animals. Reefs also shelter young fish from larger predators.” What is this paragraph mostly about?

tip: Ask what single topic every sentence describes.

stem: Choose the best word: “Coral reefs shelter fish. ____, they protect young sea turtles.”
options / answer: A) Furthermore | B) Finally | C) Therefore | D) Unlike
why correct: “Furthermore” adds another fact about what reefs protect.
tip: Also/furthermore/in addition add more description.

stem: Read: “A volcano is a mountain with an opening that can release melted rock called lava. options / answer: A) Some volcanoes stay quiet for hundreds of years. | B) Thick clouds of ash sometimes rise from the opening. | C) The ground around it can tremble before an eruption. | D) A volcano is a mountain with an opening that can release lava.
why correct: This sentence specifically describes the trembling ground.
tip: Match each detail to exactly what it is describing.

stem: A classmate claims the volcano paragraph above narrates a single eruption from start to finish, step by step. Is the classmate right?
options / answer: True | False
why correct: The paragraph lists general facts about volcanoes, not a single eruption unfolding in order.
tip: Description gives facts; sequence tells a time-ordered story.

stem: Read: “A bicycle has two wheels connected by a frame, with pedals that turn a chain to move the back wheel. Handlebars let the rider steer, and brakes squeeze the wheels to slow down. stem: Read the paragraph above about bicycles. Which detail explains how a bicycle's gears help the rider?
options / answer: A) Some bicycles also have gears to make hills easier to climb. | B) Handlebars let the rider steer. | C) A bicycle has two wheels connected by a frame. | D) Brakes squeeze the wheels to slow down.
why correct: This sentence specifically explains what the gears are for.
tip: Match the question to the exact detail that answers it.

stem: Read: “A lighthouse is a tall tower built near dangerous coastlines. A bright, rotating light at the top warns ships of rocks below. Many lighthouses also have a foghorn that sounds when visibility is poor.” Which statement best explains the structure of this paragraph?
options / answer: A) It explains why lighthouses are no longer used today. | B) It lists separate features of a lighthouse and what each one does for ships. | C) It compares lighthouses built in different countries. | D) It tells a story about a ship that crashed near a lighthouse.

tip: Count how many separate features are described about the subject.

stem: Read the paragraph above about lighthouses. Which detail tells how the lighthouse warns ships in fog?
options / answer: A) A bright, rotating light at the top warns ships of rocks below. | B) Lighthouses are painted in bright colors. | C) Many lighthouses also have a foghorn that sounds when visibility is poor. | D) A lighthouse is a tall tower built near dangerous coastlines.

tip: Find the sentence that matches the exact condition asked about.

stem: Read: “Tropical rainforests are warm and extremely wet, with rain falling almost every day. Tall trees form a thick canopy that blocks most sunlight from reaching the ground. tip: Ask what single place or thing every sentence is about.

stem: Match each rainforest detail with what it describes.
options / answer: Rain falling almost every day = the climate | A thick canopy of tall trees = the plant layers | Thousands of species living there = the animal life
why correct: Each detail describes a different part of the rainforest.
tip: Sort details by what part of the topic they belong to.

stem: Read: “Most spiders have eight legs and two body sections. Many spin silk webs to trap insects, while others hunt their prey by chasing it. Spider silk is extremely strong for its thin size.” Which detail describes how some spiders catch food?
options / answer: A) Many spin silk webs to trap insects, while others hunt their prey by chasing it. | B) Spider silk is extremely strong for its thin size. | C) Most spiders have eight legs and two body sections. | D) Spiders live mostly in cold climates.

tip: Find the sentence that directly answers the question asked.

stem: Choose the best word: “A spider has eight legs. ____, it has two main body sections.”
options / answer: A) Next | B) Additionally | C) Instead | D) So
why correct: “Additionally” adds another physical detail about the spider.

stem: Read: “A bakery fills its shelves with warm loaves of bread, flaky pastries, and sweet cakes. The smell of fresh dough drifts through the open door, and large ovens hum in the back room. stem: Read the paragraph above about the bakery. Which detail appeals to the reader's sense of smell?
options / answer: A) Warm loaves of bread, flaky pastries, and sweet cakes fill the shelves. | B) Bakers knead dough early each morning. | C) The smell of fresh dough drifts through the open door. | D) Large ovens hum in the back room.

tip: Look for words naming what you would smell, see, or hear.

stem: Read: “A freight train pulls dozens of long cars loaded with coal, grain, or steel. Powerful engines at the front provide the strength to pull such heavy loads. Loud horns warn nearby cars and pedestrians at crossings.” Which detail describes how the train warns people nearby?

why correct: This sentence directly describes the horn as a warning.
tip: Match the question to the exact detail that answers it.

stem: Someone argues the freight-train paragraph above is built from general facts rather than from a story about one particular trip. Do you agree?
options / answer: True | False
why correct: The sentences give general facts about freight trains, not a single timed event.
tip: Facts about a subject in general signal a description structure.

stem: Read: “Many mosques have a tall tower called a minaret, where the call to prayer can be heard. Inside, patterned carpets cover the floor, and arched doorways lead into a large open hall. options / answer: A) Domes on the roof help carry sound throughout the building. | B) Patterned carpets cover the floor. | C) Arched doorways lead into a large open hall. | D) Many mosques have a tall tower called a minaret.

tip: Check which part of the building each detail belongs to.

stem: Match each mosque feature with what it is used for.
options / answer: minaret = calling people to prayer | carpets = covering the floor | domes = carrying sound
why correct: Each architectural feature has its own descriptive purpose.
tip: Pair each feature with its function.

stem: Read: “A glacier is a huge, slow-moving sheet of ice formed from packed snow. Deep cracks called crevasses can form as the ice moves over uneven ground. tip: Ask why the author added each extra fact about the topic.

stem: Choose the best word: “A glacier moves slowly over land. ____, it can carve out deep valleys.”
options / answer: A) Because | B) However | C) On top of that | D) Before

tip: Also/in addition/on top of that add more description.

stem: Read: “An orchard is a large area planted with rows of fruit trees such as apple, orange, or fig trees. Bees fly between the blossoms, helping the trees produce fruit. Workers pick the ripe fruit by hand each season.” Which sentence structure best describes how this paragraph is organized?
options / answer: A) It explains the cause of poor fruit harvests. | B) It narrates one specific day of picking fruit. | C) It lists separate facts about the trees, the bees, and the workers in an orchard. | D) It compares an orchard to a vegetable garden.

options / answer: A) pact | B) parent | C) panic | D) palace
why correct: “Panic” falls alphabetically between “pamphlet” and “parade.”
tip: Compare letter by letter after the matching guide-word start.

stem: Put these words in the order they would appear in a dictionary.
options / answer: sequence → serene → serious → settle → seven
why correct: Compare letters one by one: seq, ser(e), ser(i), set, sev.
tip: When the first letters match, compare the next different letter.

stem: You need several paragraphs of background information about the history of the Roman Empire, not just a short definition. Which resource is the better choice?
options / answer: A) A thesaurus, because it lists many related words | B) A dictionary, because it lists every meaning of every word | C) A glossary, because it only covers words from one book | D) An encyclopedia, because it gives detailed explanations rather than brief definitions
why correct: An encyclopedia provides detailed, multi-paragraph explanations of topics, unlike a brief dictionary definition.
tip: Choose an encyclopedia when you need depth, not just a quick definition.

stem: A dictionary app suggests “photosynthesis” as soon as you type “photo.” What is the main benefit of this autocomplete feature?
options / answer: A) It helps you find and spell long or difficult words more quickly | B) It replaces the need to read the definition once you find the word | C) It only works for very short, simple words | D) It automatically defines every word you have ever searched for
why correct: Autocomplete speeds up finding long or hard-to-spell words.
tip: Use autocomplete to save time looking up tricky spellings.

stem: A dictionary respelling shows “dic·tion·ar·y (DIK-shuh-ner-ee).” Which syllable receives the primary stress?
options / answer: A) ee | B) DIK | C) shuh | D) ner
why correct: Capital letters in a respelling show the syllable with the primary stress.
tip: Look for the capitalized syllable to find the stressed part of a word.

stem: A dictionary shows “ob·ject (noun) OB-jekt: a thing; ob·ject (verb) ob-JEKT: to disagree.” Which pronunciation fits “Many parents object to the new school schedule”?
options / answer: A) Both pronunciations fit equally well here | B) OB-jekt, because here “object” is used as a noun | C) ob-JEKT, because here “object” is used as a verb meaning to disagree | D) Neither pronunciation fits, since this must be a typo
why correct: Used as a verb meaning to disagree, “object” is pronounced ob-JEKT.
tip: Check the part of speech to choose the correct pronunciation.

stem: “The stars winked at us from the night sky.” Which type of figurative language is this, and why?
options / answer: A) Hyperbole, because it is a wild exaggeration | B) Idiom, because it is a common saying with a hidden meaning | C) Simile, because it compares two things using “like” or “as” | D) Personification, because the stars are given the human action of winking.
why correct: Giving the stars the human action of winking is personification.
tip: Personification gives human actions or feelings to something non-human.

stem: “Her tears fell like rain.” What does this simile help the reader understand?
options / answer: A) That she was crying heavily, with many tears falling | B) That it was raining outside while she cried | C) That she stopped crying suddenly | D) That her tears were cold like rain
why correct: Comparing tears to rain shows that many tears fell steadily.
tip: In a simile, think about what quality the two things share.

stem: “I asked a million questions before the test.” What does this hyperbole mean?
options / answer: A) She was too shy to ask any questions | B) She asked many questions, even though she did not ask exactly one million | C) She asked exactly one million questions | D) She asked one short question
why correct: Hyperbole uses an obvious exaggeration to show that she asked a lot of questions.
tip: Hyperbole exaggerates to make a strong impression, not to state a fact.

stem: “The classroom was a zoo during the fire drill.” What does this metaphor suggest?
options / answer: A) The classroom actually contained animals | B) The classroom smelled bad | C) The classroom was noisy, chaotic, and hard to control | D) The classroom was calm and orderly
why correct: Comparing the classroom to a zoo suggests loud, chaotic behavior.
tip: A metaphor says one thing IS another to highlight a shared quality.

stem: “The giant stood like a mountain over the village.” Which type of figurative language is this, and why?
options / answer: A) Hyperbole, since the claim is wildly exaggerated | B) A metaphor, since one thing is called another thing directly | C) Personification, since a non-living thing acts human | D) Simile, because it uses “like” to compare the giant to a mountain.
why correct: The word “like” signals a direct comparison between the giant and a mountain.
tip: Look for “like” or “as” to spot a simile.

stem: “The old gate groaned as it opened.” What does this personification suggest?
options / answer: A) The gate made a loud, creaky sound, as if it were complaining | B) The gate was painted a dull gray color | C) The gate opened silently and smoothly | D) The gate opened by itself without anyone touching it
why correct: Giving the gate a human sound like groaning suggests it made a loud, unpleasant creak.
tip: Personification gives human actions or feelings to objects or animals.

stem: “The library was silent as a tomb, and the clock ticked like a patient heartbeat.” Which statement best explains how these two comparisons work together?
options / answer: A) Both comparisons suggest the library was crowded with people | B) Both comparisons build a picture of a still, hushed place where only a slow, steady sound can be heard | C) The first comparison shows noise, and the second shows silence, so they contradict each other | D) The comparisons describe how fast time was passing
why correct: Comparing the library to a tomb and the clock to a heartbeat both emphasize deep stillness broken only by one steady sound.
tip: When two comparisons appear together, look for what feeling or picture they build as a pair.

stem: True or false: This sentence contains a simile: “The kite danced in the wind.”
options / answer: True | False
why correct: There is no “like” or “as” comparing the kite to something else; giving the kite the human action of dancing makes this personification, not a simile.
tip: A simile always uses “like” or “as” to compare two things.

stem: Choose the best word to complete the simile: “The ice was as ____ as glass.”
options / answer: A) loud | B) smooth | C) happy | D) heavy
why correct: Glass is known for being smooth, so this word completes the simile's comparison.
tip: A good simile compares a quality the two things truly share.

stem: “The news spread through the school like wildfire.” What does this simile show?
options / answer: A) That the news was kept secret | B) That very few people heard the news | C) That the news spread extremely quickly to many people | D) That the news was about an actual fire
why correct: Wildfire spreads fast and widely, so this simile shows the news reached many people quickly.
tip: Think about the well-known quality of the second thing in a simile.

stem: “The wind argued with the trees all night.” Which type of figurative language is this, and why?
options / answer: A) Hyperbole, because it describes an impossible exaggeration | B) Idiom, because it is a well-known saying | C) Simile, because it uses “like” or “as” to compare two things | D) Personification, because the wind is described doing the human action of arguing.
why correct: Giving the wind the human action of arguing is personification.
tip: Personification gives human actions, thoughts, or feelings to something non-human.

stem: “Her mind was a locked door when asked about the accident.” What does this metaphor suggest?
options / answer: A) She refused to share any information about the accident | B) She had forgotten everything about the accident | C) She had never heard about the accident | D) She was eager to explain every detail of the accident
why correct: Comparing her mind to a locked door suggests she is deliberately keeping information from others.
tip: A metaphor replaces one thing with another to highlight a shared quality — here, being closed off.

stem: “I could sleep for a hundred years after that race.” What does this hyperbole mean?
options / answer: A) She felt too energized to sleep at all after the race | B) She was extremely tired after the race | C) She finished the race in record time | D) She actually planned to sleep for a hundred years
why correct: The impossible exaggeration of sleeping for a hundred years shows how exhausted she felt.
tip: Hyperbole exaggerates far beyond reality to express a strong feeling.

stem: “Her voice was a melody that calmed the whole room.” Which type of figurative language is this, and why?
options / answer: A) Personification, because an object is given human traits | B) Hyperbole, because it describes an impossible exaggeration | C) Metaphor, because her voice is directly called a melody without using “like” or “as.” | D) Simile, because it compares two things using “like” or “as”
why correct: Saying her voice IS a melody, without “like” or “as,” makes this a metaphor.
tip: A metaphor states that one thing is another thing.

stem: “The old computer wheezed and groaned before finally starting.” What does this personification suggest?
options / answer: A) The computer was brand new | B) The computer started instantly and silently | C) The computer played music when it started | D) The computer made rough, labored sounds, as if it were struggling to start
why correct: Giving the computer human sounds like wheezing and groaning suggests it struggled to start, like an exhausted person.
tip: Personification can make a machine seem tired or unwell.

stem: The author compares the approaching storm to “a wolf prowling closer every hour.” What does this comparison suggest about the storm?
options / answer: A) That the storm felt slow but threatening, like a predator stalking its prey | B) That the storm was moving away from the area | C) That the storm arrived suddenly without warning | D) That the storm was harmless and gentle
why correct: Comparing the storm to a prowling wolf suggests a slow, patient, and dangerous approach.
tip: Think about what qualities the comparison's second image usually has.

stem: True or false: This sentence contains personification: “The shy moon peeked from behind the clouds.”
options / answer: True | False
why correct: Giving the moon the human qualities of shyness and peeking is personification.
tip: Personification gives human feelings or actions to something non-human.

stem: Choose the best word to complete the simile: “The crowd roared as loud as ____.”
options / answer: A) a feather | B) a whisper | C) thunder | D) silence
why correct: Thunder is known for being extremely loud, which fits the roaring crowd.
tip: Pick a comparison word that is famous for the exact quality you need.

stem: “Life is a winding road full of unexpected turns.” What does this metaphor mean?
options / answer: A) Life is literally shaped like a road | B) Life has many unpredictable changes and challenges along the way | C) Life stays the same without any changes | D) Life always follows a straight, easy path
why correct: Comparing life to a winding road highlights the unexpected changes and challenges people face.
tip: In an extended metaphor, think about what the whole comparison represents.

stem: “Fear is a shadow that follows without a sound.” Which type of figurative language is this, and why?
options / answer: A) Hyperbole, since the statement exaggerates wildly | B) Personification, since a lifeless thing is acting human | C) A metaphor, since the feeling fear is called a shadow outright. | D) A simile, since a connecting word sets up the comparison
why correct: Saying fear IS a shadow, without “like” or “as,” makes this a metaphor.
tip: A metaphor states directly that one thing is another.

stem: “This backpack weighs a ton.” What does this hyperbole mean?
options / answer: A) The backpack actually weighs 2,000 pounds | B) The backpack is completely empty | C) The backpack is a normal, light weight | D) The backpack feels extremely heavy, though it does not literally weigh a ton
why correct: Saying the backpack weighs a ton is an obvious exaggeration to show how heavy it feels.
tip: Hyperbole uses impossible numbers or claims to stress a feeling.

stem: “The city never sleeps, its lights blinking through the night.” What does this personification suggest?
options / answer: A) The city stays active and lively through the night, without truly stopping | B) The city only has activity during the day | C) The city's lights turn off automatically at night | D) The city is completely empty after dark
why correct: Giving the city the human trait of never sleeping suggests constant nighttime activity.
tip: Personification can describe a place as if it has human habits like sleeping.

stem: “Her excuses dissolved like sugar in hot tea.” Which type of figurative language is this, and why?
options / answer: A) Metaphor, because it states one thing is another without “like” or “as” | B) Simile, because it uses “like” to compare her excuses dissolving to sugar dissolving in tea. | C) Hyperbole, because it describes an impossible exaggeration | D) Personification, because an object is given human traits
why correct: The word “like” signals a direct comparison between her excuses disappearing and sugar dissolving.
tip: Look for “like” or “as” to spot a simile.

stem: The author describes the old oak tree as “a silent witness to a hundred years of change.” What does this personification suggest about the tree?
options / answer: A) That the tree has changed its own location many times | B) That the tree is younger than it appears | C) That the tree has stood through many years of history without being able to speak about what it has seen | D) That the tree can actually talk about the past
why correct: Calling the tree a silent witness suggests it has observed a century of change without being able to tell anyone about it.
tip: Personification can suggest a long, quiet history for something non-human.

stem: “The soldier's courage was a flame that no storm could extinguish, burning quietly even in the coldest nights.” Which statement best explains how the metaphor and the idea of persistence work together here?
options / answer: A) The storm represents the soldier's own doubts about fighting | B) The metaphor suggests the soldier's courage depended on warm weather | C) The flame metaphor shows that the soldier's courage eventually burned out completely | D) The flame metaphor shows that the soldier's courage stayed steady and strong no matter how difficult or discouraging things became
why correct: Comparing courage to an unextinguishable flame burning through storms and cold nights emphasizes that it remained steady despite hardship.
tip: When a metaphor is extended with more details, each detail should strengthen the same main idea.

stem: True or false: This sentence contains a hyperbole: “I nearly died of embarrassment when I tripped in the hallway.”
options / answer: True | False
why correct: Saying she “nearly died” of embarrassment is an obvious exaggeration, which is hyperbole.
tip: Hyperbole uses extreme, impossible language to express a strong feeling.

stem: Choose the best word to complete the simile: “The debate became as tense as a ____ about to snap.”
options / answer: A) pillow | B) feather | C) cloud | D) rubber band
why correct: A rubber band stretched to its limit captures the feeling of extreme tension right before something breaks.
tip: Pick a comparison that is known for being able to “snap” under tension.

stem: Read: “Everyone cheered when the carnival came to town, but Yusuf stayed home because loud crowds made him anxious.” What is Yusuf's perspective on the carnival?
options / answer: A) He feels uneasy about crowded, noisy events, unlike most people. | B) He thinks the carnival is boring. | C) He does not know the carnival is happening. | D) He is excited to go to the carnival with his friends.
why correct: Yusuf's choice to stay home because of loud crowds shows he feels anxious in that situation, unlike everyone who cheered.
tip: Look at a character's actions and the reason given for them to find their perspective.

stem: Read: “The teacher said the field trip was canceled due to rain, but Mariam smiled because she had forgotten her permission slip anyway.” True or false: Mariam is disappointed by the news like the rest of the class.
options / answer: True | False
why correct: Mariam smiled at the news, showing relief rather than disappointment, because she would not have been able to go anyway.
tip: Compare a character's reaction to what you would expect, to notice a different perspective.

stem: Read: “Khalid thought the broken clock should be thrown away, but his sister Rania wanted to keep it on the shelf because their grandfather had given it to her.” How is Rania's perspective different from Khalid's?
options / answer: A) Rania does not know who gave her the clock. | B) Rania values the clock for its connection to their grandfather, while Khalid only sees it as broken and useless. | C) Khalid also wants to keep the clock for sentimental reasons. | D) Rania thinks the clock still works perfectly.
why correct: Khalid judges the clock only by its condition, while Rania values its sentimental connection to their grandfather.
tip: Two characters can view the same object differently based on what it means to them.

stem: Read: “Adham groaned when the coach announced extra practice, but Dina punched the air with excitement because she loved any chance to improve her serve.” What is Dina's perspective on the extra practice?
options / answer: A) She is upset about having to miss her other plans. | B) She agrees with Adham that the extra practice is unwelcome. | C) She is excited about the extra practice because it gives her more time to improve a skill she cares about. | D) She does not care about volleyball or her serve.
why correct: Dina's excited reaction shows she values the extra chance to practice, unlike Adham.
tip: Contrasting reactions to the same event reveal different perspectives.

stem: Read: “Zain's mother called the thunderstorm beautiful and powerful, but Zain hid under his blanket, convinced the loud booms meant something terrible was about to happen.” How do Zain and his mother see the thunderstorm differently?
options / answer: A) Neither of them notices the thunderstorm happening. | B) Zain thinks the storm is beautiful, just like his mother. | C) Zain's mother is also frightened by the thunder. | D) His mother admires the storm's power, while Zain feels frightened and expects something bad to happen.
why correct: The mother's admiration contrasts with Zain's fear, showing two different perspectives on the same storm.
tip: Opposite feelings about the same event point to different perspectives.

stem: A story about a lost puppy is told only from the puppy's owner's point of view. How would the story change if it were also told from the puppy's point of view?
options / answer: A) Readers would also learn what the puppy was thinking and feeling while it was lost, not just the owner's worry. | B) The story would no longer include the puppy at all. | C) The owner's feelings would no longer matter to the story. | D) The events of the story would completely change.
why correct: Adding another character's point of view adds their inner thoughts and feelings to the story, without erasing the original viewpoint.
tip: Think about what new feelings or thoughts a different point of view would reveal.

stem: A class trip story is told only through Hassan's diary entries. How would readers' understanding of the trip change if Hassan's teacher's diary entries were added?
options / answer: A) Readers would lose Hassan's original thoughts about the trip. | B) Readers would see the trip from an adult's perspective too, which might reveal concerns or plans Hassan never noticed. | C) The events of the trip itself would change. | D) Readers would only learn the exact same information twice.
why correct: A second point of view, like the teacher's, often reveals thoughts, worries, or details the first narrator did not notice.
tip: A new point of view usually adds information the original narrator could not have known or noticed.

stem: Read: “Everyone groaned when the museum guide announced a two-hour lecture, but Lina leaned forward eagerly, since she loved learning the history behind every object.” What is Lina's perspective on the lecture?
options / answer: A) She is bored and wants to leave early. | B) She does not understand what the lecture is about. | C) She is eager and interested because she enjoys learning historical details. | D) She agrees with everyone else that the lecture is too long.
why correct: Lina's eager reaction shows she enjoys the historical details, unlike the rest of the group.
tip: Notice when a character's reaction is different from everyone else's.

stem: Read: “Karim's older brother said moving to a new city would be a great adventure, but Karim cried in his room because he did not want to leave his friends behind.” True or false: Karim shares his brother's excited view of the move.
options / answer: True | False
why correct: Karim feels upset about leaving his friends, which is the opposite of his brother's excitement about an adventure.
tip: A character's actions, like crying, often reveal their true feelings.

stem: Read: “Salma thought the old, dusty attic looked spooky and unwelcoming, but her cousin Nadia thought it looked like the perfect hideout for secret adventures.” How is Nadia's perspective different from Salma's?
options / answer: A) Neither girl has an opinion about the attic. | B) Salma thinks the attic would make a great hideout too. | C) Nadia also finds the attic frightening. | D) Nadia sees the attic as exciting and full of possibility, while Salma sees it as scary and unpleasant.
why correct: Nadia's excitement about secret adventures contrasts with Salma's fear of the spooky attic.
tip: The same place can seem very different depending on who is looking at it.

stem: Read: “The coach called the tournament loss a disappointing result, but Hassan smiled, proud that his team had improved so much since the season began.” What is Hassan's perspective on the loss?
options / answer: A) He focuses on his team's improvement and feels proud, rather than only seeing the loss as disappointing. | B) He is embarrassed that his team lost the tournament. | C) He thinks the team did not improve at all this season. | D) He agrees completely with the coach that the result was only disappointing.
why correct: Hassan sees the loss through the lens of his team's progress, giving him a more positive perspective than the coach's.
tip: A character can focus on a different part of the same event to form a different perspective.

stem: Read: “Dina's father said the city's new noisy construction site was a sign of exciting progress, but Dina covered her ears and wished for the quiet park that used to be there.” How do Dina and her father see the construction site differently?
options / answer: A) Dina's father also dislikes the noise from the construction. | B) Her father views it hopefully as progress, while Dina misses the quiet park and dislikes the noise. | C) Neither of them has noticed the construction site yet. | D) Dina is excited about the new construction, just like her father.
why correct: The father's hopeful view of progress contrasts with Dina's longing for the quiet park that used to be there.
tip: A change can feel like progress to one person and a loss to another.

stem: Read: “Everyone congratulated Hana on winning the debate, but she quietly wondered if she had only won because her opponent seemed nervous.” What is Hana's perspective on her win?
options / answer: A) She believes she definitely lost the debate. | B) She feels completely confident that she won fairly. | C) She feels uncertain about whether she truly deserved the win. | D) She is angry at her opponent for losing.
why correct: Hana's private doubt about her opponent's nervousness shows she questions whether her win was fully deserved.
tip: A character's private thoughts can reveal a different perspective than their public reaction.

stem: Read: “The principal announced that uniforms would now be required, calling it a step toward fairness among students. Yusra argued it would only hide the real differences in students' lives outside school.” How does Yusra's perspective differ from the principal's?
options / answer: A) The principal also doubts that uniforms will help. | B) Yusra has no opinion about the new uniform policy. | C) Yusra agrees that uniforms create true fairness among students. | D) Yusra believes uniforms only mask inequality rather than truly solving it, unlike the principal's view of fairness.
why correct: Yusra sees the policy as a surface-level fix, while the principal sees it as a genuine step toward fairness.
tip: Look for the reasoning behind each character's opinion, not just whether they agree or disagree.

stem: Read: “Samir's coach praised his aggressive playing style as determined, but Samir's teammate Lina thought it was reckless and put the team at risk.” How do Lina and the coach view Samir's playing style differently?
options / answer: A) The coach sees determination in his style, while Lina sees it as risky and careless. | B) Neither of them has an opinion about how Samir plays. | C) Lina also admires Samir's playing style as determined. | D) The coach also worries that Samir's style is too risky.
why correct: The same aggressive style is read as admirable determination by the coach and as careless risk by Lina.
tip: The same behavior can be judged very differently depending on a person's priorities.

stem: Read: “Dina's grandmother spoke fondly of the old neighborhood before it was rebuilt, remembering the noisy markets and narrow streets. Dina, who had only seen photos, found the new wide avenues and modern shops far more appealing.” How is Dina's perspective different from her grandmother's?
options / answer: A) Dina also wishes the old noisy markets had never been replaced. | B) Dina appreciates the modern changes she has grown up with, while her grandmother misses the neighborhood's earlier character. | C) Dina's grandmother prefers the new modern shops over the old markets. | D) Neither of them has any opinion about the neighborhood's changes.
why correct: Having only known the new neighborhood, Dina values its modern features, while her grandmother's memories make her miss what was lost.
tip: A person's own experience, even secondhand through photos or stories, shapes their perspective.

stem: Read: “The scientist explained that the experiment's failure provided valuable data about what did not work, while the new intern saw only a wasted afternoon.” How do the scientist and the intern view the failed experiment differently?
options / answer: A) The intern also sees the failure as valuable information. | B) Neither of them reacts to the experiment's result. | C) The scientist values the failure as useful information, while the intern sees it only as wasted time. | D) The scientist agrees that the afternoon was wasted.
why correct: Experience lets the scientist see value in a failed result that the less experienced intern views only as lost time.
tip: A person's experience with a situation can shape whether they see a setback as useful or wasted.

stem: A story about a difficult hiking trip is narrated only by the group's most experienced hiker. How might readers' understanding change if it were also narrated by the least experienced hiker in the group?
options / answer: A) Both narrators would notice and feel exactly the same things. | B) Readers would lose all the details the experienced hiker already shared. | C) The actual events of the hiking trip would be completely different. | D) Readers would also learn about struggles, fears, or doubts that the experienced hiker might not have noticed or felt as strongly.
why correct: A less experienced narrator would likely notice difficulties and fears that a confident, experienced hiker might overlook.
tip: A character's background and experience shape what they notice and how they feel.

stem: A historical event is described in a textbook mainly through the decisions of a king, with little mention of ordinary villagers. How would adding a villager's account change readers' understanding of the event?
options / answer: A) Readers would see how the king's decisions actually affected daily life for ordinary people, not just the decisions themselves. | B) Readers would learn nothing new from the villager's account. | C) The king's decisions would no longer be part of the story. | D) The historical facts of what happened would change completely.
why correct: A villager's account would reveal the everyday human impact of the king's decisions, adding depth the textbook's focus on the king alone misses.
tip: Whose perspective a text centers shapes which effects and feelings get mentioned.

stem: Read: “Everyone at the party admired the tall, elaborate cake, but Reem, the baker's younger sister, only saw the uneven frosting she had tried and failed to smooth out.” What is Reem's perspective on the cake?
options / answer: A) She thinks the cake looks perfect, just like everyone else. | B) She focuses critically on a flaw others do not notice, because she knows how it was made. | C) She does not care about the cake at all. | D) She believes the cake is the ugliest one she has ever seen.
why correct: Knowing the effort and mistakes behind the cake, Reem notices a flaw that guests, who only see the finished result, miss entirely.
tip: Someone close to how something was made often notices different details than an outside observer.

stem: Read: “The manager called the store's slow afternoon a chance to reorganize the shelves calmly, while the new cashier found the empty hours boring and worried about losing hours.” True or false: The manager and the cashier share the same positive view of the slow afternoon.
options / answer: True | False
why correct: The manager sees the slow afternoon positively as a chance to reorganize, while the cashier finds it boring and worries about losing work hours.
tip: Two people can experience the exact same situation with very different feelings.

stem: Read: “Omar's father insisted that saving every spare coin was simply responsible, while Omar, saving for a new bicycle, felt it was an unbearably slow way to reach his goal.” How is Omar's perspective different from his father's?
options / answer: A) Neither of them has an opinion about saving money. | B) Omar agrees that saving slowly is the responsible choice. | C) Omar feels impatient about the slow pace of saving, while his father views the same habit as simply being responsible. | D) Omar's father also feels impatient about saving slowly.
why correct: Omar's goal-driven impatience contrasts with his father's calm view of saving as simply a responsible habit.
tip: A specific goal, like buying a bicycle, can change how someone feels about a general habit.

stem: Read: “The travel writer described the crowded, chaotic market as full of vibrant energy and life, while a local shopkeeper, tired after a twelve-hour shift, only wished for a quiet moment to rest.” How do the travel writer and the shopkeeper see the market differently?
options / answer: A) The travel writer also wishes the market were quieter. | B) Neither of them has a reaction to the market's atmosphere. | C) The shopkeeper also finds the market's energy exciting and refreshing. | D) The writer admires the market's energy as an outsider, while the exhausted shopkeeper longs for the quiet the writer does not need.
why correct: A visitor experiencing the market briefly can enjoy its energy, while someone working there all day may simply feel exhausted by the same chaos.
tip: A short visit and a long workday can create very different perspectives on the same place.

stem: Read: “The committee praised the new policy as a quick, efficient solution, but the employee who would have to follow it every day worried it ignored small but important details of daily work.” How do the committee and the employee view the new policy differently?
options / answer: A) The committee sees the policy as efficient overall, while the employee worries it overlooks details that matter in daily practice. | B) Neither group has formed an opinion about the new policy. | C) The committee also worries about small daily details being ignored. | D) The employee also believes the policy is a perfect, efficient solution.
why correct: Those who design a policy from a distance may focus on overall efficiency, while those who must carry it out daily notice details that could cause problems.
tip: People closer to the daily impact of a decision often notice different concerns than those who made it.

stem: Read the pun: "The baker almost closed his shop, but a new recipe finally brought in more dough." Which word creates the double meaning?
options / answer: A) recipe | B) dough | C) baker | D) shop
why correct: “Dough” can mean bread dough or, informally, money, which is why the sentence is funny.
tip: A pun hides two meanings inside one word.

stem: Read the pun: "The river otter kept its savings at the bank, right on the river’s own bank." Which word creates the double meaning?
options / answer: A) river | B) savings | C) bank | D) otter
why correct: “Bank” can mean the edge of a river or a place to keep money.
tip: Look for the word that fits two different pictures.

stem: Read the pun: "The new puppy loved sitting under the old oak tree, barking at its own bark." Which word creates the double meaning?
options / answer: A) oak | B) puppy | C) tree | D) bark
why correct: “Bark” can mean the sound a dog makes or the covering of a tree trunk.
tip: Puns often hide a second meaning inside a common word.

stem: Read the pun: "The feather was so light that it floated straight up toward the light." Which word creates the double meaning?
options / answer: A) light | B) straight | C) feather | D) floated
why correct: “Light” can mean not heavy or a glowing source of brightness.

tip: “Despite” introduces an obstacle that did not stop the main action.

tip: Think about what normally happens when a living thing is missing something it needs.

tip: Look for details that show steady progress toward a goal.

why correct: Since this happens every time the bell rings, the same pattern is likely to repeat tomorrow.

why correct: Taking direct action—adding irrigation—right after the forecast shows he is actively preparing for dry weather.
tip: An action taken because of a clue is stronger evidence than the clue alone.

tip: “Whose” = belonging to whom; “who’s” = who is.

stem: Choose the correct word: “____ bringing the snacks today?”
options / answer: A) Whose | B) Who’se | C) Whos | D) Who’s
why correct: “Who’s” is the contraction for “who is,” which fits this question.
tip: Try replacing the word with “who is” to check if it still makes sense.

stem: Which sentence correctly shows the possessive of the name Chris?
options / answer: A) Chris’s backpack is on the bus. | B) Chrises backpack is on the bus. | C) Chris backpack is on the bus. | D) Chriss’ backpack is on the bus.
why correct: For a singular name ending in s, add ’s to show possession: Chris’s.
tip: Singular owner: add ’s, even if the name already ends in s.

stem: Choose the correct word: “The kitten hid beneath ____ favorite blanket.”
options / answer: A) its | B) it’s | C) it's’ | D) its’
why correct: “Its” shows that the blanket belongs to the kitten, with no apostrophe needed.
tip: “Its” with no apostrophe always shows ownership.

stem: Which sentence uses an apostrophe correctly?
options / answer: A) We could’nt find the children’s shoes. | B) We couldn’t find the children’s shoes. | C) We couldn’t find the childrens’ shoes. | D) We couldnt find the childrens shoes.
why correct: “Couldn’t” needs its apostrophe before the t, and “children’s” adds ’s because “children” is already plural without an s.
tip: Irregular plurals like “children” and “men” still just add ’s for possession.

stem: Choose the correct word: “The children lost ____ library books.”
options / answer: A) there | B) their | C) theirs | D) they’re
why correct: “Their” shows that the books belong to the children.
tip: “Their” shows ownership; “there” shows place; “they’re” means “they are.”

stem: Which sentence correctly fixes the error in: “The teams uniform's were in the van.”
options / answer: A) The teams uniforms were in the van. | B) The team’s uniform’s were in the van. | C) The team’s uniforms were in the van. | D) The teams’ uniform's were in the van.
why correct: “Team’s” shows ownership, while “uniforms” is just a plain plural and needs no apostrophe.
tip: Only add an apostrophe when a word shows ownership, never just because a word is plural.

stem: Which sentence correctly fixes the error in: “Its a shame the puppy hurt it’s paw.”
options / answer: A) It’s a shame the puppy hurt it’s paw. | B) Its a shame the puppy hurt its paw. | C) Its’ a shame the puppy hurt its’ paw. | D) It’s a shame the puppy hurt its paw.
why correct: “It’s” (it is) starts the sentence, and “its” (ownership) describes the puppy's own paw.
tip: “It’s” = it is. “Its” = belonging to it. “Its’” is never correct.

stem: In the sentence “The girls’ bikes were parked outside,” more than one girl owns a bike.
options / answer: True | False
why correct: The apostrophe after the s in “girls’” shows that the bikes belong to several girls.
tip: Apostrophe after a plural s usually signals more than one owner.

stem: Which sentence uses contractions and possessives correctly?
options / answer: A) We’re sure the cat’s bowl is empty again. | B) Were sure the cat’s bowl is empty again. | C) Were sure the cats bowl is empty again. | D) We’re sure the cats’ bowl is empty again.
why correct: “We’re” means “we are,” and “cat’s” correctly shows the bowl belongs to one cat.
tip: Read each short word aloud as its full form to check it fits the sentence.

stem: Choose the contraction for “should not”: “You ____ run near the pool.”
options / answer: A) should’n’t | B) should’nt | C) shouldn’t | D) shouldnt
why correct: “Should not” contracts to “shouldn’t,” with the apostrophe replacing the o.
tip: The apostrophe in “not” contractions almost always sits right before the final t.

stem: Which sentence correctly shows that MORE THAN ONE sister shares a bedroom?
options / answer: A) My sisters bedroom is upstairs. | B) My sisters’ bedroom is upstairs. | C) My sisters’s bedroom is upstairs. | D) My sister’s bedroom is upstairs.
why correct: Since “sisters” already ends in s, the possessive for the plural owners is formed by adding only an apostrophe: sisters’.
tip: Plural noun already ending in s: add just an apostrophe, no extra s.

stem: Write the contraction for “would have”: “If I had known, I ____ called sooner.”
options / answer: (typed)
why correct: “Would have” contracts to “would’ve,” with the apostrophe replacing “ha.”
tip: Be careful not to write “would of,” which is an incorrect spelling of this contraction.

stem: Choose the correct word: “The museum changed ____ opening hours.”
options / answer: A) their | B) it’s | C) its’ | D) its
why correct: “Its” shows that the opening hours belong to the museum, with no apostrophe.
tip: If you can swap in “it is” and the sentence still makes sense, use “it’s”; otherwise use “its.”

stem: Which sentence correctly fixes the error in: “The childrens coats were soaked.”
options / answer: A) The childrens’ coats were soaked. | B) The childs coats were soaked. | C) The children’s coats were soaked. | D) The childrens's coats were soaked.
why correct: “Children” is an irregular plural that does not end in s, so its possessive simply adds ’s: children’s.
tip: Irregular plurals (children, men, women, people) add ’s even though they are already plural.

stem: Tap the part of the sentence that has an error.
options / answer: The jurys |  verdict |  shocked |  the courtroom.
why correct: Only one jury reached the verdict, so the singular possessive “jury’s” is needed.
tip: If there is a single owner, add ’s, even when the owner's name ends in a vowel sound.

stem: Choose the correct word: “The two scientists shared ____ research notes.”
options / answer: A) their | B) there | C) theirs | D) they’re
why correct: “Their” shows that the research notes belong to the two scientists.
tip: “Their” shows ownership; “they’re” means “they are”; “there” points to a place.

stem: Which sentence correctly fixes the error in: “Its unclear whose going to lead the project.”
options / answer: A) It’s unclear whose going to lead the project. | B) Its unclear whose going to lead the project. | C) It's unclear who's going to lead the project. | D) It’s unclear who’s going to lead the project.
why correct: “It’s” means “it is,” and “who’s” means “who is”; both fit the meaning of this sentence.
tip: Test each word by replacing it with its full two-word form.

stem: Choose the correct word: “Each team practiced ____ routine for weeks.”
options / answer: A) theirs | B) its | C) their | D) it’s
why correct: “Each team,” though made of many people, is treated as one unit, so the singular possessive “its” is correct.
tip: Words like “each” and “every” usually take a singular pronoun.

stem: Which sentence correctly shows a possessive for a plural noun that does NOT end in s?
options / answer: A) The geese’s nests were hidden in the reeds. | B) The gooses’ nests were hidden in the reeds. | C) The geese nests were hidden in the reeds. | D) The geeses’ nests were hidden in the reeds.
why correct: “Geese” is already plural without an s, so its possessive adds ’s: geese’s.
tip: First find the correct plural form, then add ’s if it does not already end in s.

stem: Tap the part of the sentence that has an error.
options / answer: The companys |  profits |  rose |  sharply this year.
why correct: Only one company earned the profits, so the singular possessive “company’s” is needed.
tip: Check whether the apostrophe is missing entirely before deciding where it goes.

stem: Choose the contraction for “I would”: “____ rather walk than wait for the bus.”
options / answer: A) Id | B) I’ld | C) I’d | D) I’d’ve
why correct: “I would” contracts to “I’d.”
tip: “I’d” can mean “I would” or “I had” — check the context to be sure which one fits.

stem: Which sentence correctly fixes the error in: “Theyre bringing there own lunch to the picnic.”
options / answer: A) They’re bringing they’re own lunch to the picnic. | B) They’re bringing their own lunch to the picnic. | C) Their bringing their own lunch to the picnic. | D) There bringing there own lunch to the picnic.
why correct: “They’re” means “they are,” and “their” shows that the lunch belongs to them.
tip: They’re = they are. Their = belonging to them. There = a place.

stem: Which sentence correctly fixes the error in: “The witness’ story didnt match the officers’ report.”
options / answer: A) The witnesses story didn’t match the officers report. | B) The witness’s story didn’t match the officers’ report. | C) The witness’s story didn’t match the officer’s report. | D) The witness’ story didnt match the officer’s report.
why correct: “Witness’s” and “officer’s” each show a single owner, and “didn’t” needs its apostrophe for the missing letter o.
tip: Check possessives and contractions separately; a sentence can have errors in both.

stem: In the sentence “The babies’ toys were scattered across the floor,” the apostrophe shows that more than one baby owns toys.
options / answer: True | False
why correct: “Baby” becomes “babies” in the plural, and adding an apostrophe after the s shows plural possession: babies’.
tip: Form the plural first, then add the apostrophe based on whether it already ends in s.

stem: Write the contraction for “you are not”: “____ allowed to park here after six.”
options / answer: (typed)
correct: You're not / You’re not / you're not / you’re not
why correct: “You are” contracts to “you’re,” and the word “not” stays separate to make “you’re not.”
tip: Only the “you are” part contracts; “not” is not shortened in this phrase.

stem: Which sentence demonstrates correct use of BOTH a contraction and a possessive?
options / answer: A) She has’nt finished reading her brother’s favorite book yet. | B) She hasnt finished reading her brothers favorite book yet. | C) She hasn’t finished reading her brothers’ favorite book yet. | D) She hasn’t finished reading her brother’s favorite book yet.
why correct: “Hasn’t” correctly contracts “has not,” and “brother’s” correctly shows a single owner.
tip: Check each apostrophe separately: is it forming a contraction or showing ownership?

stem: Choose the correct word: “____ sure the printer is broken again.”
options / answer: A) Were | B) Wer’e | C) We’er | D) We’re
why correct: “We’re” is the contraction for “we are,” which fits at the start of this sentence.
tip: Replace the short word with “we are” to check whether the sentence still makes sense.

stem: Which sentence correctly shows the possessive form of a hyphenated family term?
options / answer: A) My brother-in-law’s new truck is parked outside. | B) My brother’s-in-law new truck is parked outside. | C) My brothers-in-law’s new truck is parked outside. | D) My brother-in-laws new truck is parked outside.
why correct: For a hyphenated compound noun, the possessive ’s attaches to the final word in the term.
tip: Treat the whole hyphenated phrase as one word and add ’s only at its very end.

stem: Read the sentence: “The campfire crackled and popped as orange sparks jumped into the dark sky.” Which sense does this sentence appeal to MOST?
options / answer: A) taste | B) hearing | C) touch | D) smell
why correct: “Crackled and popped” are sound words that let you hear the fire.
tip: Look for words that describe a sound to find hearing imagery.

stem: Which phrase uses imagery that helps you SMELL what is happening? “The kitchen filled with the sharp smell of fresh mint tea.”
options / answer: A) “fresh mint tea” | B) “the kitchen filled” | C) “the sharp smell of fresh mint tea” | D) “in the kitchen”
why correct: The phrase names a smell directly, letting you imagine the scent of mint.
tip: Smell imagery often uses the word “smell” or “scent” along with a description.

stem: Choose the word that best completes this imagery about touch: The wool blanket felt ____ against my cold hands.
options / answer: A) scratchy | B) quiet | C) colorful | D) sweet
why correct: “Scratchy” describes a rough texture you feel with your hands.
tip: Touch words describe how something feels, such as its texture or temperature.

stem: Read the sentence: “Layla bit into the lemon and her whole face puckered at the sour taste.” Which sense is this sentence mainly about?
options / answer: A) smell | B) sight | C) hearing | D) taste
why correct: The sour taste of the lemon is the main sensory detail described.
tip: Taste words often describe flavors like sour, sweet, salty, or bitter.

stem: The sentence “The puppy's fur was soft and warm against my cheek” appeals mostly to the sense of touch.
options / answer: True | False
why correct: Soft and warm describe how the fur feels, which is a touch detail.
tip: Touch imagery describes texture, temperature, or pressure.

stem: Which sentence uses imagery that helps the reader SEE a clear picture?
options / answer: A) The sky turned a deep purple as the first stars began to glitter. | B) It got dark outside after a while. | C) The evening was nice and calm. | D) The weather changed later that evening.
why correct: The specific colors and the image of glittering stars let the reader clearly picture the sky.
tip: Strong imagery uses specific, colorful details instead of vague words.

stem: Read the sentence: “The thunder rumbled low, then cracked so loudly that the windows rattled.” Which sense does this appeal to?
options / answer: A) touch | B) hearing | C) smell | D) taste
why correct: Rumbling, cracking, and rattling are all sound details.
tip: Sound words such as rumble, crack, and rattle signal hearing imagery.

stem: Choose the word that creates smell imagery: The bakery air was thick with the ____ of cinnamon rolls.
options / answer: A) shape | B) aroma | C) sound | D) weight
why correct: “Aroma” describes a smell, letting you imagine the scent of cinnamon rolls.
tip: “Aroma” and “scent” are common words used to create smell imagery.

stem: Which sentence combines TWO different senses in its imagery?
options / answer: A) She poured the lemonade carefully into the glass. | B) The glass of lemonade sat near the window. | C) The icy lemonade was so cold it made her teeth ache, and its sourness made her eyes water. | D) The lemonade was in a tall glass on the table.
why correct: The sentence describes both the cold feeling (touch) and the sour taste.
tip: Look for more than one sensory detail packed into a single sentence.

stem: Why might an author choose to describe “the metallic taste of blood after biting her lip” instead of simply writing “she hurt her lip”?
options / answer: A) To make the sentence shorter and easier to read. | B) To change what actually happened in the story. | C) To avoid describing any feelings at all. | D) To let the reader feel exactly what the character experienced, not just know that it happened.
why correct: Vivid sensory imagery helps readers experience events through the character's senses rather than just being told facts.
tip: Ask: does this detail let me imagine the moment, or just report a fact?

stem: Read the paragraph: “Sand scorched the soles of Mariam's bare feet as the salty ocean breeze tangled her hair. Somewhere nearby, a gull shrieked.” Which senses are used?
options / answer: A) touch (hot sand), smell (salty breeze), and hearing (the gull's shriek) | B) sight only | C) touch only | D) taste and sight only
why correct: The paragraph layers hot sand (touch), the salty breeze (smell), and the gull's shriek (hearing) together.
tip: In longer passages, imagery often combines several senses to build one full scene.

stem: Read the line: “The old violin's strings hummed a low, trembling note that seemed to shiver through the empty hall.” Which sense does the imagery mainly appeal to?
options / answer: A) taste | B) hearing | C) sight | D) smell
why correct: “Hummed” and “trembling note” describe sound, letting the reader hear the violin.
tip: Look past the setting word to find the sensory detail doing the describing.

stem: Which phrase from “The frost had etched silver ferns across the window, and the air smelled faintly of wood smoke” appeals to the sense of smell?
options / answer: A) “across the window” | B) “frost had etched silver ferns” | C) “smelled faintly of wood smoke” | D) “the air”
why correct: The phrase directly names a smell, letting the reader imagine the scent of smoke.
tip: Smell imagery usually names the scent itself, not just the object producing it.

stem: Choose the word that best completes this sight imagery: The lighthouse beam swept a ____ arc of gold across the black water.
options / answer: A) rough | B) silent | C) glowing | D) bitter
why correct: “Glowing” describes how the light appears, creating a visual image.
tip: Sight imagery describes color, brightness, shape, or movement that can be seen.

stem: Read the sentence: “Her palms stung from the rope's rough fibers as she pulled herself up, inch by burning inch.” Which TWO senses does this imagery appeal to?
options / answer: A) hearing only | B) sight and hearing | C) taste and smell | D) touch and a feeling of pain or burning
why correct: “Stung,” “rough fibers,” and “burning” all describe physical sensations felt through touch.
tip: Physical sensations like burning, stinging, or aching usually signal touch imagery.

stem: In the sentence “Steam curled off the noodles, carrying the sharp bite of ginger and garlic across the room,” the imagery appeals mainly to smell.
options / answer: True | False
why correct: The phrase “sharp bite of ginger and garlic” describes a strong smell carried through the air.
tip: Words like “carrying” an odor across a space often signal smell imagery.

stem: Which revision adds vivid SIGHT imagery to the plain sentence “The garden had flowers in it”?
options / answer: A) Crimson tulips and golden daffodils lined the winding garden path. | B) The garden smelled wonderful in spring. | C) There were flowers growing in the garden. | D) The garden was nice and had some plants.
why correct: Specific colors and flower names let the reader clearly picture the garden.
tip: Replace vague words like “nice” with exact colors, shapes, or names.

stem: Match each descriptive phrase with the sense it appeals to most.
options / answer: the engine's steady growl = Hearing | the rusty gate's jagged edge = Touch | the tang of unripe mangoes = Taste | smoke drifting over the valley = Sight
why correct: Each phrase focuses on one dominant sensory detail.
tip: Ask which sense would notice this detail first in real life.

stem: Read the passage: “The diesel fumes stung Fatima's throat as the ferry's horn blasted twice, and spray from the waves soaked her shoes.” Which THREE senses are used?
options / answer: A) sight, taste, and smell | B) smell, hearing, and touch | C) sight only | D) taste, touch, and hearing
why correct: “Stung” (smell), the horn's “blasted” (hearing), and the soaking spray (touch) each appeal to a different sense.
tip: In longer passages, list each sensory clue separately before deciding which senses are used.

stem: Why might an author choose the phrase “the chalky, bitter taste of the medicine” instead of simply writing “the medicine tasted bad”?
options / answer: A) To change the reader's opinion about the character. | B) To make the sentence more confusing for the reader. | C) To let the reader imagine the exact unpleasant flavor rather than just knowing it was unpleasant. | D) To avoid describing the medicine at all.
why correct: Specific sensory words like “chalky” and “bitter” create a sharper, more precise image than a general word like “bad.”
tip: Precise sensory words almost always create a stronger image than vague ones.

stem: How does the imagery in “The rain hissed against the tin roof while mud squelched under every step” shape the mood of the scene?
options / answer: A) It creates an exciting, celebratory mood. | B) It creates a peaceful, sunny mood. | C) It creates a silent, empty mood. | D) It creates an uncomfortable, messy mood through unpleasant sounds and textures.
why correct: The harsh sound of hissing rain and the unpleasant feel of squelching mud together build a gloomy, uncomfortable mood.
tip: Ask what feeling the specific sounds and textures would give you if you experienced them yourself.

stem: Read the line: “The engine's exhaust left a bitter, oily taste at the back of his throat as the truck rattled over the gravel.” Which TWO senses dominate this imagery?
options / answer: A) taste and hearing | B) touch only | C) sight and smell | D) smell and sight
why correct: “Bitter, oily taste” appeals to taste, and “rattled” is a sound detail appealing to hearing.
tip: Separate each descriptive phrase and match it to exactly one or two senses.

stem: Which phrase from “Frost silvered the fence, and the air bit sharply at any exposed skin” creates touch imagery?
options / answer: A) “any exposed skin” | B) “bit sharply at any exposed skin” | C) “Frost silvered the fence” | D) “the air”
why correct: “Bit sharply” describes a painful, stinging feeling on the skin, which is a touch sensation.
tip: Touch imagery often uses words for pain, pressure, temperature, or texture.

stem: Choose the word that best completes this imagery about hearing: The old floorboards ____ under every careful step.
options / answer: A) sparkled | B) tasted | C) smelled | D) groaned
why correct: “Groaned” describes a sound the floorboards make, creating an auditory image.
tip: Sound verbs like groan, creak, and rattle usually signal hearing imagery.

stem: Read the sentence: “The alley reeked of rotting fruit, and flies droned lazily over the overflowing bins.” Which TWO senses does this sentence appeal to?
options / answer: A) taste and touch | B) touch and taste | C) smell and hearing | D) sight only
why correct: “Reeked” describes a smell, and “droned” describes the sound the flies make.
tip: Look for one verb or adjective tied to each specific sense.

stem: In the sentence “The marble floor radiated a biting cold that crept through her thin socks,” the imagery appeals mainly to touch.
options / answer: True | False
why correct: “Biting cold” and “crept through her thin socks” describe a physical sensation felt through the skin.
tip: Temperature and physical pressure described against the body usually signal touch imagery.

stem: Which revision strengthens the plain sentence “The street market was busy and loud” with more vivid SENSORY imagery?
options / answer: A) People walked around the busy market quickly. | B) The market was crowded with shoppers that day. | C) The street market had many people and sounds. | D) Vendors shouted over clattering carts, and the smoky scent of grilled corn drifted between the stalls.
why correct: Specific sound details (shouting, clattering) and smell details (smoky scent of corn) replace the vague words “busy and loud.”
tip: Trade vague words like “busy” for precise sounds, smells, or sights.

stem: Match each descriptive phrase with the sense it appeals to most.
options / answer: the diesel's acrid sting in the nose = Smell | gears grinding somewhere below deck = Hearing | the raw sting of a rope burn = Touch | neon signs smeared across the wet pavement = Sight
why correct: Each phrase centers on one specific sensory impression.
tip: Identify the exact body part or sense organ each detail would affect.

stem: Read the passage: “Diesel fumes stung his eyes as gulls screeched overhead, and the dock planks, slick with spray, threatened to send him sliding.” Which combination of senses is at work?
options / answer: A) smell (diesel fumes), hearing (screeching gulls), and touch (slick, sliding planks) | B) taste and sight | C) sight, taste, and smell | D) touch only
why correct: Each clause in the sentence targets a different sense: fumes for smell, screeching for hearing, and slick planks for touch.
tip: Break a long, layered sentence into clauses and assign each one its own sense.

stem: How does the imagery in “The silence pressed against his ears like a physical weight, broken only by his own ragged breathing” affect the mood of the scene?
options / answer: A) It creates a busy, chaotic mood. | B) It builds a tense, unsettling mood by making even the absence of sound feel heavy and oppressive. | C) It creates a cheerful, relaxed mood. | D) It creates a mood of celebration.
why correct: Describing silence itself as a “weight” and breathing as “ragged” builds tension and discomfort rather than calm.
tip: Even the absence of sound can be turned into imagery that shapes mood.

stem: Why might an author describe a character's fear as “a cold hand closing slowly around her ribs” instead of writing “she felt afraid”?
options / answer: A) To avoid naming the emotion at all. | B) To make the sentence easier to understand at a glance. | C) To use a physical, sensory comparison that lets readers feel the fear in their own bodies rather than just being told about it. | D) To shorten the description as much as possible.
why correct: Comparing fear to a physical sensation, a cold hand tightening, makes the abstract feeling vivid and felt rather than simply stated.
tip: Writers often turn feelings into physical sensations to make emotions more vivid.

stem: An author is writing about how a frog and a toad look alike and different. Which structure best fits this topic?
options / answer: A) Sequence | B) Cause and effect | C) Description | D) Compare and contrast
why correct: Comparing how a frog and toad are alike and different is exactly what compare-and-contrast structure does.
tip: If a text is about two or more things side by side, think compare-and-contrast.

stem: Which signal words most likely show a COMPARISON (a similarity)?
options / answer: A) both, similarly, also | B) because, so, as a result | C) unlike, in contrast, however | D) first, next, finally
why correct: Words like “both,” “similarly,” and “also” point out that two things share something in common.
tip: Learn one short list of comparison words and one short list of contrast words.

stem: Choose the word that signals a CONTRAST: Bicycles need pedaling to move, ____ scooters can be pushed with one foot.
options / answer: A) whereas | B) and | C) similarly | D) also
why correct: “Whereas” introduces a difference between how bicycles and scooters are moved.
tip: Contrast words include but, however, unlike, and whereas.

stem: A paragraph explains how camels and horses both have four legs, but only camels have humps that store fat. What is this paragraph mainly doing?
options / answer: A) Explaining why camels have humps | B) Comparing and contrasting camels and horses | C) Explaining the steps to care for a camel | D) Describing only camels
why correct: The paragraph shows one similarity (four legs) and one difference (humps) between camels and horses.
tip: Look for both a similarity and a difference in the same paragraph.

stem: An article that explains how solar panels and wind turbines both produce electricity, but work in very different ways, uses a compare-and-contrast structure.
options / answer: True | False
why correct: The article discusses a similarity (both produce electricity) and a difference (how they work), which is compare-and-contrast.
tip: Check for at least one similarity and one difference between the two subjects.

stem: Which sentence uses a compare-and-contrast structure?
options / answer: A) First, the owl spots its prey from a branch. | B) Owls build nests high in tree branches. | C) Owls hunt mainly at night, while hawks hunt mainly during the day. | D) Because owls have excellent night vision, they can hunt in darkness.
why correct: The sentence shows a clear difference between when owls and hawks hunt.
tip: Look for two subjects being discussed side by side in the same sentence.

stem: Match each short description with the text structure it mostly matches.
options / answer: How ants and bees are alike and different = Compare and contrast | The steps to plant a seed, in order = Sequence | Why the ice melted in the sun = Cause and effect | Facts about one kind of shark = Description
why correct: Each description matches the text structure that fits its purpose.
tip: Ask what the paragraph is mainly trying to do: compare, order, explain why, or describe.

stem: An author writes an article comparing city life and country life. Why might the author choose a compare-and-contrast structure instead of a simple description?
options / answer: A) To describe only city life in great detail. | B) To explain why cities became crowded over time. | C) To explain the order that cities were built in history. | D) To help readers clearly see how the two kinds of life are alike and different.
why correct: Comparing two subjects side by side helps readers notice similarities and differences they might otherwise miss.
tip: Authors choose compare-and-contrast when their main goal is to show how two things relate.

stem: Which pair of sentences uses signal words to show both a similarity AND a difference?
options / answer: A) Both sharks and dolphins live in the ocean. However, sharks are fish while dolphins are mammals. | B) Sharks and dolphins both live in the ocean. | C) Sharks have been on Earth for millions of years. | D) Dolphins are mammals, and sharks are fish.
why correct: “Both” signals the similarity, and “however” signals the difference, in the very same pair of sentences.
tip: Strong compare-and-contrast writing often pairs a similarity signal with a contrast signal.

stem: Which topic would be BEST suited to a compare-and-contrast structure?
options / answer: A) A description of what one library's reading room looks like | B) How a public library and a bookstore are similar and different | C) The steps for checking out a library book | D) Why a library might run out of copies of a popular book
why correct: This topic names two subjects, a library and a bookstore, and asks how they are alike and different.
tip: A compare-and-contrast topic always needs at least two subjects to put side by side.

stem: An author organizes an article by first describing how volcanoes and earthquakes are both caused by shifting tectonic plates, then explaining how their effects differ. What is the overall structure of this article?
options / answer: A) Sequence | B) Problem and solution | C) Compare and contrast | D) Description
why correct: The article explicitly discusses a shared cause and then contrasting effects, which is a compare-and-contrast structure.
tip: An article can use compare-and-contrast for part of itself even if it mixes in other details.

stem: Which sentence signals a comparison used to make an unfamiliar idea easier to understand?
options / answer: A) Because the nucleus is damaged, the cell cannot function properly. | B) First, the nucleus sends out instructions to the rest of the cell. | C) A cell's nucleus contains the cell's genetic material. | D) A cell's nucleus works much like a city's control center, directing most of the city's major decisions.
why correct: Comparing the nucleus to a city's control center helps readers understand an unfamiliar idea using something familiar.
tip: Authors often compare a hard science idea to something everyday to make it clearer.

stem: Choose the signal word that best shows a DIFFERENCE: Renewable energy sources can be replenished naturally, ____ fossil fuels take millions of years to form and cannot be quickly replaced.
options / answer: A) additionally | B) whereas | C) furthermore | D) likewise
why correct: “Whereas” introduces the contrast between how quickly each type of energy source can be replaced.
tip: Build a list of contrast signal words: whereas, unlike, on the other hand, in contrast.

stem: A paragraph explains that both bats and dolphins use echolocation to find prey, but bats use it in the air while dolphins use it underwater. What is the paragraph's purpose?

stem: Why might an author choose a compare-and-contrast structure to explain the difference between a democracy and a monarchy?

stem: Read this description: “The scientist listened to the glacier groan and crack beneath her boots, a sound she had once found beautiful and now found impossible to listen to without counting the years it had left.” How does the phrase “impossible to listen to without counting the years it had left” affect the tone of this description?

tip: A character measuring time running out often signals a mournful, urgent tone.

stem: Read this description: “Three people stood at the bus stop stamping their feet against the cold, none of them speaking, all of them watching the same empty road for a bus that was already fifteen minutes late.” How does the phrase “a bus that was already fifteen minutes late” affect the tone of this description?

stem: Read this description: “Dust floated in the single beam of light as Huda lifted the lid of the old box, and a photograph of her mother at seven years old looked back at her, younger than Huda had ever imagined she could be.” How does the phrase “younger than Huda had ever imagined she could be” affect the tone of this description?

stem: Read this description: “The flashlight beam shook slightly in Bilal's hand as it swept across shelves he usually passed without a glance, each shadow stretching a little longer than he remembered the room being.” How does the phrase “each shadow stretching a little longer than he remembered” affect the tone of this description?

stem: Read this description: “Waves slammed against the rocks below as the keeper climbed the spiral stairs one more time, refusing to let the light go dark no matter how hard the wind pushed against the glass.” How does the phrase “refusing to let the light go dark no matter how hard the wind pushed” affect the tone of this description?

stem: Read this description: “Steel beams caught the first light as the crew gathered below, and Khalid looked up at the half-finished frame, already picturing the building that didn't exist yet but somehow already felt real to him.” How does the phrase “already felt real to him” affect the tone of this description?
options / answer: A) It creates a tone of bitter sarcasm. | B) It creates a tone of hopeful ambition. | C) It creates a tone of quiet despair. | D) It creates a tone of calm indifference.

stem: Read this passage: “Volcanoes form when melted rock, called magma, rises up through cracks in the Earth's crust. When a volcano erupts, the magma is called lava once it reaches the surface. options / answer: A) Which country has the most volcanoes? | B) How many volcanoes are there in the world? | C) What is lava called before it reaches the surface? | D) How long does an eruption usually last?

stem: Read this passage: “Recycling centers sort glass, plastic, and paper into separate bins. Glass is crushed and melted down to make new jars and bottles. options / answer: A) workers | B) money | C) history | D) glass

tip: Look for the exact process described step by step.

stem: Read this passage: “Camels store fat in their humps, not water. This fat can be used for energy when food is scarce in the desert. A camel's wide feet also keep it from sinking into soft sand.” This passage explains that a camel's hump is used to store water.

tip: Watch for details that correct a common misunderstanding.

stem: Read this passage: “Rainforest trees grow so close together that their leaves form a thick ceiling called a canopy. Very little sunlight reaches the forest floor below. stem: Read this passage: “Solar panels convert sunlight directly into electricity using special materials that release electrons when struck by light. stem: Read this passage: “Carbohydrates are the body's quickest source of energy, broken down rapidly into glucose for the bloodstream. stem: Which sentence correctly uses an irregular past-tense verb?
options / answer: A) The old rope had tore apart under the heavy load. | B) The old rope had teared apart under the heavy load. | C) The old rope had torn apart under the heavy load. | D) The old rope tore apart under the heavy load, has it?
why correct: tear → tore → (have/had) torn.
tip: The past participle after had often differs from the simple past form.

stem: Choose the past tense: “The sailors ____ to the mast as the waves crashed over the deck.”
options / answer: A) clung | B) clang | C) clinged | D) clings
why correct: cling → clung.
tip: cling/clung follows the same pattern as sting/stung and sling/slung.

stem: Which sentence correctly uses an irregular past-tense verb?
options / answer: A) Had the committee known the true cost sooner, it would have choose a cheaper plan. | B) Had the committee knowed the true cost sooner, it would have chosen a cheaper plan. | C) Had the committee knew the true cost sooner, it would have chosen a cheaper plan. | D) Had the committee known the true cost sooner, it would have chosen a cheaper plan.
why correct: had + known, and would have + chosen: both use the correct past participles.
tip: In past-perfect “if” sentences, every helping verb needs a past participle after it.
