stem: Which sentence correctly uses an irregular past-tense verb?
options / answer: A) Overcome with relief, the climbers wept at the summit. | B) Overcome with relief, the climbers weep at the summit. | C) Overcome with relief, the climbers weeped at the summit. | D) Overcome with relief, the climbers have wept at the summit, and left.
why correct: The irregular past tense of “weep” is “wept.”
tip: Several irregular verbs change -eep to -ept: sleep/slept, keep/kept, weep/wept.

stem: Where does this story take place? “Mona tied her donkey to a post outside the mudbrick house and carried a basket of dates up the narrow lane.”
options / answer: A) In a big city | B) In a village | C) In a classroom | D) On a ship
why correct: The donkey, mudbrick house, and narrow lane show a small village setting.
tip: Look for small details like animals and building materials to picture the setting.

stem: Which detail tells you WHEN this story takes place? “Khalid lit an oil lamp because the house had no electricity, and he wrote his letter by its flickering light.”
options / answer: A) flickering light | B) his letter | C) no electricity | D) the house
why correct: No electricity suggests the story happens long ago or somewhere without modern power.
tip: Clues about technology often reveal when a story is set.

stem: How does the setting create a problem in this story? “Snow piled against the cabin door, and the family had only enough firewood for one more night.”
options / answer: A) The family does not like snow. | B) The firewood is the wrong kind. | C) The cabin is too small for the family. | D) The snow and shortage of firewood threaten the family’s safety.
why correct: Being snowed in with little firewood creates danger, which is the story’s problem.
tip: Ask how the time and place make the character’s situation harder.

stem: Which words help you picture the setting? “Waves slapped against the fishing boat as seagulls circled overhead and salty spray stung the sailors’ eyes.”
options / answer: A) waves, seagulls, salty spray | B) stung, circled | C) fishing boat, sailors | D) eyes, boat
why correct: Waves, seagulls, and salty spray are sensory details that build the ocean setting.
tip: Setting details often appeal to the senses: sight, sound, smell.

stem: In the sentence “The marketplace buzzed with vendors calling out prices for mangoes and spices,” the setting is a quiet library.
options / answer: True | False
why correct: A buzzing marketplace with vendors is a busy, noisy place, not a quiet library.
tip: Compare the mood of a sentence to the setting it describes.

stem: Why might the author have set this story in a desert instead of a forest? “Yara counted her remaining water carefully, knowing the next well was two days away.”
options / answer: A) To make the story funny. | B) To make finding water the main source of danger and tension | C) To describe many different plants. | D) To show Yara likes hot weather.
why correct: A desert setting makes scarce water the central danger, driving the plot forward.
tip: Think about what problems a setting naturally creates for the characters.

stem: Which sentence best shows a change in setting that affects the mood of a story?
options / answer: A) The beach was sandy and the boat was red. | B) The crew ate lunch on the deck. | C) The sunny beach gave way to dark storm clouds as the boat drifted farther from shore. | D) The captain checked his watch twice.
why correct: The shift from sunny beach to dark storm clouds creates a sudden, tense mood.
tip: A change in weather or light often signals a change in mood.

stem: What does the detail “the clock tower’s bell had been silent for fifty years” suggest about the setting?
options / answer: A) The town just built the clock tower. | B) The bell rings every hour. | C) The town has no clock tower. | D) The town has been quiet or unchanged for a long time.
why correct: A bell silent for fifty years hints at a town stuck in the past.
tip: Details about how long something has been true reveal clues about a setting’s history.

stem: A story opens: “Inside the spaceship, red warning lights flashed along the metal corridor.” What can you tell about the setting?
options / answer: A) It is a futuristic, possibly dangerous place. | B) It is an old wooden cabin. | C) It is a peaceful garden. | D) It is a quiet library.
why correct: A spaceship with flashing warning lights signals a futuristic and tense setting.
tip: Setting details can hint at danger before any action happens.

stem: Two stories are set during the same flood, but one is told from a rooftop and the other from a rescue boat. How would the settings most likely change each story?
options / answer: A) The stories would be exactly the same. | B) Each character would notice different dangers and details based on their exact location. | C) The flood would not matter in either story. | D) Only the rooftop story could mention water.
why correct: Being on a rooftop versus a boat changes what each character can see and fear.
tip: Even within one big event, a character’s exact spot shapes what they experience.

stem: Where does this scene take place? “Nadia adjusted her goggles before diving past the coral toward the sunken ship.”
options / answer: A) In a desert canyon | B) In a school gymnasium | C) Underwater near a shipwreck | D) On a mountain trail
why correct: Goggles, diving, coral, and a sunken ship all point to an underwater setting.
tip: List every detail before deciding on the setting.

stem: Which detail best reveals WHEN this story is set? “Omar sent a telegram to his brother, knowing it would take three days to arrive.”
options / answer: A) sending a message | B) his brother | C) Omar’s name | D) a telegram that takes three days
why correct: Telegrams and multi-day delivery suggest an earlier time before instant communication.
tip: Look at how characters communicate to guess the time period.

stem: How does the setting increase the conflict in this scene? “The bridge swayed over the canyon, and the rope holding it was already fraying.”
options / answer: A) The unstable bridge makes crossing the canyon dangerous. | B) The canyon is very colorful. | C) The bridge is painted red. | D) The canyon is narrow.
why correct: A swaying, fraying bridge over a canyon creates real physical danger for the characters.
tip: A dangerous setting often becomes the obstacle characters must overcome.

stem: Which setting detail would most likely help a character solve a problem later in the story? “Deep in the cave, Layla noticed a faint draft coming from a crack in the back wall.”
options / answer: A) Layla’s flashlight | B) the draft from the crack in the wall | C) Layla’s footsteps | D) the cave’s darkness
why correct: A draft often signals an opening to the outside, which could become an escape route.
tip: Setting details that seem small, like a draft or a smell, often matter later.

stem: In the sentence “Neon signs lit the crowded night market as scooters weaved between food stalls,” the setting is most likely a quiet rural farm at dawn.
options / answer: True | False
why correct: Neon signs, a crowded market, and scooters describe a busy city at night, not a quiet farm.
tip: Match the energy and details in a sentence to the kind of place it describes.

stem: Why might an author set a mystery in an old, creaky mansion rather than a new apartment?
options / answer: A) Mansions are always haunted. | B) Apartments are always happy places. | C) The mansion’s age and strange sounds build suspense and hide secrets. | D) A mansion is easier to draw.
why correct: An old mansion’s creaks, shadows, and history naturally create mystery and suspense.
tip: Authors often choose settings that match the mood their genre needs.

stem: A story is set during a heat wave in a crowded apartment with no air conditioning. How does this setting most likely affect the characters?
options / answer: A) It makes the characters feel cold. | B) It has no effect on the characters’ moods. | C) It makes the characters want to stay inside longer. | D) It makes the characters irritable and eager to escape the heat.
why correct: Heat and crowding in an enclosed space would naturally make characters uncomfortable and short-tempered.
tip: Think about how a setting’s physical conditions would realistically affect people in it.

stem: What mood does this setting create? “Fog rolled silently over the empty pier, and a single lantern swung from its post.”
options / answer: A) An eerie, lonely mood | B) A cheerful, festive mood | C) A bright, sunny mood | D) A busy, crowded mood
why correct: Fog, emptiness, and a single swinging lantern create an eerie, lonely feeling.
tip: Weather and lighting details are strong clues to a setting’s mood.

stem: Two scenes happen during the same war, but one is set in a quiet village and the other in a bombed-out city street. How would the settings most likely shape each scene differently?
options / answer: A) The war would not affect either setting. | B) The village scene might focus on waiting and fear, while the city scene might focus on danger and destruction. | C) Both scenes would describe identical events. | D) Only the city scene could include any characters.
why correct: A quiet village and a bombed city would expose characters to very different sights and dangers.
tip: The same historical event can create very different settings depending on exact location.

stem: Which detail shows that this scene takes place long after a disaster, not during it? “Vines now curled over the collapsed roof, and moss covered the broken steps.”
options / answer: A) the disaster itself | B) the collapsed roof | C) vines and moss covering the ruins | D) the broken steps
why correct: Vines and moss take time to grow, showing the ruins have sat untouched for a while.
tip: Plants slowly reclaiming a place are a common clue that time has passed.

stem: Which detail most strongly establishes the time period of this scene? “She tucked her phone away and checked the brass pocket watch her grandfather had carried in the war.”
options / answer: A) tucking away a phone | B) her grandfather | C) checking the time | D) the brass pocket watch from the war
why correct: A pocket watch tied to a specific war gives a concrete historical reference point.
tip: Look for objects linked to specific historical events for precise time clues.

stem: How does the isolated setting intensify the conflict? “The research station sat three hundred miles from the nearest town, and the only radio had just gone dead.”
options / answer: A) It leaves the characters without help if something goes wrong. | B) It gives the characters extra supplies. | C) It allows the characters to call for help easily. | D) It makes the station very warm.
why correct: Extreme distance and a dead radio cut the characters off from rescue, raising the stakes.
tip: Isolation in a setting often removes a character’s safety net.

stem: What does the setting reveal about the character’s state of mind? “Dishes piled in the sink, curtains stayed drawn at noon, and dust coated the piano no one played anymore.”
options / answer: A) The character is extremely organized. | B) The character is likely struggling with grief or neglect. | C) The character just moved in. | D) The character loves hosting parties.
why correct: A neglected, closed-up home mirrors a character who has withdrawn, often from grief.
tip: A setting can reflect a character’s inner emotional state.

stem: Why might the author set this chapter in a crowded train station rather than an empty field? “Amid shouted announcements and shoving crowds, Tariq realized he had lost sight of his sister.”
options / answer: A) Train stations are always exciting. | B) The author simply prefers trains. | C) The chaos and crowd make it realistically hard to find someone, raising tension. | D) An empty field would be too quiet to write about.
why correct: A crowded, noisy station makes losing a person both believable and tense.
tip: Choose the setting detail that most directly explains the problem in the scene.

stem: In the sentence “Dust devils spun across the cracked, sun-baked flats as the caravan’s water barrels ran dry,” the setting is a lush, rainy rainforest.
options / answer: True | False
why correct: Dust devils, cracked ground, and dry water barrels describe a scorched desert, not a rainforest.
tip: Check whether every detail actually matches the setting you think a sentence describes.

stem: How do the settings of a bustling port city and a silent mountain monastery most likely shape two different characters in the same story?
options / answer: A) Both characters would develop in identical ways. | B) Neither setting would influence the characters at all. | C) Only the monastery character could show any emotion. | D) The port city character would likely be shaped by constant activity and trade, while the monastery character would be shaped by solitude and reflection.
why correct: Contrasting settings like a busy port and a silent monastery typically produce contrasting character traits.
tip: Compare how daily life in each setting would train a character’s habits and outlook.

stem: What is the effect of the author shifting the setting from a sunlit garden to a locked basement within the same chapter?
options / answer: A) It creates a sudden, unsettling contrast that signals danger ahead. | B) It shows the character is bored. | C) It proves the garden was never real. | D) It has no effect on the story’s mood.
why correct: Moving abruptly from a bright, open garden to a dark, locked basement signals a sharp tonal shift toward danger.
tip: A sudden setting contrast is often used deliberately to unsettle the reader.

stem: Which detail best explains why characters in this scene speak in hushed voices? “Stone archways funneled every whisper into an echo throughout the ancient library’s reading hall.”
options / answer: A) The characters are reading very difficult books. | B) The echoing stone architecture would amplify any noise they made. | C) The library has no other visitors. | D) The characters are shy by nature.
why correct: The echoing stone architecture explains why any sound, even a whisper, would carry loudly.
tip: Setting details like materials and architecture can explain character behavior.

stem: A story set on a long sea voyage shows the ship’s supplies dwindling week by week. What does this passage of time within the setting most likely foreshadow?
options / answer: A) A sudden change to a city setting | B) The voyage ending exactly on schedule | C) A coming crisis over food or water as supplies run out | D) An unrelated subplot about a festival
why correct: Supplies running low over time typically builds toward a crisis the characters must face.
tip: When a setting detail changes gradually, it often signals rising tension to come.

stem: How does the setting of a one-room schoolhouse on the frontier shape the kinds of conflicts likely to arise in a story set there?
options / answer: A) Conflicts would mainly involve advanced technology failing. | B) Conflicts would mainly involve disputes between rival sports teams. | C) Conflicts would mainly involve traffic and crowded hallways. | D) Conflicts would likely involve limited resources, mixed ages learning together, and isolation from other towns.
why correct: A small, isolated frontier school naturally creates conflicts tied to scarce resources and mixed-age learning, not modern school issues.
tip: Think about what problems actually fit the time and place of a setting.

stem: A reader finishes a paragraph about honeybees but cannot remember how many legs a bee has. What should the reader do?
options / answer: A) Reread the paragraph to find the detail about the bee’s legs. | B) Ask a friend instead of checking the text. | C) Skip to the next paragraph. | D) Guess a number and move on.
why correct: Rereading lets the reader find the exact detail instead of guessing.
tip: When you forget a detail, look back at the text before guessing.

stem: After reading about how camels survive in the desert, a student is unsure why camels have thick eyelashes. Which part of the text should the student reread?
options / answer: A) The title of the article | B) The sentence that explains what the eyelashes protect the camel from | C) The last sentence of the whole article | D) The picture caption only, without any text
why correct: The sentence describing the eyelashes’ purpose directly answers the question.
tip: Find the sentence that matches your question, not just any part of the text.

stem: Rereading a confusing sentence can help a reader understand words they missed the first time.
options / answer: True | False
why correct: Reading slowly a second time often clears up confusion caused by skimming too fast.
tip: Slow down and reread any sentence that confuses you.

stem: A paragraph about the pyramids says they were built using ramps and levers. A reader does not understand how a lever works. What is the best next step?
options / answer: A) Stop reading the article completely. | B) Change the meaning of “lever” in your head. | C) Reread the sentence about the lever and look for an example in the text. | D) Skip the whole paragraph.
why correct: Rereading the sentence can reveal an example or explanation of how levers work.
tip: Looking for an example in the text can make a hard word clearer.

stem: A text explains that rainforests get over seventy inches of rain a year. A reader wants to know why rainforests have so many plants. What should the reader do?
options / answer: A) Count the inches of rain instead of rereading. | B) Only reread the first sentence of the article. | C) Assume rainfall has nothing to do with plants. | D) Reread the paragraph to see if it connects the rainfall to plant growth.
why correct: Rereading can reveal how the text links heavy rainfall to plentiful plant growth.
tip: Reread to find connections between two facts in a text.

stem: After finishing an article about volcanoes, a student cannot explain why lava sometimes moves slowly and sometimes quickly. Which part should the student reread?
options / answer: A) The section describing what affects the speed of lava | B) The introduction sentence only | C) The section about volcano names | D) The last paragraph about safety tips
why correct: The section about lava’s speed is the exact part that answers the question.
tip: Match your confusing question to the section most likely to answer it.

stem: A reader is confused by the sentence “The ants left a scent trail so others could follow it back to the nest.” What should the reader do first?
options / answer: A) Reread only the last word of the sentence. | B) Reread the sentence slowly, paying attention to each part. | C) Skip to the next sentence right away. | D) Decide the sentence is unimportant.
why correct: Reading the whole sentence again, slowly, helps the reader connect each part of the idea.
tip: Reread an entire confusing sentence, not just a single word.

stem: A text about recycling states that aluminum cans can be recycled again and again without losing quality. A reader wonders if this is true for all materials. What is the best step?
options / answer: A) Change the topic to something easier. | B) Assume every material recycles the same way. | C) Reread the text to see if it compares aluminum to other materials. | D) Stop reading because the question seems too hard.
why correct: Rereading can show whether the text explains differences between materials.
tip: Reread to check if the text answers a question you are curious about.

stem: Which TWO are good reasons to reread a paragraph about bats using echoes to find insects?
options / answer: A) To avoid finishing the article | B) To find a detail you forgot | C) To make the paragraph longer | D) To understand a confusing science term
why correct: Rereading helps clarify confusing words and recover forgotten details.
tip: Reread for understanding, not to delay or avoid reading.

stem: A student reads that lighthouses once used oil lamps and mirrors to create a bright beam. The student is confused about why mirrors were needed. What should the student do?
options / answer: A) Reread only the title of the article. | B) Guess that mirrors were just decoration. | C) Skip ahead to a different article. | D) Reread the sentence to look for the mirrors’ specific purpose.
why correct: The sentence about mirrors likely explains how they focused or strengthened the light.
tip: Reread the specific sentence connected to your confusion, not the whole article randomly.

stem: An article says spiders use silk for webs, safety lines, and wrapping eggs. A reader cannot remember which use came first in the text. What should the reader do?
options / answer: A) Reread the paragraph in order to find the sequence of uses listed. | B) Decide the order does not matter. | C) Skip to a different paragraph about spiders. | D) Guess the order from memory.
why correct: Rereading in order lets the reader confirm exactly how the uses were listed.
tip: When a question is about order, reread looking specifically for sequence words.

stem: If a reader understands a paragraph completely the first time, they must still reread it five more times.
options / answer: True | False
why correct: Rereading is a strategy for confusion, not a required rule for every paragraph regardless of understanding.
tip: Reread when something is unclear, not automatically every single time.

stem: A text explains that a desert tortoise can survive a year without drinking water. A reader wants to know how this is possible. What should the reader do?
options / answer: A) Ignore the question and move on. | B) Reread the text looking for an explanation of how the tortoise stores water. | C) Assume the text made a mistake. | D) Reread only the picture, not the words.
why correct: Rereading can reveal details about how the tortoise’s body conserves water.
tip: When a fact seems surprising, reread for the text’s own explanation.

stem: A student rereads a paragraph about coral reefs and notices a sentence they missed the first time: “Coral reefs shelter thousands of fish species.” What did rereading help the student do?
options / answer: A) Change the author’s words. | B) Avoid learning new information. | C) Find a detail that was missed during the first reading. | D) Make the paragraph shorter.
why correct: Rereading often uncovers details that were skipped or missed the first time.
tip: A careful second read can reveal sentences your eyes skipped over.

stem: An article explains how bread rises because yeast produces gas bubbles in the dough. A reader does not understand what yeast is. What should the reader do?
options / answer: A) Skip to an article about a different food. | B) Guess that yeast is a type of flour. | C) Decide yeast is not important to the article. | D) Reread the sentence about yeast to look for a definition or clue.
why correct: Rereading the sentence can reveal a definition or description of yeast.
tip: Look for a definition near a confusing science word before guessing its meaning.

stem: A paragraph about the water cycle explains evaporation, condensation, and precipitation in that order. A reader mixes up which step comes first. What is the best fix?
options / answer: A) Reread the paragraph, tracking the order the steps are introduced. | B) Only look at the title of the section. | C) Make up a new order that sounds right. | D) Skip the paragraph and read the next one.
why correct: Rereading with attention to sequence words (first, then, finally) clarifies the correct order.
tip: Reread for sequence clues like first, next, and finally.

stem: A student rereads an article about ancient Egyptian boats twice and now understands why the boats were made from papyrus reeds instead of wood. What is the BEST explanation for this improvement?
options / answer: A) The student read it faster the second time. | B) The second reading let the student focus on details that were unclear the first time. | C) The article changed between readings. | D) The student ignored the details about papyrus.
why correct: A careful second reading allows a reader to focus more closely on confusing details.
tip: Slower, more careful rereading—not speed—usually builds better understanding.

stem: Rereading only helps with long articles, never with a single confusing sentence.
options / answer: True | False
why correct: Rereading can help with a single sentence just as much as with a long article.
tip: Rereading works at any size—one sentence or a whole article.

stem: After reading about how beavers build dams, a student is confused about why beavers use mud as well as sticks. What should the student do?
options / answer: A) Skip the whole section about beaver homes. | B) Assume mud is not important to the dam. | C) Reread the sentence explaining the purpose of the mud. | D) Guess that beavers like the taste of mud.
why correct: Rereading the sentence can show that mud is used to seal and strengthen the dam.
tip: If a material is named specifically, reread to find out why it matters.

stem: A reader finishes a paragraph about how electricity travels through a circuit but cannot recall what a conductor is. What should the reader do?
options / answer: A) Decide the term is not worth understanding. | B) Skip ahead to a new topic. | C) Guess a definition that sounds reasonable. | D) Reread the paragraph to find where a conductor is explained.
why correct: Rereading lets the reader locate the exact definition instead of guessing.
tip: When a key term is unclear, reread the sentence right around it.

stem: A text on photosynthesis says plants convert sunlight into stored energy. A reader is unsure what “stored energy” means in this context. Which part should be reread?
options / answer: A) The sentence or two explaining what the plant does with that energy | B) A completely different paragraph about animals | C) The paragraph’s final summary sentence only | D) The title of the article
why correct: The explanation of how the plant uses that energy clarifies what “stored energy” means.
tip: Find the sentence closest to the confusing phrase, not a distant one.

stem: Rereading a paragraph can help a reader notice how two ideas within it are connected.
options / answer: True | False
why correct: A careful second reading often reveals connections, like cause and effect, missed the first time.
tip: Reread to notice connections between sentences, not just to re-read words.

stem: An article explains that earthquakes happen when tectonic plates suddenly shift. A reader does not understand why the plates shift in the first place. What is the best next step?
options / answer: A) Skip the whole article. | B) Reread the section discussing the cause of plate movement. | C) Reread only the glossary, if there is one, and nothing else. | D) Decide tectonic plates move randomly for no reason.
why correct: The section on causes likely explains the buildup of pressure that leads to shifting.
tip: Look specifically for the section discussing causes, not effects.

stem: A text states that the Great Barrier Reef is made of billions of tiny coral polyps. A reader wants to know how such small creatures build something so large. What should the reader do?
options / answer: A) Assume the number given must be a typo. | B) Stop reading because it seems unbelievable. | C) Reread the text to find the explanation of how polyps build the reef over time. | D) Switch to reading about a different ocean topic.
why correct: Rereading can reveal how the text explains gradual reef-building over long periods of time.
tip: When a fact feels surprising, reread for the text’s explanation of how it happens.

stem: After finishing an article about ancient trade routes, a student cannot explain why merchants traveled in large groups called caravans. Which part should the student reread?
options / answer: A) The map caption alone | B) The section listing trade goods only | C) The concluding sentence about trade today | D) The section explaining the reasons merchants grouped together
why correct: The section about grouping reasons directly answers why caravans formed.
tip: Match your specific question to the section most likely to address it.

stem: A reader is confused by the sentence “Suspension bridges use cables to transfer the weight of traffic to the towers at each end.” What should the reader do first?
options / answer: A) Reread the sentence slowly, focusing on each part of the process. | B) Reread only the word “bridge.” | C) Decide the sentence is unimportant. | D) Skip ahead without rereading.
why correct: Slowly rereading the whole sentence helps connect cables, weight, and towers.
tip: Break a complex sentence into its parts during a careful reread.

stem: A text about bacteria explains that some bacteria are helpful while others cause illness. A reader wonders if this applies to all microscopic organisms. What is the best step?
options / answer: A) Assume all tiny organisms behave the same way. | B) Reread the text to see if it compares bacteria to other microscopic organisms. | C) Change the subject to something unrelated. | D) Stop reading because the question feels too broad.
why correct: Rereading can reveal whether the text draws distinctions between organism types.
tip: Reread to check whether the text actually answers your broader question.

stem: Which TWO are good reasons to reread a section about how glaciers carve valleys?
options / answer: A) To notice how one process leads to another | B) To clarify a confusing geology term | C) To make the section shorter | D) To avoid finishing the article
why correct: Rereading helps with both vocabulary and understanding cause-and-effect processes.
tip: Reread to connect ideas and clarify terms, not to stall.

stem: A student reads that early bicycles had no pedals and riders pushed off the ground with their feet. The student is confused about how this was safer or less safe than modern bikes. What should the student do?
options / answer: A) Guess that early bicycles were always safer. | B) Reread only the picture caption. | C) Reread the paragraph to look for a comparison to modern bicycles. | D) Skip ahead to an unrelated article.
why correct: The paragraph may directly compare safety features of early and modern bicycles.
tip: Reread for direct comparisons the text makes between two things.

stem: An article says the human heart has four chambers that each play a different role. A reader cannot remember which chamber does what. What should the reader do?
options / answer: A) Guess the roles from memory. | B) Skip to a paragraph about a different organ. | C) Decide the chambers all do the same thing. | D) Reread the paragraph, matching each chamber to its specific role.
why correct: Rereading carefully lets the reader match each chamber to the role the text describes.
tip: When a text lists several similar parts, reread slowly to tell them apart.

stem: A reader who already understands a passage perfectly the first time should still reread it ten times before moving on.
options / answer: True | False
why correct: Rereading is meant to resolve confusion, not a required number of repeats regardless of understanding.
tip: Reread based on need, not a fixed number of times.

stem: A text explains that some fish can detect electric fields produced by other animals. A reader wants to know how this ability works. What should the reader do?
options / answer: A) Reread the text looking for the explanation of the sensing organ involved. | B) Assume the text is exaggerating. | C) Ignore the detail and move on. | D) Reread only the diagram, not the words.
why correct: Rereading can reveal details about the specialized organ that senses electric fields.
tip: When an ability seems surprising, reread for the text’s explanation of the mechanism.

stem: A student rereads a paragraph about forest fires and notices a sentence they missed: “Some seeds only sprout after being exposed to intense heat.” What did rereading help the student do?
options / answer: A) Avoid new information. | B) Find an important detail that was missed during the first reading. | C) Shorten the paragraph. | D) Change the author’s original wording.
why correct: A careful second read can surface sentences that were skipped the first time.
tip: Rereading slowly can catch details your eyes glossed over at first.

stem: An article explains that medieval castles had moats, drawbridges, and thick walls. A reader does not understand the specific purpose of a moat. What should the reader do?
options / answer: A) Skip to an article about a different building. | B) Guess that the moat was for swimming. | C) Reread the sentence about the moat to look for its stated purpose. | D) Decide the moat was just decoration.
why correct: Rereading the sentence likely reveals that the moat was meant to slow or stop attackers.
tip: Look for the stated purpose near the term you are confused about.

stem: A paragraph about solar panels explains how sunlight, electrons, and wiring work together to create electricity, in that order. A reader mixes up the sequence. What is the best fix?
options / answer: A) Make up an order that sounds logical. | B) Only reread the heading of the section. | C) Skip the paragraph entirely. | D) Reread the paragraph, tracking the order each part is introduced.
why correct: Rereading with attention to sequence clues clarifies the correct order of the process.
tip: Reread for words like first, then, and finally to track a process.

stem: A student rereads an article about submarines twice and now understands why they must carefully control both their weight and air supply underwater. What is the BEST explanation for this improvement?
options / answer: A) The second reading let the student focus on details that were confusing at first. | B) The student read it much faster the second time. | C) The student skipped the confusing parts both times. | D) The article’s content changed between readings.
why correct: A slower, more careful second reading allows focus on previously confusing details.
tip: Careful, attentive rereading—not speed—builds deeper understanding.

stem: Rereading is useful only for science articles and never helps with history or social studies texts.
options / answer: True | False
why correct: Rereading is a general strategy that helps with confusing text in any subject, not just science.
tip: Rereading works across all subjects, not just one.

stem: After reading about satellites orbiting Earth, a student is confused about why satellites do not fall out of the sky. What should the student do?
options / answer: A) Assume gravity does not affect satellites. | B) Reread the section explaining the balance between gravity and speed. | C) Guess that satellites have engines running constantly. | D) Skip the whole section about orbits.
why correct: Rereading the section can reveal how a satellite’s speed balances Earth’s gravity to keep it in orbit.
tip: When a fact seems to defy common sense, reread for the text’s scientific explanation.

stem: A writer claims, “Our school should start an hour later because teenagers need more sleep.” What is the claim in this argument?
options / answer: A) Our school has classes. | B) Sleep is healthy. | C) The school should start an hour later. | D) Teenagers need more sleep.
why correct: The claim is the specific position the writer wants readers to accept.
tip: The claim is usually the main opinion the whole argument is trying to prove.

stem: A student argues against homework by saying, “Homework is just busywork, and everyone knows busywork is pointless.” What is weak about this reasoning?
options / answer: A) It uses too many big words. | B) It does not mention homework at all. | C) It is too short to be an argument. | D) It assumes something is true just because many people supposedly believe it.
why correct: Claiming “everyone knows” something is a bandwagon appeal, not real evidence.
tip: Watch for arguments that rely on popularity instead of facts.

stem: An article argues cities should add more bike lanes and supports this with data showing bike injuries dropped 40% in cities that added protected lanes. Is this evidence relevant to the claim?
options / answer: A) Yes, because it directly connects bike lanes to fewer injuries, supporting the claim’s safety benefit. | B) No, because the article does not mention bike lanes at all. | C) No, because injury statistics have nothing to do with bike lanes. | D) Yes, but only because it mentions a percentage.
why correct: The statistic shows a direct link between the proposed action and a real safety outcome.
tip: Relevant evidence directly supports the specific claim being made.

stem: A letter to the editor says, “We must ban plastic bags immediately, or our oceans will be completely dead within five years.” What technique does this sentence use?
options / answer: A) A balanced comparison of two solutions | B) An extreme, exaggerated prediction to create fear | C) A direct quotation from a marine scientist | D) A calm explanation of recycling methods
why correct: The extreme claim about oceans being “completely dead” in five years is an exaggeration meant to scare readers.
tip: Watch for absolute, dramatic predictions that lack supporting evidence.

stem: An essay claims school uniforms reduce bullying and supports this only by saying, “My cousin’s school has uniforms, and nobody there gets bullied.” Why is this evidence weak?
options / answer: A) It is weak because it is written in first person. | B) It is weak because uniforms are mentioned. | C) A single personal example cannot prove something is true for schools in general. | D) It is weak because the cousin attends school.
why correct: One anecdote is not enough evidence to support a broad claim about all schools.
tip: A single example, or anecdote, is weaker evidence than data from many cases.

stem: An opinion piece argues against raising the driving age by saying, “Lowering the driving age last year clearly caused the rise in traffic jams this year.” What is the flaw in this reasoning?
options / answer: A) It fails to mention traffic jams at all. | B) It focuses only on pedestrians, not drivers. | C) It uses too much statistical data. | D) It assumes one event caused another just because it happened first, without real proof.
why correct: This is a false-cause fallacy: one event happening before another does not prove it caused the other.
tip: Just because B follows A does not prove A caused B.

stem: A city council member argues for a new community garden, citing a university study of 50 cities showing gardens reduced local food costs by 15% on average. Compared to a single resident’s opinion, why is this evidence stronger?
options / answer: A) It is based on data from many cities rather than one person’s impression. | B) It is stronger because it mentions gardens. | C) It is stronger because it includes a percentage. | D) It is stronger because a council member said it.
why correct: A large study across many cities is more reliable than one person’s limited experience.
tip: Evidence from many cases is generally stronger than a single opinion or example.

stem: A debate speaker says, “My opponent wants to cut the art budget, so clearly she hates creativity and wants children to suffer.” What is wrong with this statement?
options / answer: A) It correctly summarizes the opponent’s budget proposal. | B) It unfairly attacks the opponent’s character instead of addressing her actual argument. | C) It provides strong evidence for cutting the art budget. | D) It focuses only on factual spending numbers.
why correct: This is an ad hominem attack: it insults the opponent’s character instead of addressing her reasoning.
tip: A fair argument responds to ideas, not insults aimed at a person.

stem: An article claims, “Video games cause violence,” and supports this only by describing one teenager who played violent games and later got in a fight. Is this evidence sufficient to prove the claim?
options / answer: A) Yes, because fights are a serious topic. | B) No, because video games are not mentioned. | C) No, because one isolated case cannot prove a broad claim about all video games. | D) Yes, because the teenager definitely played video games.
why correct: A single example is not enough to support a sweeping claim about video games in general.
tip: A broad claim needs broad evidence, not just one story.

stem: A persuasive essay about ocean cleanup states, “According to a 2023 marine biology study, plastic debris in the Pacific has tripled since 2000.” Why might this source be considered credible?
options / answer: A) It is credible because it uses the word “tripled.” | B) It is credible because it appears in an essay. | C) It is credible because the topic is about the ocean. | D) It cites a specific, dated scientific study rather than a vague or unnamed claim.
why correct: Naming a specific, dated study gives readers a way to verify the claim, which builds credibility.
tip: Specific, named sources are generally more credible than vague references.

stem: A classmate argues, “If we allow students to use phones during lunch, soon they’ll want phones during tests, and eventually school will have no rules at all.” What flaw does this argument show?
options / answer: A) It assumes one small change will lead to extreme, unlikely consequences. | B) It uses a specific statistic about phone use. | C) It correctly predicts a realistic and likely chain of events. | D) It focuses only on lunchtime rules, ignoring other topics.
why correct: This is a slippery-slope fallacy: it assumes a small change must lead to a drastic, unproven outcome.
tip: Be suspicious of arguments claiming one step must lead to an extreme chain reaction.

stem: An article argues for mandatory recess and acknowledges, “Some worry recess cuts into learning time, but studies show short breaks actually improve focus afterward.” What does acknowledging this counterargument do for the essay?
options / answer: A) It weakens the essay by admitting the writer is wrong. | B) It makes the argument more credible by showing the writer considered an opposing view. | C) It is irrelevant because recess is unrelated to learning. | D) It contradicts the main claim entirely.
why correct: Addressing and responding to an opposing view shows the writer has considered multiple sides fairly.
tip: A strong argument often anticipates objections and explains why they do not outweigh the claim.

stem: A speech claims cafeteria food should be healthier, citing a nutritionist’s expert opinion, a survey of 500 students, and a comparison to three other districts’ menus. What makes this argument strong?
options / answer: A) It is strong because it is a speech, not an essay. | B) It is strong because it mentions the number three. | C) It combines several different, credible types of evidence rather than relying on just one. | D) It is strong because it is about food.
why correct: Using expert opinion, a large survey, and real comparisons together builds a well-rounded, convincing case.
tip: Arguments that combine multiple kinds of credible evidence are generally stronger than those relying on one type.

stem: A blog post argues against zoos, stating only, “Zoos are sad places.” Which revision would make this argument more convincing?
options / answer: A) Repeating the phrase “zoos are sad” three more times. | B) Making the font of the claim larger. | C) Adding more exclamation points to the sentence. | D) Adding specific evidence about animal stress levels or enclosure sizes compared to natural habitats
why correct: Specific, factual evidence about animal welfare would support the claim far better than an unsupported feeling.
tip: Vague emotional claims become convincing arguments only once specific evidence is added.

stem: An editorial argues for a four-day school week and provides this evidence: a pilot program in one district showed improved test scores. What additional information would help evaluate whether this evidence is sufficient?
options / answer: A) Whether other factors in that district, besides the schedule, might explain the improved scores | B) The exact date the editorial was published | C) The name of the newspaper that printed it. | D) How many pages the editorial is.
why correct: Checking for other possible causes helps determine whether the schedule change, and not something else, truly caused the improvement.
tip: Before accepting a cause-and-effect claim, consider whether other factors could explain the result.

stem: A student writer claims minimum wage for teens should rise, using a single friend's unfairly low paycheck as the only evidence, while the article overall discusses national wage statistics elsewhere. Which revision would most improve the argument's evidence?
options / answer: A) Repeating the claim at the end of every paragraph | B) Replacing or supplementing the anecdote with broader data on teen wages across the region | C) Mentioning the friend's favorite school subject | D) Describing the friend's paycheck in greater emotional detail
why correct: Broader regional data would make the case far more representative than one friend's experience.
tip: When an argument relies on a single story, ask what wider data could replace or support it.

stem: An article about youth sports argues early specialization in one sport increases injury risk, citing a sports-medicine association’s position statement and three peer-reviewed studies. A reader claims this argument is weak because “sports articles are always biased.” Is this a fair evaluation?
options / answer: A) Yes, because all articles about sports are untrustworthy. | B) No, because the article never mentions any evidence. | C) No, because it dismisses solid medical evidence without pointing to any specific flaw in it. | D) Yes, because peer-reviewed studies are rarely accurate.
why correct: Dismissing credible, cited evidence with a vague generalization is not a fair or specific critique.
tip: A fair evaluation points to a specific weakness in the evidence, not a blanket dismissal.

stem: A flyer states, “Vote for the new playground proposal because it will make our park better.” What is missing from this argument?
options / answer: A) Any mention of voting. | B) A claim about the park. | C) A title for the flyer. | D) Specific evidence or reasons explaining how the playground will improve the park
why correct: The flyer states an opinion but gives no specific reasons or evidence to support it.
tip: A claim without supporting reasons is an opinion, not yet a complete argument.

stem: An article about renewable energy states, “Solar panels are getting cheaper, and some cities report lower electricity bills after installing them.” Is this evidence relevant to an argument for using more solar energy?
options / answer: A) Yes, because cost and savings are directly related to whether solar energy is worth adopting. | B) No, because electricity bills have nothing to do with solar panels. | C) No, because cities are not involved in solar energy use. | D) Yes, but only because the sentence is short.
why correct: Falling cost and lower bills are directly relevant facts for deciding whether solar energy is worthwhile.
tip: Ask whether the evidence actually bears on the specific claim being made.

stem: A letter about protecting coral reefs says, “Reefs are beautiful, so we should ban all boats near them.” What is the weakness in this reasoning?
options / answer: A) It focuses only on economic costs. | B) A reef’s beauty alone does not logically prove that banning all boats is the right solution. | C) It fails to mention coral reefs. | D) It uses a scientific study as evidence.
why correct: The reasoning jumps from an emotional appeal (beauty) straight to an extreme solution without real evidence connecting the two.
tip: A strong solution needs evidence linking the problem to that specific fix, not just an appeal to emotion.

stem: A writer argues against a new highway, stating, “Every single person I asked at the grocery store opposes it, so clearly the whole town is against it.” What is the flaw here?
options / answer: A) It focuses only on cost estimates. | B) It fails to mention the highway at all. | C) A small, unrepresentative group cannot reliably stand for the opinion of an entire town. | D) It relies on a government report.
why correct: A hasty generalization draws a broad conclusion about a whole town from a very small, biased sample.
tip: A small sample from one location cannot represent an entire population's views.

stem: An op-ed about space exploration funding cites NASA’s publicly released budget reports and interviews with three astrophysicists. Compared to an anonymous online comment making the same claim, why would this evidence be considered more trustworthy?
options / answer: A) It is more trustworthy because it is longer. | B) It is more trustworthy because it discusses space. | C) It is more trustworthy because it was published online. | D) It comes from named, verifiable sources with relevant expertise.
why correct: Named experts and official reports can be checked and verified, unlike an anonymous, unsupported comment.
tip: Evidence from identifiable, qualified sources is generally more trustworthy than anonymous claims.

stem: An argument for self-driving cars states, “Self-driving cars will eliminate all car accidents forever.” What is problematic about this claim?
options / answer: A) It makes an absolute, overly confident prediction that no technology could realistically guarantee. | B) It fails to mention cars at all. | C) It cites too many statistics. | D) It focuses only on pedestrian safety.
why correct: Claiming a technology will eliminate something “forever” and completely is an unsupported, extreme overstatement.
tip: Be cautious of arguments using words like “always,” “never,” or “forever” without strong evidence.

stem: An article supports remote learning by describing one student who improved grades while learning from home, without mentioning any other students' experiences. Why might this evidence be considered one-sided?
options / answer: A) It is one-sided because the student is named. | B) It presents only a success story without acknowledging students who may have struggled with remote learning. | C) It is one-sided because it mentions grades. | D) It is one-sided because it is about school.
why correct: Presenting only a positive example while ignoring students who struggled gives an incomplete, biased picture.
tip: A balanced argument should acknowledge both successes and struggles, not just one side.

stem: An article arguing for later school start times cites a sleep-medicine association’s guidelines and a three-year study across twelve school districts. A critic claims the argument is weak because it is “too long.” Is this a fair critique?
options / answer: A) No, because the article never actually cites any evidence. | B) Yes, because twelve districts is too small a number to matter. | C) No, because length does not determine whether evidence is strong or relevant. | D) Yes, because longer arguments are always less convincing.
why correct: A fair critique addresses the quality or relevance of evidence, not simply how long the argument is.
tip: Length is not a valid reason to dismiss an argument; focus on the evidence itself.

stem: A proposal to add a school garden includes a farmer’s expert advice, a cost estimate from the district budget office, and results from three similar school gardens elsewhere. What makes this combination of evidence effective?
options / answer: A) It is effective only because it was written for school. | B) It is effective only because it mentions a garden. | C) It is effective only because three numbers are used. | D) It draws on expert knowledge, financial reality, and real-world results together.
why correct: Combining expert advice, financial facts, and real outcomes addresses the proposal from multiple important angles.
tip: Strong proposals often combine expert opinion, practical cost data, and real examples.

stem: A speaker argues, “Anyone who disagrees with building the new stadium clearly doesn’t care about our town’s future.” Why is this reasoning flawed, even if the speaker also provides some economic data later?
options / answer: A) It unfairly implies that any disagreement must come from not caring, ignoring other valid reasons someone might object. | B) It is flawed because it is addressed to the town. | C) It is flawed because it mentions a stadium. | D) It is flawed because it includes economic data.
why correct: This statement unfairly dismisses valid objections by implying only one bad motive explains disagreement.
tip: Watch for arguments that insult opposing views instead of responding to their actual reasons.

stem: An article claims a town’s new recycling program failed because “litter on Main Street increased the same month the program began.” A classmate points out that a large festival also happened that month. How does this affect the article’s argument?
options / answer: A) It strengthens the article’s claim about the program. | B) It shows another likely cause exists, weakening the claim that the recycling program caused the increase. | C) It proves the recycling program is working perfectly. | D) It has no effect, because festivals never produce litter.
why correct: Identifying another possible cause, like the festival, shows the original argument may have overlooked a more likely explanation.
tip: Before accepting a single cause, check whether another event could explain the same result.

stem: A reviewer argues a new library policy is bad, writing only, “I don’t like change.” What is the main problem with this argument?
options / answer: A) It includes too much data about the library. | B) It fails to state an opinion. | C) It gives a personal preference instead of a reason connected to the actual policy. | D) It focuses only on other libraries.
why correct: Simply disliking change says nothing specific about why the policy itself is actually harmful.
tip: A real argument needs reasons tied to the specific issue, not just a general preference.

stem: An essay favoring community service requirements cites a single star student who loved volunteering, then concludes, “So every student will love community service.” What is the flaw in this conclusion?
options / answer: A) It uses a large, representative survey. | B) It focuses only on students who dislike volunteering. | C) It fails to mention community service. | D) It generalizes one enthusiastic student's experience to predict how every student will feel.
why correct: One enthusiastic student's experience cannot reliably predict how an entire student body will react.
tip: A conclusion about “everyone” needs evidence from many people, not just one example.

stem: An article defending a longer lunch period states, “Students who eat lunch for 45 minutes report feeling less rushed and more focused in afternoon classes, according to a survey of 300 students.” Is this evidence relevant and sufficient?
options / answer: A) It is relevant and reasonably sufficient, since it directly connects lunch length to a measurable outcome across many students. | B) It is relevant but not sufficient, because surveys are never useful evidence. | C) It is irrelevant, because lunch length has nothing to do with focus. | D) It is sufficient only because the number 300 is mentioned.
why correct: A sizable survey directly linking lunch length to focus is both relevant and reasonably strong evidence.
tip: Check both whether evidence connects to the claim and whether it comes from a reasonably large, credible source.

stem: A speaker claims, “Everyone knows that students who play sports get worse grades,” without citing any source. What is the main issue with this argument?
options / answer: A) It fails to mention sports at all. | B) It presents an unsupported generalization as if it were an established fact. | C) It focuses only on grades in one specific class. | D) It cites a peer-reviewed study.
why correct: Saying “everyone knows” something does not make it true; it simply avoids providing real evidence.
tip: A claim is not proven just because it is stated as common knowledge.

stem: An argument for banning junk-food ads aimed at children states, “Removing these ads will instantly make every child healthy.” What makes this claim weak?
options / answer: A) It fails to mention children. | B) It uses a specific, cited statistic. | C) It overstates what removing ads could realistically achieve, ignoring other factors in children's health. | D) It focuses only on advertising techniques.
why correct: Health depends on many factors besides advertising, so claiming an “instant” and total fix is an overstatement.
tip: Watch for claims that promise a single simple fix will solve a complicated problem entirely.

stem: An editorial favoring solar panels on school roofs discusses a pilot program’s energy savings, addresses the concern about installation cost by citing a ten-year payback estimate, and compares outcomes to two similar schools. What makes this a strong argument overall?
options / answer: A) It is strong only because panels are mentioned twice. | B) It is strong only because it is about schools. | C) It is strong only because it mentions ten years. | D) It presents evidence, directly responds to a likely objection, and provides comparable real-world examples.
why correct: Combining evidence, a response to objections, and real comparisons builds a well-rounded, convincing argument.
tip: The strongest arguments present evidence, address objections, and offer comparable real examples.

stem: A town-hall speaker argues against a curfew for teens, stating, “Curfews insult every responsible teenager in this town.” What logical problem does this statement show?
options / answer: A) It assumes all responsible teens would be personally insulted, without evidence that this is actually true. | B) It fails to mention teenagers. | C) It focuses only on curfews for adults. | D) It cites a city council report.
why correct: The statement assumes a strong emotional reaction without any evidence that teens in general actually feel insulted.
tip: An emotional assumption is not the same as evidence that something is actually true.

stem: An article about lowering the voting age cites political-science research showing 16-year-olds in test programs voted at similar informed rates as adults. How does this evidence support the argument?
options / answer: A) It does not support the argument at all. | B) It provides specific, research-based data suggesting younger teens can vote responsibly. | C) It supports the argument only because it is from an article. | D) It supports the argument only because it mentions an age.
why correct: Specific research comparing informed voting rates directly supports the claim about younger teens' readiness to vote.
tip: Look for evidence that directly measures the exact outcome the claim is about.

stem: An op-ed opposing a proposed amusement park states, “The one time I visited a similar park, the lines were long, so this park will definitely fail.” What is the flaw in this reasoning?
options / answer: A) It fails to mention an amusement park. | B) It focuses only on ticket prices. | C) It bases a broad prediction about a different, new park on a single unrelated past experience. | D) It cites a formal business analysis.
why correct: One unrelated experience at a different park is not strong evidence for predicting this new park's success or failure.
tip: A single, unrelated personal experience is weak evidence for predicting an unrelated future outcome.

stem: An essay in favor of grading on a curve addresses the objection that curving is “unfair to top students” by explaining that curves are recalculated so top scores are never lowered, only middle and low scores adjusted upward. Does this response adequately address the concern?
options / answer: A) Yes, but only because it uses the word “fair.” | B) No, because it ignores the concern completely. | C) No, because curves are always unfair by definition. | D) Yes, because it directly explains why the specific fairness concern raised does not actually apply.
why correct: Explaining exactly how the method works directly answers the specific fairness objection raised.
tip: A strong rebuttal explains precisely why a specific objection does not hold up, not just that the writer disagrees.

stem: A student argues that mandatory summer homework improves fall test scores, citing a study from one small private school with unusually small class sizes. A classmate says the evidence is “fine because it’s a real study.” Is this classmate’s evaluation complete?
options / answer: A) No, because it overlooks whether the small school’s unique conditions might limit how well the results apply elsewhere. | B) Yes, because any real study is automatically sufficient evidence. | C) Yes, because private schools are always representative of all schools. | D) No, because the study does not mention test scores.
why correct: A study's being real does not guarantee its findings apply broadly; unusual conditions can limit how general the results are.
tip: Consider whether a study’s specific conditions might limit how well its findings apply to other situations.

stem: An argument for building a new skate park states, “A few teens wrote supportive letters, so clearly the whole community wants this.” A second argument for the same park cites a city survey of 2,000 residents showing 68% support. How do these two pieces of evidence compare in strength?
options / answer: A) Neither piece of evidence is relevant to the skate park. | B) The survey of 2,000 residents is far stronger evidence of community-wide support than a few letters. | C) The letters are stronger because they are personal and emotional. | D) Both pieces of evidence are equally strong.
why correct: A large, broad survey represents the community far better than a handful of individual letters.
tip: When comparing evidence, consider how well each piece represents the whole group being discussed.

stem: An investigative report argues a factory’s new filter reduced river pollution, citing water-quality data from upstream and downstream testing stations over eighteen months, expert analysis from an environmental engineer, and acknowledgment that a nearby farm’s runoff could also affect results. How does acknowledging the farm’s runoff affect the overall strength of this argument?
options / answer: A) It proves the filter had no effect on pollution at all. | B) It is irrelevant because farms have nothing to do with rivers. | C) It strengthens the argument’s credibility by showing the writer considered and weighed another possible cause. | D) It completely destroys the argument’s claim about the filter.
why correct: Honestly acknowledging another possible cause, while still presenting strong supporting data, makes an argument more credible, not less.
tip: A thorough argument considers alternative explanations rather than ignoring them.

stem: Two articles both argue for stricter coral reef protections. Article A cites a single tour guide’s opinion that “tourists are ruining the reefs.” Article B cites peer-reviewed marine biology data on coral bleaching rates near high-traffic tourist sites over ten years. Which argument provides stronger support for action, and why?
options / answer: A) Both articles are equally strong since they reach the same conclusion. | B) Article A, because tour guides see the reefs most often. | C) Article A, because opinions are always more persuasive than data. | D) Article B, because long-term, peer-reviewed data provides far more reliable evidence than one person’s opinion.
why correct: Peer-reviewed, long-term data is far more reliable and representative than a single person’s personal opinion.
tip: When comparing arguments, weigh systematic data more heavily than a single, unverified opinion.

stem: True or false style check turned question: does paragraph 2 of “Should Homework Be Optional?” tell a story about one specific student’s day, or does it use research to respond to a claim?
options / answer: A) It uses research evidence to respond to a claim — it counters the idea that homework improves scores with findings from multiple studies. | B) It describes what a typical homework assignment looks like. | C) It lists homework rules from several different countries. | D) It tells a story about one specific student’s homework routine.
why correct: Paragraph 2 states a common claim and then counters it with a review of research studies.
tip: In argument paragraphs, check whether a claim is being tested against evidence.

stem: True or false: paragraph 3 of “Should Homework Be Optional?” is organized as a chronological account of a single school year.
options / answer: True | False
why correct: Paragraph 3 explains what an optional-homework system would look like in practice, not a year-by-year account.
tip: Check what a paragraph is actually doing, not just its general topic.

stem: Which structure describes paragraph 5 of “Should Homework Be Optional?” (the one about stress and sleep) on its own?
options / answer: A) problem and solution — it proposes a specific fix for student stress | B) cause and effect — heavy mandatory homework is shown to cause higher stress and less sleep in students | C) compare and contrast — it compares two different named schools’ homework policies | D) chronological order — it lists stress levels recorded each month of the school year
why correct: The paragraph links one cause (heavy mandatory homework) to two effects (stress and poor sleep).
tip: Look for words like “linked to” that connect a cause to its effects.

stem: How does the author organize paragraph 4 of “Should Homework Be Optional?”, the one addressing the worry about struggling students falling behind?
options / answer: A) It simply restates the article’s main claim three times in a row. | B) It compares struggling students in two different grade levels. | C) It raises a counterargument and then answers it with a new reason, rather than simply repeating the original claim. | D) It lists the exact daily schedule of a struggling student.
why correct: The paragraph names a worry (falling behind), then offers a new, specific reason why flexible homework could actually help.
tip: A strong rebuttal paragraph often follows a worry with a fresh reason, not a repeated claim.

stem: Put these paragraph functions from “Should Homework Be Optional?” in the order they appear in the text.
options / answer: Introduce the issue and state the author’s claim that homework should be optional → Counter the claim that mandatory homework improves achievement, using research → Explain what an optional-homework system would actually look like in practice → Answer the worry that struggling students would fall behind → Link heavy mandatory homework to stress and poor sleep → Restate that flexible homework would likely help both wellbeing and learning
why correct: The article builds step by step: claim, evidence against mandatory homework, a practical explanation, a rebuttal, a wellbeing cost, and a closing restatement.
tip: Identify the JOB each paragraph does, then put those jobs in the order they appear.

stem: Match each paragraph’s main structural job in “Should Homework Be Optional?” with its paragraph number.
options / answer: Paragraph 1 = introduces the issue and states the author’s claim | Paragraph 2 = counters the achievement claim using research evidence | Paragraph 4 = raises and answers the falling-behind counterargument | Paragraph 6 = restates the claim to close the argument
why correct: Each numbered paragraph plays a specific structural role in building the overall argument.
tip: Identify the JOB each paragraph does within the text’s overall structure.

stem: What is paragraph 1 of “Coral Reefs Under Pressure” primarily organized to do?
options / answer: A) list the exact steps scientists use to study a reef | B) explain a single cause-and-effect chain about reef damage | C) compare two different oceans’ reef populations | D) describe several specific ways reefs matter to ocean life, using examples such as fish shelter, sea turtle food and storm protection
why correct: The paragraph lists several distinct examples of why reefs matter, one after another.
tip: A paragraph that names several separate examples about one topic is usually a description structure.

stem: True or false: paragraph 4 of “Coral Reefs Under Pressure” describes two different solutions scientists are trying to help reefs recover.
options / answer: True | False
why correct: Paragraph 4 names both growing corals in nurseries and breeding heat-tolerant corals as two separate responses.
tip: When a paragraph lists more than one fix for the same problem, it is still organized as problem-and-solution.

passage: Should Schools Switch to a Four-Day Week?
stem: Which structure best describes paragraph 3 of “Should Schools Switch to a Four-Day Week?”, the paragraph about saving money?
options / answer: A) claim and evidence — it states the money-saving claim, then presents cost data that undercuts it | B) description only — it simply lists what a school budget contains | C) compare and contrast — it compares bus costs in two different districts | D) chronological order — it lists a school’s budget month by month
why correct: The paragraph states supporters’ money-saving claim and then responds with specific cost figures.
tip: In argumentative texts, check whether a paragraph tests a claim with evidence.

passage: Should Schools Switch to a Four-Day Week?
stem: True or false: the article as a whole, “Should Schools Switch to a Four-Day Week?”, uses chronological order, describing how a single school week changes hour by hour.
options / answer: True | False
why correct: The article is organized around testing supporters’ separate claims with evidence, not around an hour-by-hour account of one week.
tip: Do not assume a structure just from a text’s topic — check how the paragraphs actually connect.

stem: Read this paragraph: “Houseplants kept away from windows often grow pale and droopy. Without enough sunlight, a plant cannot make the food it needs, so its leaves turn yellow and its stems grow weak.” How is this paragraph organized?
options / answer: A) compare and contrast — it compares plants in sunlight to plants without sunlight | B) cause and effect — a lack of sunlight causes the plant’s leaves and stems to weaken | C) problem and solution — it proposes a fix for pale houseplants | D) chronological order — it lists what happens to a plant day by day
why correct: The paragraph explains that one condition (low light) produces a specific effect (weak, pale growth).
tip: Signal words like “so” often point to cause and effect.

stem: Read this paragraph: “The fennec fox has several features suited to desert life. Its huge ears release body heat. Thick fur on its paws protects against hot sand. Its kidneys are built to need very little water.” How is this paragraph organized?
options / answer: A) compare and contrast — it compares the fox to another desert animal | B) cause and effect — each feature causes the next feature to develop | C) description — it lists several separate features that help the fox survive the desert | D) chronological order — the features are listed in the order the fox develops them
why correct: The paragraph lists separate traits of one animal rather than connecting them by cause, time or comparison.
tip: A paragraph listing several traits about one subject is usually a description structure.

stem: Read this paragraph: “First, workers collect used paper and soak it in water until it breaks apart into pulp. Next, the pulp is pressed flat into thin sheets. Finally, the sheets are dried and rolled onto large spools.” How is this paragraph organized?
options / answer: A) compare and contrast — it compares old paper to new paper | B) description — it simply describes what a paper mill looks like | C) cause and effect — each step is a cause that explains why paper is recycled | D) chronological order — it describes the steps of recycling paper in the order they happen
why correct: Words like “first,” “next” and “finally” signal a step-by-step, time-ordered process.
tip: Order words (first, next, then, finally) are the clearest clue to chronological structure.

stem: Read this paragraph: “Bicycles have two wheels and are pedaled by the rider’s legs. Electric scooters also have wheels, but a small motor powers them instead of leg muscles. Both are used for short trips around a neighborhood.” How is this paragraph organized?
options / answer: A) compare and contrast — it shows how bicycles and scooters are alike and different | B) chronological order — it tells the history of how scooters were invented | C) problem and solution — it explains a transportation problem and a fix | D) cause and effect — pedaling causes the scooter’s motor to run
why correct: The paragraph points out a shared feature (wheels, short trips) and a key difference (legs versus motor).
tip: Watch for words like “also” and “but” that signal similarities and differences.

stem: Read this paragraph: “Students at Rawda Middle School complained that the library was too noisy to study in during lunch. The librarian set up a separate quiet room with a sign-in sheet and moved group projects to the cafeteria instead. Within a week, students reported the library felt calm enough to focus.” How is this paragraph organized?
options / answer: A) description — it only describes what the library building looks like | B) problem and solution — it describes a noise problem and the specific steps taken to fix it | C) chronological order — it lists the school’s full daily schedule | D) compare and contrast — it compares the library to the cafeteria
why correct: A specific problem (noise) is named, followed by the concrete actions taken to solve it.
tip: Look for a named problem followed by a fix — that pattern signals problem and solution.

stem: Read this paragraph: “When more cars idle in traffic, engines burn fuel without actually moving anywhere. This wasted fuel releases extra exhaust into the air, and in cities with heavy traffic jams, air quality often gets worse during rush hour.” How is this paragraph organized?
options / answer: A) chronological order — it lists what happens during each hour of a commute | B) compare and contrast — it compares traffic in two different cities | C) cause and effect — idling cars in traffic cause more exhaust, which worsens air quality | D) description — it simply describes what a traffic jam looks like
why correct: One condition (idling traffic) leads directly to a result (worse air quality).
tip: Ask: does one event make another event happen? That is cause and effect.

stem: Read this paragraph: “Clouds come in several basic shapes. Cumulus clouds look like puffy cotton balls. Stratus clouds spread out in flat, gray sheets. Cirrus clouds form thin, feathery streaks high in the sky.” How is this paragraph organized?
options / answer: A) problem and solution — it explains a weather problem clouds create | B) cause and effect — each cloud type causes the next type to form | C) chronological order — it describes clouds in the order they appear each day | D) description — it lists different types of clouds and describes what each one looks like
why correct: The paragraph simply lists separate categories and their features, without connecting them by cause, time or problem.
tip: A paragraph naming several types or categories, one after another, usually uses a description structure.

stem: Read this paragraph: “Keeping savings in a jar at home means the money is easy to reach anytime, but it earns nothing extra over time. Putting the same money in a savings account makes it slightly harder to access quickly, but the bank adds a small amount of interest every year.” How is this paragraph organized?
options / answer: A) compare and contrast — it weighs the trade-offs of keeping money in a jar versus a bank account | B) chronological order — it explains the history of how banks were invented | C) problem and solution — it identifies one single correct way to save money | D) cause and effect — saving in a jar causes people to open a bank account
why correct: The paragraph sets two options side by side and names an advantage and disadvantage of each.
tip: Look for “but” paired with matching features — that is comparison.

stem: Read this paragraph: “When a hillside is cleared of trees, there are no longer any roots to hold the soil in place. Heavy rain then washes the loose topsoil downhill, leaving the land harder for new plants to grow in. Over time, the bare hillside can become almost impossible to farm.” How is this paragraph organized?
options / answer: A) compare and contrast — it compares hillsides with trees to hillsides without rain | B) cause and effect — clearing trees sets off a chain of results, from loose soil to erosion to land that is hard to farm | C) chronological order — it lists the exact dates when hillsides were cleared | D) description — it only describes what a bare hillside looks like
why correct: Each sentence shows one event producing the next: no trees, then loose soil, then erosion, then unfarmable land.
tip: When one effect becomes the cause of the next effect, that is a cause-and-effect chain.

stem: Read this paragraph: “Many students who rode bikes to Al-Nour School left them leaning against the fence, where they often got knocked over or blocked the sidewalk. The student council proposed installing numbered bike racks near the main gate, and the school agreed to install twenty of them before the new term began.” How is this paragraph organized?
options / answer: A) cause and effect — leaning bikes against the fence caused the fence to break | B) compare and contrast — it compares bike racks at two different schools | C) problem and solution — it names a bike-parking problem and the specific solution the council proposed and the school carried out | D) description — it only describes what the bikes looked like
why correct: A specific problem (poorly parked bikes) is followed by a concrete plan that solves it.
tip: Problem-and-solution paragraphs usually name a difficulty, then describe exactly what fixed it.

stem: Read this paragraph: “In the 1950s, farmers in Deir al-Wadi sold vegetables from the backs of trucks parked along the main road. By the 1980s, the town had built a covered market with permanent stalls. Today, the same market also hosts a weekend crafts fair alongside the vegetable sellers.” How is this paragraph organized?
options / answer: A) problem and solution — it describes a problem with the covered market | B) description — it only describes what the market stalls look like | C) cause and effect — the crafts fair caused the vegetable sellers to leave | D) chronological order — it traces how the town’s market changed from the 1950s to today
why correct: Specific time markers (1950s, 1980s, today) trace the market’s development across decades.
tip: Dates or decades lined up in order are a strong signal of chronological structure.

stem: Read this paragraph: “A violin has four main parts. The body is a hollow wooden box that makes the sound louder. The neck holds the fingerboard where a player presses the strings.
