The bridge lifts the strings above the body. The scroll at the top holds the tuning pegs.” How is this paragraph organized?
options / answer: A) description — it names and explains each main part of a violin, one at a time | B) chronological order — it explains the steps for building a violin over time | C) cause and effect — the bridge causes the scroll to hold the tuning pegs | D) compare and contrast — it compares a violin to another instrument
why correct: Each sentence introduces one labeled part and what it does, without connecting them by time or cause.
tip: A list of labeled parts, each explained separately, is a description structure.

stem: Read this paragraph: “Basketball requires a hoop at a fixed height and rewards players who can dribble while running. Volleyball, on the other hand, is played over a net and depends on quick reactions rather than ball-handling while moving. Both games, however, reward teamwork and communication between teammates on the move.” How is this paragraph organized?
options / answer: A) chronological order — it explains the history of each sport | B) compare and contrast — it points out key differences between basketball and volleyball while noting one shared quality | C) cause and effect — dribbling in basketball causes volleyball players to react quickly | D) problem and solution — it solves a disagreement about which sport is better
why correct: The paragraph sets the two sports side by side, naming a difference for each and then a shared trait.
tip: Phrases like “on the other hand” and “both … however” are strong compare-and-contrast signals.

stem: Read this paragraph: “During deep sleep, the brain strengthens connections between neurons that were active while a person was learning something new that day. Students who sleep fewer than six hours tend to remember less of what they studied the day before, because this strengthening process is cut short. Over weeks of poor sleep, this effect can add up to noticeably weaker test performance.” How is this paragraph organized?
options / answer: A) description — it only describes what happens physically inside the brain during sleep | B) compare and contrast — it compares students who sleep six hours to students who sleep eight hours | C) cause and effect — too little sleep interrupts memory strengthening, which weakens memory and eventually test performance | D) chronological order — it lists the stages of a person’s sleep cycle in order
why correct: The paragraph traces a chain: less sleep interrupts a brain process, which lowers memory, which lowers test scores.
tip: When a result keeps leading to a further result, trace the whole chain of causes and effects.

stem: Read this paragraph: “Fishing fleets off one coastal town had been catching so many young sardines that the overall sardine population began shrinking every year. Marine officials introduced a seasonal catch limit and required nets with wider holes so young fish could escape. Within three years, sardine numbers in the area had begun to recover.” How is this paragraph organized?
options / answer: A) description — it only describes what a fishing net looks like | B) compare and contrast — it compares sardine fishing to tuna fishing | C) chronological order — it lists every year’s exact catch numbers | D) problem and solution — it names a shrinking-fish-population problem and the specific rules that helped fix it
why correct: A clear problem (shrinking sardine population) is followed by the specific actions that reversed it.
tip: Look for a result (recovery, improvement) that follows directly after a described fix.

stem: Read this paragraph: “In 1876, the first working telephone could only connect two specific points joined by a single wire. By the 1890s, cities had built switchboards so that any customer’s call could be connected to any other customer in town. By the mid-1900s, long-distance cables let callers reach other cities and even other countries.” How is this paragraph organized?
options / answer: A) chronological order — it traces how telephone networks expanded from 1876 through the mid-1900s | B) compare and contrast — it compares telephones to telegraphs | C) cause and effect — switchboards caused the invention of the telephone | D) problem and solution — it describes one single problem with modern phones
why correct: Specific years (1876, 1890s, mid-1900s) mark each stage of the network’s growth in order.
tip: A string of dates or eras, each building on the last, signals chronological structure.

stem: Read this paragraph: “A rural village had no streetlights, so people avoided walking after dark because of poor visibility. The village council installed solar-powered lamps along the main road, which charge during the day and turn on automatically at dusk. Since the lamps needed no wiring to the village's main power grid, installation took only two weeks. Residents now report walking after dark far more often than before.” How is this paragraph organized?
options / answer: A) cause and effect only, with no solution described | B) problem and solution — it names a safety problem from the dark and explains how solar lamps solved it quickly | C) chronological order — it lists the full history of solar lamp technology | D) compare and contrast — it compares solar lamps to lamps connected to the power grid
why correct: A specific problem (unsafe darkness) is followed by a specific, quickly installed fix (solar lamps) and a result (more walking after dark).
tip: Look for a named problem followed by an action that fixes it.

stem: Read this paragraph: “A few years after zebra mussels were accidentally introduced to a freshwater lake, fishers noticed the water had become unusually clear. The mussels filter huge amounts of plankton from the water as they feed, and plankton is the main food source for many small native fish. As plankton grew scarce, several native fish species that once thrived in the lake began to decline sharply.” How is this paragraph organized?
options / answer: A) description — it only describes what zebra mussels look like | B) problem and solution — it proposes a way to remove the mussels from the lake | C) cause and effect — the mussels’ feeding reduces plankton, which then causes native fish populations to decline | D) compare and contrast — it compares zebra mussels to a native mussel species
why correct: The clearer water, the mussels’ feeding, the shrinking plankton and the declining fish form one connected chain of causes and effects.
tip: In nature articles, trace how one species’ feeding habit can ripple through to affect other species.

stem: Read this paragraph: “Solar panels generate the most electricity around midday, when sunlight is strongest, but produce almost nothing at night. Wind turbines can generate power at any hour, as long as the wind is blowing, but calm days leave them nearly idle. Because the two sources tend to be weak at different times, many power grids combine both to keep electricity flowing more steadily.” How is this paragraph organized?
options / answer: A) cause and effect — solar panels cause wind turbines to generate more power | B) chronological order — it explains the order in which solar and wind technology were invented | C) description — it only describes what a wind turbine looks like | D) compare and contrast — it contrasts when solar and wind power are strong or weak, then explains why combining them helps
why correct: The paragraph lines up a weakness of each source and shows how pairing them offsets those weaknesses.
tip: When two things are each strong where the other is weak, that pairing itself is a form of comparison.

stem: Read this paragraph: “Patients at a busy clinic were often waiting more than two hours past their scheduled appointment time, mostly because urgent walk-in cases kept interrupting the daily schedule. The clinic began setting aside two short blocks each day reserved only for walk-ins, so scheduled appointments would no longer be bumped. Average wait times for scheduled patients dropped by almost half within a month.” How is this paragraph organized?
options / answer: A) problem and solution — it identifies the cause of long waits and explains the scheduling change that reduced them | B) compare and contrast — it compares this clinic’s wait times to another clinic’s | C) description — it only describes what the clinic’s waiting room looks like | D) chronological order — it lists the clinic’s exact opening and closing times
why correct: A specific cause of delay is diagnosed, a scheduling fix is applied, and a clear result (reduced wait time) follows.
tip: Good problem-and-solution paragraphs often name why the problem happened, not just what the problem was.

stem: Read this paragraph: “Coffee cherries are first picked by hand when they turn deep red. They are then either dried whole in the sun for several weeks or washed to remove the outer fruit immediately after picking. Once dried, the inner beans are hulled, sorted by size, and finally roasted just before shipping.” How is this paragraph organized?
options / answer: A) compare and contrast — it only compares sun-dried coffee to washed coffee | B) chronological order — it follows coffee cherries through each stage of processing, from picking to roasting | C) problem and solution — it explains a problem with roasting coffee too early | D) cause and effect — picking the cherries causes them to turn red
why correct: The paragraph moves step by step through the stages a coffee cherry passes through, ending in roasting.
tip: Process paragraphs that move from raw material to finished product are chronological in structure.

stem: Read this paragraph: “Canned vegetables can sit safely in a pantry for a year or more because the sealed can and the heat used during canning kill the bacteria that cause spoilage. Fresh vegetables keep their vitamins and texture better, but they spoil within days unless refrigerated, since nothing stops bacteria from growing on them right away. Because of this trade-off, many families buy some of each, choosing fresh vegetables for the week ahead and canned ones for longer storage.” How is this paragraph organized?
options / answer: A) chronological order — it explains the history of how canning was invented | B) problem and solution — it identifies one single best way to store all vegetables | C) compare and contrast — it weighs shelf life against freshness for canned versus fresh vegetables and explains how that trade-off affects shopping choices | D) cause and effect only — refrigeration is shown as the one cause of all food spoilage
why correct: The paragraph names an advantage and disadvantage of each storage method, then shows how that comparison shapes a real choice.
tip: When a paragraph ends by explaining how people act because of a trade-off, trace back to the comparison that created it.

stem: Read this paragraph: “Dark asphalt and concrete absorb far more sunlight than grass or trees do, and they release that heat back into the surrounding air for hours after sunset. Because many cities are covered mostly in these materials, nighttime temperatures downtown can stay several degrees warmer than in nearby suburbs with more greenery. Some cities have responded by painting rooftops white and planting trees along streets to reduce this effect.” How is this paragraph organized?
options / answer: A) pure description — it only describes what asphalt looks like | B) pure compare and contrast — it only compares two specific named cities to each other | C) pure chronological order — it lists the exact hour each city planted its first tree | D) cause and effect, with a brief problem-and-solution ending — dark surfaces trap heat and raise city temperatures, and the final sentence adds a response some cities have tried
why correct: Most of the paragraph builds a cause-and-effect chain (dark materials, trapped heat, warmer nights), and the last sentence briefly shifts to a solution being tried.
tip: A paragraph can blend two structures — look at where a shift happens, often in the final sentence.

stem: Read this paragraph: “Rain-fed farms depend entirely on seasonal rainfall, so a dry year can cut their harvest drastically, but farmers save on the cost and labor of watering. Irrigated farms water their crops on a steady schedule regardless of rainfall, which protects yields during dry years, but the pumps and canals needed are expensive to build and maintain. Because of this trade-off, many regions use rain-fed farming where rainfall is reliable and irrigation only where it is not.” How is this paragraph organized?
options / answer: A) compare and contrast — it weighs the risks and costs of rain-fed versus irrigated farming and explains how that trade-off shapes farmers’ choices | B) cause and effect only — dry years are shown as the single cause of all farming decisions | C) problem and solution — it identifies irrigation as the one correct fix for all farms | D) chronological order — it explains how irrigation technology developed over the centuries
why correct: The paragraph sets the two farming methods side by side, naming a benefit and a drawback for each, then explains how that comparison guides a choice.
tip: When a paragraph names a trade-off for each option and then draws a conclusion from comparing them, that is compare and contrast.

stem: Read this paragraph: “Many recycling programs found that bins meant only for paper and plastic were filled with food waste, greasy pizza boxes and broken glass, ruining otherwise recyclable material. Several cities responded by printing clear picture guides on every bin lid and fining repeat offenders who ignored the rules. Contamination rates in those cities fell by nearly a third within two years, though officials noted that ongoing public education remained necessary to keep rates low.” How is this paragraph organized?
options / answer: A) description only — it simply describes what is typically found inside a recycling bin | B) problem and solution — it names the contamination problem, describes two specific fixes, and reports a result while noting the fix still needs upkeep | C) chronological order only — it lists each city’s recycling program by the year it was founded | D) compare and contrast only — it compares recycling rules in different countries
why correct: A specific problem (contamination) leads to specific fixes (guides, fines) and a measured result, with a closing note about ongoing effort.
tip: A strong problem-and-solution paragraph often ends by noting whether the fix was complete or still needs more work.

stem: Read this paragraph: “After a severe flood destroyed hundreds of homes along the river in 1962, the city built its first levee system within five years. A second, larger flood in 1998 revealed that the original levees were too low, so engineers raised and reinforced them throughout the early 2000s. Because of these upgrades, a comparably large flood in 2019 caused far less damage to the same neighborhoods.” How is this paragraph organized?
options / answer: A) problem and solution with no time order — it treats all three floods as happening at the same time | B) pure description — it only describes what a levee looks like | C) chronological order built around cause and effect — each flood (1962, 1998, 2019) prompts a response, and the paragraph tracks how those responses changed outcomes over time | D) pure compare and contrast — it only compares the 1962 flood to the 2019 flood, ignoring everything else
why correct: Three dated floods are presented in order, and each one’s cause-and-effect relationship to the city’s levee response is tracked across time.
tip: When dates anchor a chain of causes and effects, the structure is chronological but driven by cause and effect.

stem: Read this paragraph: “Bacteria reproduce so quickly that a population exposed to an antibiotic may include a few individuals with a random mutation that happens to resist the drug. Because the antibiotic kills off the non-resistant bacteria, the resistant ones survive and reproduce, passing the resistance trait to their offspring. Over many rounds of this process, especially when antibiotics are overused or not finished as prescribed, a bacterial population can become mostly or entirely resistant. Doctors have responded by prescribing antibiotics more selectively and completing full treatment courses to reduce how often this cycle repeats.” How is this paragraph organized?
options / answer: A) chronological order with specific dates for each stage of resistance | B) a single, one-time cause and effect — one antibiotic dose permanently makes all bacteria resistant forever | C) compare and contrast between two different bacteria species | D) a repeating cause-and-effect cycle that builds to a problem, followed by a brief solution — each round of antibiotic use causes resistant bacteria to multiply, and the final sentence adds how doctors are responding
why correct: The paragraph explains a repeating mechanism (mutation, survival, reproduction, repeat) that builds toward a problem, then closes with how doctors are addressing it.
tip: Some structures repeat in a cycle rather than happening only once — look for words like “over many rounds” or “repeats.”

stem: Read this paragraph: “When a key factory that supplied a specific computer chip shut down after a storm, several electronics companies that depended on that single supplier could not finish assembling their products, even though every other part was ready. Prices for finished electronics using that chip rose within weeks, since the remaining chip supply could not meet demand. In response, some companies began sourcing the same chip from two or more factories instead of just one, even though this raised their costs slightly, in order to avoid being stopped completely by a single factory’s shutdown again.” How is this paragraph organized?
options / answer: A) cause and effect leading into a problem-and-solution ending — the factory shutdown causes a supply shortage and price increase, and companies then adopt a strategy to prevent the same cause from stopping them again | B) compare and contrast between two competing computer chip brands | C) description only, detailing what the factory building looked like after the storm | D) chronological order listing the exact date of every price increase
why correct: A single cause (the shutdown) triggers a chain of effects (shortage, price rise), and the paragraph ends by describing a solution companies adopted to prevent a repeat.
tip: In cause-and-effect writing about business or systems, look for a shift at the end toward prevention — that often signals an added problem-and-solution layer.

stem: Read this paragraph: “A species of migratory bird has relied for centuries on wetlands along its route to rest and refuel during a journey of several thousand kilometers. As many of those wetlands have been drained for farmland over the past fifty years, the birds now face longer stretches without a safe place to stop, and researchers have recorded a steady decline in the number of birds completing the full migration each year. Conservation groups in several countries along the route have begun restoring small sections of wetland and coordinating the timing of protections so that no single country’s efforts are undone by another’s lack of action.” How is this paragraph organized?
options / answer: A) a simple list of facts about the bird’s appearance and diet | B) cause and effect across a long time span, ending with a solution that requires coordination among several causes of the original problem — wetland loss (cause) reduces migration success (effect), and the final sentence describes a multi-country response | C) chronological order with each country’s protection law dated individually | D) compare and contrast between two different bird species that share the same route
why correct: The paragraph traces how a decades-long cause (wetland loss) produces a specific effect (fewer successful migrations), then closes with a coordinated, multi-country solution.
tip: When several separate causes (draining wetlands in different places) combine to create one large effect, solving it usually also requires coordinated action.

stem: Read this paragraph: “Bus ridership in one mid-sized city fell by nearly a third after routes were cut and fares were raised during a budget shortfall, forcing many riders to rely on cars instead and worsening downtown traffic. City planners later restored the cut routes and froze fares for two years while also adding real-time arrival screens at major stops so riders could trust the schedule again. Ridership slowly climbed back over the following three years, though it still has not fully returned to its earlier levels.” How is this paragraph organized?
options / answer: A) pure compare and contrast between bus ridership in two different cities | B) pure description of what the city’s buses and bus stops look like | C) cause and effect followed by problem and solution — budget cuts cause falling ridership and worse traffic, and the city’s multi-part response only partially reverses that effect over time | D) pure chronological order with no cause-and-effect connections between events
why correct: A budget cut causes a specific effect (falling ridership), and the city’s later actions address that problem, though the paragraph notes the fix is still incomplete.
tip: Look for a result described as only partly fixed, such as “still has not fully returned” — that often signals a blended cause-effect and problem-solution structure.

stem: Read this paragraph: “Along one stretch of coastline, a storm destroyed homes built behind a cleared beach, while homes behind a stretch of mangrove forest just a few kilometers away suffered far less damage, because the mangroves’ dense roots absorbed much of the wave energy before it reached land. Engineers initially proposed building a concrete seawall to replace the lost protection, but a mangrove-restoration project turned out to cost less and also created a fish nursery that supported the area’s fishing economy. Because of these added benefits, the restoration plan was eventually chosen over the seawall.” How is this paragraph organized?
options / answer: A) pure chronological order, with every event dated to a specific year | B) pure description of what a mangrove tree looks like | C) pure problem and solution, with no comparison between the two proposed solutions | D) cause and effect combined with compare and contrast, ending in problem and solution — the mangroves’ root structure explains the damage difference, two solutions are compared, and one is chosen for its added benefits
why correct: The paragraph blends three patterns: a cause-and-effect explanation for the damage difference, a comparison of two proposed fixes, and a final choice based on added benefits.
tip: Longer paragraphs often blend structures — identify each piece (why something happened, what options were compared, what was finally decided) separately.

stem: Read this paragraph: “A disease that spreads easily needs a certain percentage of a population to be immune before outbreaks stop spreading widely, a point researchers call the herd immunity threshold; for a highly contagious disease, that percentage can be quite high. When vaccination rates in one region fell below that threshold after a period of low turnout at clinics, a localized outbreak spread quickly among unvaccinated children, even though most adults in the same region were already immune. Health officials responded with a focused campaign at schools specifically, rather than a general public campaign, because the gap was concentrated almost entirely among that one age group.” How is this paragraph organized?
options / answer: A) a definition followed by cause and effect and then a targeted solution — the paragraph first explains a concept, then shows how falling below it caused an outbreak in one group, then describes a response matched specifically to that group | B) pure chronological order, with the outbreak and the campaign given specific calendar dates | C) pure compare and contrast between two different diseases | D) pure description of what the disease’s symptoms look like
why correct: The paragraph opens by defining a concept, then traces how falling below that threshold caused a specific outbreak, then explains a solution matched to the specific group affected.
tip: When a paragraph defines a term before explaining an event, check whether the definition itself is doing structural work — setting up the cause that follows.

stem: Choose the correct word: “The ____ nest fell from the tree.”
options / answer: A) birds | B) bird’s | C) birds’ | D) bird
why correct: One bird owns the nest, so add an apostrophe and s: bird’s.
tip: Singular owner: add ’s.

stem: Choose the correct word: “The ____ bones were buried under the porch.”
options / answer: A) dog’s’s | B) dog’s | C) dogs’ | D) dogs
why correct: More than one dog owns the bones, so the plural dogs takes only an apostrophe: dogs’.
tip: Plural ending in s: add only an apostrophe.

stem: Which sentence uses a possessive noun correctly?
options / answer: A) My neighbors garden is full of roses. | B) My neighbor’s garden is full of roses. | C) My neighbors’s garden is full of roses. | D) My neighbor’s are full of roses.
why correct: One neighbor owns the garden, so “neighbor’s” is correct.
tip: Read the sentence aloud — does it sound like “belonging to”?

stem: Choose the correct word: “The ____ shells were scattered on the beach.”
options / answer: A) turtle’s | B) turtle | C) turtles | D) turtles’
why correct: Many turtles own the shells, so the plural turtles takes only an apostrophe.
tip: Plural already ending in s: add only an apostrophe.

stem: Tap the part of the sentence that has an error.
options / answer: The three puppies |  tails |  wagged happily.
why correct: Three puppies own the tails, so add an apostrophe after the s: puppies’.
tip: Plural nouns ending in s only need an apostrophe, not an extra s.

stem: Choose the correct word: “The ____ boots were covered in mud.”
options / answer: A) men’s | B) mens’ | C) mens | D) man’s
why correct: “Men” is already plural and does not end in s, so add ’s: men’s.
tip: Irregular plurals (men, women, mice, geese) add ’s just like singular nouns.

stem: Which sentence uses a possessive noun correctly?
options / answer: A) The gooses’ feathers covered the pond. | B) The geese feathers covered the pond. | C) The geese’s feathers covered the pond. | D) The geeses’ feathers covered the pond.
why correct: “Geese” is the irregular plural of goose, and since it does not end in s, add ’s.
tip: Learn irregular plurals first, then add ’s if they do not end in s.

stem: Type the correct possessive form of “girl” to complete the sentence: The ____ bike had a flat tire.
options / answer: (typed)
why correct: One girl owns the bike, so add ’s: girl’s.
tip: Singular owner: add an apostrophe and s.

stem: Which sentence shows that a set of bikes is owned by MORE THAN ONE girl?
options / answer: A) The girl bikes leaned against the fence. | B) The girl’s bikes leaned against the fence. | C) The girls bikes leaned against the fence. | D) The girls’ bikes leaned against the fence.

stem: Read this paragraph: “Volunteers at an animal shelter noticed that many dogs stayed longer when their photos online looked blurry or dark. The shelter began taking brighter, better-lit photos of every new dog and writing a short, friendly description for each one. Within two months, dogs were being adopted almost twice as quickly as before. The shelter now trains every new volunteer in basic photography before letting them help with adoptions.” What is the main idea of this paragraph?
options / answer: A) The shelter stopped posting photos of dogs online entirely. | B) Improving online photos and descriptions helped shelter dogs get adopted much faster. | C) Volunteers were no longer needed once the new photos were posted. | D) Dogs with blurry photos were adopted faster than other dogs.
why correct: The paragraph connects a specific change (better photos) to a clear result (faster adoptions), which is its main idea.
tip: Find the change a paragraph describes, then the result that followed.

stem: Read this paragraph: “A small coastal town used to lose several fishing boats every year when sudden storms caught sailors by surprise far from shore. After installing a simple weather-warning siren at the harbor, boats could return to safety before a storm fully formed. Boat losses dropped sharply in the years after the siren was installed, though a few sailors still ignored the warning when fish were plentiful.” What is the main idea of this paragraph, including the detail about sailors who ignored the siren?
options / answer: A) Sailors ignored the siren because it was too quiet to hear. | B) The siren completely ended all boat losses in the town forever. | C) A harbor warning siren greatly reduced storm-related boat losses, although not every sailor heeded it. | D) The town removed the siren because it did not work.
why correct: A complete main idea should include both the siren's clear benefit and the detail that it did not solve the problem for every sailor.
tip: When a paragraph ends with an exception, a strong main-idea statement should mention it too.

stem: Read this paragraph: “A small bakery began offering free bread to anyone who came by just before closing time, rather than throwing away unsold loaves. At first, only a handful of neighbors came by each evening, but word spread, and soon a small line formed every night. The owner noticed that many of these same visitors became regular paying customers earlier in the day, since they now trusted the bakery and visited more often. What began as a way to reduce waste ended up growing the bakery's daily business as well.” Which statement BEST captures the main idea of this paragraph?
options / answer: A) The bakery stopped selling bread during the day to focus on giving it away at night. | B) Giving away bread caused the bakery to lose money overall. | C) Only strangers who never returned came for the free bread. | D) Giving away unsold bread not only reduced waste but also unexpectedly helped the bakery gain more regular daytime customers.
why correct: A full main-idea statement should include both the original goal (reducing waste) and the surprising additional benefit (growing the daytime business).
tip: When a paragraph describes an unexpected extra result, a strong main-idea statement captures both the original purpose and that result.

stem: Read this paragraph: “Octopuses are known for their remarkable intelligence among invertebrates. They can solve simple puzzles to reach hidden food. Many octopuses have escaped from aquarium tanks by figuring out how to open lids. Scientists have even observed them using tools, such as carrying shells to use as shelter later.” What is the central idea of this paragraph?
options / answer: A) Octopuses show several signs of surprising intelligence for an invertebrate. | B) Octopuses cannot solve any kind of puzzle. | C) No other invertebrate has ever been studied by scientists. | D) Aquariums are specially designed so octopuses can never escape.
why correct: Each example — puzzle-solving, escaping tanks and tool use — supports the same overall claim about octopus intelligence.
tip: Look for the one idea that connects every specific example in a paragraph.

stem: Read this paragraph: “Many cities are adding more bicycle lanes to busy streets. Protected lanes with a physical barrier reduce accidents between cyclists and cars. Cities with more bike lanes often see fewer traffic jams, since some drivers switch to biking instead. Bike lanes can also encourage more people to exercise as part of their daily commute.” What is the central idea of this paragraph?
options / answer: A) Protected bike lanes have no effect on cyclist safety. | B) Adding bicycle lanes brings several benefits to a city, from safety to traffic to health. | C) Bicycle lanes always make traffic jams worse. | D) People who bike to work rarely get any exercise.
why correct: The paragraph lists three separate benefits of bike lanes, all supporting one overall claim about their value to a city.
tip: When several distinct benefits are listed, the central idea usually ties them together.

stem: Read this paragraph: “Icebergs form when large chunks of ice break off from glaciers or ice shelves and drift into the ocean. Only about one-tenth of an iceberg is visible above the water's surface, while the rest remains hidden below. This hidden mass makes icebergs especially dangerous to ships, since a vessel can misjudge how far the ice actually extends underwater. Sailors have used sonar for decades to measure an iceberg's true size before sailing nearby.” What is the central idea of this paragraph?
options / answer: A) Sonar was invented specifically to study icebergs. | B) Icebergs form only from ocean water freezing in place. | C) Icebergs are more dangerous than they appear because most of their size is hidden underwater. | D) Icebergs are completely visible above the water's surface.
why correct: The paragraph's details about hidden mass and sonar use both support the central idea about hidden danger.
tip: Find the idea that explains why the paragraph includes the detail about sonar.

stem: Which TWO details support the central idea that coral reefs face serious threats from warming oceans?
options / answer: A) Warm water causes coral to expel the algae that give it color and food. | B) Some tourists enjoy snorkeling near coral reefs. | C) Coral reefs are found in oceans all around the world. | D) Prolonged high temperatures can cause bleached coral to die.
why correct: These two details directly explain how warming water damages and can kill coral.
tip: Choose details that explain the THREAT itself, not background facts about reefs.

stem: Read this paragraph: “Public libraries have begun offering more than just books to borrow. Many now lend out tools, sewing machines and even telescopes for a short period. Some libraries host free coding classes and resume-writing workshops for adults. These added services have drawn in visitors who might never have come in for books alone.” What is the central idea of this paragraph?
options / answer: A) Telescopes are the most popular item libraries now lend. | B) Libraries have stopped lending books to focus on other services. | C) Only children are interested in the new library services. | D) Libraries are attracting new visitors by offering services beyond just lending books.
why correct: The paragraph lists several new services and ends by connecting them to a central claim about attracting new visitors.
tip: Look at the final sentence of a paragraph — it often restates the central idea in general terms.

stem: Read this paragraph: “Researchers studying ant colonies have found that ants use chemical trails, called pheromones, to communicate with each other. When an ant finds food, it leaves a pheromone trail back to the colony. Other ants follow the strongest trail, which helps the colony quickly focus on the best food source. Over time, weaker trails to less useful food fade away entirely.” Which sentence BEST restates the central idea of this paragraph?
options / answer: A) Ants use chemical trails to communicate and efficiently guide the colony toward the best food sources. | B) Every ant trail leads to a different food source forever. | C) Ants communicate only through physical touch, never chemicals. | D) Ants cannot tell the difference between a strong and a weak trail.
why correct: This sentence combines the paragraph's details about pheromones, trail-following and fading trails into one general idea.
tip: A strong restatement should combine separate details into one overall claim.

stem: Read this paragraph: “A regional airline began charging passengers a small fee to check a bag, while making the fee free for passengers who booked online a week in advance. Ticket sales rose for flights booked early, since the discount gave travelers a clear reason to plan ahead instead of waiting until the last minute. Flights booked at the last minute, which used to fill up with checked bags, now carry noticeably less luggage overall. The airline credits the new fee structure with both steadier bookings and lighter planes.” What is the central idea of this paragraph?
options / answer: A) Passengers who book early now check more bags than before. | B) A new baggage fee structure changed passenger behavior in ways that benefited the airline in two separate ways. | C) The new fee structure had no effect on when people booked flights. | D) The airline removed baggage fees for all passengers.
why correct: The paragraph connects one policy change to two distinct results — steadier bookings and lighter planes — which together form the central idea.
tip: When a paragraph names two separate results from one cause, the central idea usually covers both.

stem: Read this paragraph: “A community garden project initially struggled because most plots sat empty during the hottest summer weeks, when volunteers avoided working outside. Organizers moved the main watering and harvesting schedule to early morning and evening instead of midday. Plot usage rose significantly once volunteers no longer had to work during the worst heat, though a few plots near the garden's shadeless edge remained harder to keep staffed.” What is the central idea of this paragraph, including the detail about the shadeless plots?
options / answer: A) The shadeless plots were the only ones that were ever used. | B) Changing the schedule solved every single staffing problem completely. | C) Rescheduling garden work around the hottest hours fixed most of the staffing problem, though a few especially hot plots stayed harder to maintain. | D) Volunteers avoided the garden entirely, even after the schedule changed.
why correct: A complete central-idea statement should include both the main improvement and the specific detail about the remaining exception.
tip: When a paragraph closes with “though” or “however,” check whether that detail belongs in a complete central-idea statement.

stem: Read this paragraph: “A regional hospital introduced color-coded wristbands to flag patients with specific allergies, replacing handwritten notes that staff sometimes missed during busy shifts. Allergy-related medication errors dropped noticeably within the first six months of using the wristbands. However, the hospital later found that wristbands sometimes slipped off during long procedures, so staff began double-checking allergy status in the patient's digital chart as well.” What is the central idea of this paragraph, including the limitation that was discovered later?
options / answer: A) The wristbands completely replaced every other safety check at the hospital. | B) The hospital stopped using wristbands once the slipping problem was discovered. | C) Handwritten notes were found to be more reliable than the wristbands. | D) Color-coded wristbands reduced allergy-related errors, but the hospital had to add a digital backup check after discovering the wristbands could slip off.
why correct: A full central-idea statement should include both the wristbands' clear benefit and the specific limitation that led to an added safeguard.
tip: When a text reports a fix and then a later discovered flaw, the central idea usually needs to mention both.

stem: Read this paragraph: “A small publishing company began offering authors a choice between a traditional contract with a larger upfront payment and a smaller upfront payment paired with a higher share of ongoing sales. Most new authors chose the larger upfront payment, valuing certainty over a book's uncertain future sales. Authors whose first books had sold unusually well, however, increasingly chose the second option for their next book, trusting their track record to earn more over time. The company found that offering both options kept both new and established authors satisfied in different ways.” Which statement BEST captures the central idea of this paragraph?
options / answer: A) Giving authors a choice between two payment structures satisfied different authors differently, based on their experience and confidence in future sales. | B) Authors with successful first books always regretted choosing the second option. | C) The company eliminated the traditional upfront-payment contract entirely. | D) Every author at the company always prefers the same payment option.
why correct: A full central-idea statement should capture that the options appealed to different groups for different, text-stated reasons.
tip: When a paragraph explains WHY different groups made different choices, the central idea should reflect that reasoning, not just the choices themselves.

stem: What is the central idea of “Should Homework Be Optional?”
options / answer: A) Teachers dislike grading homework assignments. | B) Homework should be optional and matched to each student's needs rather than required for everyone the same way. | C) All homework should be eliminated completely. | D) Students who get less homework always score higher on tests.
why correct: Every paragraph builds toward the idea that flexible, needs-based homework serves students better than a required, one-size-fits-all approach.
tip: The central idea usually appears near the beginning and is restated at the end.

stem: Which detail BEST supports the central idea that mandatory homework may not actually raise achievement?
options / answer: A) Heavy homework loads are linked to stress and poor sleep. | B) Teachers could still assign practice problems under an optional system. | C) A review of multiple studies found a weak connection between homework and achievement for younger students. | D) Students spend hours on homework after a full school day.
why correct: This research finding directly challenges the claim that homework improves test scores.
tip: Look for the detail that is evidence, not just background information.

stem: Which TWO sentences belong in an objective summary of the homework article's central ideas?
options / answer: A) Every teacher secretly agrees that homework should end. | B) Heavy mandatory homework is linked to higher stress and less sleep for students. | C) Research shows a weak link between required homework and achievement, especially for younger students. | D) Homework is the most stressful part of being a student.
why correct: Objective summaries include only facts and findings stated in the text, not opinions.
tip: Ask whether the article itself states the sentence as evidence, or whether it is an added opinion.

stem: How does the central idea of “Should Homework Be Optional?” develop across the text?
options / answer: A) It lists homework rules from several different countries. | B) It focuses only on one single piece of evidence, repeated five times. | C) It tells a personal story about one struggling student. | D) Each paragraph adds a new piece of evidence — achievement, flexibility, targeted support and wellbeing — building toward the same recommendation.
why correct: The article layers several different kinds of evidence, each supporting the same central recommendation.
tip: Track how each new paragraph adds a different kind of support for the same idea.

stem: Which sentence would BEST conclude a summary of the central idea of “Should Homework Be Optional?”?
options / answer: A) Matching homework to what each student actually needs would likely help both learning and wellbeing more than requiring the same amount for everyone. | B) Homework should always be assigned on Fridays. | C) Students who finish homework quickly should receive extra assignments. | D) Parents should check their children's homework every night.
why correct: This sentence captures the article's final recommendation, which ties together all the evidence presented.
tip: A strong concluding sentence should connect back to the article's opening claim.

stem: A reader claims the homework article argues homework should be banned entirely for all grade levels. Is this an accurate statement of the article's central idea?
options / answer: A) Yes, because the article never mentions homework being assigned at all. | B) No — the article argues homework should become optional and flexible, not banned, and it focuses specifically on elementary and middle school students. | C) Yes, because test scores always drop when homework is assigned. | D) No, because the article argues homework should increase for struggling students only.
why correct: The article's actual claim is for flexibility and optionality, not elimination, and it is specific about which age groups the evidence applies to.
tip: Check a restated central idea carefully against both WHAT the text claims and WHO it is about.

stem: Read this paragraph: “Urban beekeeping has grown quickly in several major cities over the past decade. Rooftop hives give bees access to park flowers without competing with rural farmland. City-produced honey often sells at a premium because customers see it as a novelty. Beyond honey, these urban bee colonies help pollinate street trees and community gardens that might otherwise produce less fruit.” What is the central idea of this paragraph?
options / answer: A) Urban honey always costs less than honey from rural farms. | B) Rooftop hives compete directly with rural farms for the same bees. | C) Keeping bees in cities benefits both beekeepers and the surrounding urban environment in more than one way. | D) Community gardens cannot survive without rooftop beehives nearby.
why correct: The paragraph names several distinct benefits — honey, novelty value and pollination — that together support one overall idea about the value of urban beekeeping.
tip: When several different benefits are listed, the central idea usually ties them together with one general claim.

stem: Read this paragraph: “A growing number of companies now let employees choose between working from an office, working from home, or splitting their week between the two. Early data suggests that fully remote workers report the most flexibility but also the most difficulty feeling connected to coworkers. Employees who split their time report feeling nearly as flexible while staying better connected to their teams, which is why many companies are now encouraging this hybrid option over either extreme.” Which sentence BEST states the central idea of this paragraph?
options / answer: A) Fully remote work is always the best option for every employee. | B) Working in an office at all times guarantees strong teamwork. | C) Companies should let employees choose any schedule without tracking results. | D) A mix of in-office and remote work may balance flexibility and connection better than choosing only one extreme.
why correct: The paragraph compares three work arrangements and builds toward a recommendation for the middle option, which is the central idea.
tip: When a paragraph compares options and ends by favoring one, that favored option is usually the central idea.

stem: Read this paragraph: “Several hospitals recently began offering patients a short recovery survey by text message instead of a lengthy phone call days after a procedure. Response rates rose sharply because patients could reply in a free moment rather than scheduling a call, and hospitals received feedback faster, letting staff address complications sooner. However, patients without reliable phone access or who were less comfortable with texting were sometimes missed entirely, so several hospitals also kept a phone-call option available for those patients.” Which statement BEST captures the central idea of this paragraph, including its limitation?
options / answer: A) Text-message surveys sped up and improved patient feedback overall, though hospitals still had to keep a phone option to avoid leaving some patients out. | B) Hospitals abandoned the text-message survey once they noticed a problem. | C) Text-message surveys completely replaced phone calls at every hospital. | D) Patients overwhelmingly prefer phone calls to text messages after a procedure.
why correct: A full statement of the central idea must include both the main benefit (faster, better feedback) and the stated limitation (some patients were missed), since the paragraph explicitly balances both.
tip: When a paragraph ends with a limitation or exception, a strong central-idea statement should account for it, not just the main benefit.

why correct: “Barked” tells what the puppy did.

stem: Which word is a linking verb? “The cookies appeared delicious as soon as they left the oven.”
options / answer: A) delicious | B) cookies | C) appeared | D) oven
why correct: “Appeared” links the cookies to the word that describes them.
tip: Linking verbs: am, is, are, was, were, seem, become, appear.

skill: Action, Main, Helping and Linking Verbs
stem: Choose the helping verb that completes this sentence correctly: “By sunset, the neighbors ____ repaired the old fence.”
options / answer: A) is | B) had | C) has | D) having
why correct: “Had repaired” is a verb phrase using the helping verb had to show an action completed before another past moment.
tip: Helping verbs: have, has, had, is, are, will, can.

skill: Action, Main, Helping and Linking Verbs
stem: Which modal verb shows PERMISSION? “You ____ leave early if you finish your work.”
options / answer: A) shall | B) would | C) must | D) may
why correct: “May” shows that permission is being given.
tip: may/can = permission; must = requirement.

skill: Action, Main, Helping and Linking Verbs
stem: Which TWO words are verbs? “Mariam whispered the answer, so she felt proud.”
options / answer: A) whispered | B) answer | C) felt | D) proud
why correct: “Whispered” is an action verb; “felt” links Mariam to “proud.”
tip: Find every word that shows action or links ideas.

skill: Action, Main, Helping and Linking Verbs
stem: Which sentence uses a linking verb correctly after a verb of the senses?
options / answer: A) The soup tastes delicious. | B) The soup tastes deliciously. | C) The soup taste delicious. | D) The soup tasting delicious.
why correct: “Tastes” links the soup to the describing word “delicious.”
tip: After linking verbs (taste, smell, look, feel), use adjectives.

skill: Action, Main, Helping and Linking Verbs
stem: Choose the modal verb: “Students ____ bring a pencil to the exam.”
options / answer: A) would | B) could | C) must | D) might
why correct: “Must” shows the pencil is required.
tip: must = required; might/could = possible.

skill: Action, Main, Helping and Linking Verbs
stem: In the sentence “The farmers have planted rice near the river,” which word is the MAIN verb?
options / answer: A) farmers | B) planted | C) have | D) river
why correct: “Planted” shows the action; “have” helps show the tense.
tip: The main verb carries the meaning; helping verbs add detail about time.

skill: Action, Main, Helping and Linking Verbs
stem: Choose the correct helping verb: “The letter ____ delivered yesterday, since it is already in the mailbox.”
options / answer: A) could have been | B) might have been | C) should have been | D) must have been
why correct: “Must have been” shows a confident conclusion based on strong evidence.
tip: must have + past participle = a confident conclusion about the past.

skill: Action, Main, Helping and Linking Verbs
stem: Which modal verb shows the SMALLEST chance something will happen? “It ____ snow in the desert this winter.”
options / answer: A) will | B) can | C) might | D) must
why correct: “Might” shows only a small possibility.
tip: might/may = possible; will/must = more certain.

skill: Action, Main, Helping and Linking Verbs
stem: Which sentence uses the irregular verb “to be” correctly?
options / answer: A) The weather be unusually cold last March. | B) The weather were unusually cold last March. | C) The weather is unusually cold last March. | D) The weather was unusually cold last March.
why correct: “Was” agrees with the singular subject “weather” in the past tense.
tip: Match “to be” to the subject and the time of the action.

skill: Action, Main, Helping and Linking Verbs
stem: Tap the part of the sentence that has an error.
options / answer: The twins |  has practiced |  their violin solos |  every evening.
why correct: “Twins” is plural, so the helping verb must be “have,” not “has.”
tip: Match the helping verb to the subject.

skill: Action, Main, Helping and Linking Verbs
stem: Choose the correct word: “After the race, Tariq ____ exhausted.”
options / answer: A) looked | B) look | C) looks | D) looking
why correct: “Looked” links Tariq to the describing word “exhausted” in the past tense.
tip: Sense verbs like look, seem and feel can act as linking verbs.

skill: Action, Main, Helping and Linking Verbs
stem: Match each verb with the type of verb it is.
options / answer: jumped = Action verb | seems = Linking verb | has = Helping verb | might = Modal verb
why correct: Each verb plays a different role: showing action, linking, helping, or showing possibility.
tip: Ask what job the verb is doing in the sentence.

skill: Action, Main, Helping and Linking Verbs
stem: Which sentence correctly uses a helping verb with the main verb “finished”?
options / answer: A) By noon, the workers had finished painting the fence. | B) By noon, the workers had finish painting the fence. | C) By noon, the workers has finished painting the fence. | D) By noon, the workers have finished painting the fence, yesterday.
why correct: “Had finished” correctly shows an action completed before another point in the past.
tip: Had + past participle shows one past action finished before another.

skill: Action, Main, Helping and Linking Verbs
stem: Which sentence uses a modal verb to express a POLITE request?
options / answer: A) Must you please pass the water jug? | B) Would you please pass the water jug? | C) Can you please pass the water jug, immediately? | D) Will you please pass the water jug, now?
why correct: “Would” softens the request and makes it sound polite.
tip: Would/could often make requests sound more polite than will/can.

skill: Action, Main, Helping and Linking Verbs
stem: Choose the correct verb form: “By the time the bus arrived, Noor ____ waiting for twenty minutes.”
options / answer: A) was | B) had been | C) is | D) has been
why correct: “Had been waiting” shows an action that continued up until another past event.
tip: Had been + -ing shows a longer past action interrupted by a later one.

skill: Action, Main, Helping and Linking Verbs
stem: Which sentence correctly uses the subjunctive mood with a verb?
options / answer: A) If I am taller, I could reach the top shelf. | B) If I were taller, I can reach the top shelf. | C) If I were taller, I could reach the top shelf. | D) If I was taller, I could reach the top shelf.
why correct: “Were” is used after “if” for conditions that are not true, even with a singular subject.
tip: Unreal “if” clauses use “were,” no matter the subject.

skill: Action, Main, Helping and Linking Verbs
stem: Which sentence correctly distinguishes a transitive verb from an intransitive one?
options / answer: A) In both sentences, the verbs are intransitive because no helping verb is used. | B) In “Samir mailed the package,” mailed is intransitive because “package” is a noun. | C) In “Samir arrived,” arrived is transitive because it describes an action. | D) In “Samir mailed the package,” mailed is transitive because it has a direct object; in “Samir arrived,” arrived is intransitive because it has no object.
why correct: A transitive verb passes its action to a direct object; an intransitive verb does not need one.
tip: Ask “verb + what?” — if there is an answer, it is transitive.

skill: Action, Main, Helping and Linking Verbs

skill: Action, Main, Helping and Linking Verbs
stem: Choose the linking verb: “The bread ____ warm right out of the oven.”
options / answer: A) bread | B) oven | C) seemed | D) warm
why correct: “Seemed” links the bread to the describing word “warm.”
tip: Linking verbs connect a subject to a word that describes it.

skill: Action, Main, Helping and Linking Verbs

skill: Action, Main, Helping and Linking Verbs

skill: Action, Main, Helping and Linking Verbs

skill: Action, Main, Helping and Linking Verbs

skill: Action, Main, Helping and Linking Verbs

why correct: “Committee” acts as one group, so it takes the singular verb “announces.”
tip: Collective nouns usually take a singular verb when acting as one unit.

skill: Action, Main, Helping and Linking Verbs
