options / answer: Years before, = starts a flashback | Suddenly, the alarm rang. = ends a flashback | She still remembered that day. = starts a flashback | Back in the present, = ends a flashback
why correct: Certain phrases consistently open a memory, while others snap the story back to now.
tip: Learn a short list of common flashback signal phrases.

stem: A baker’s story about her bakery jumps in time. Put these events in the order they really happened.
options / answer: Nadia’s grandmother taught her to knead bread before sunrise. → Nadia opened her own small bakery as a teenager. → A fire damaged Nadia’s bakery last year. → Nadia rebuilt the bakery using her grandmother’s old recipe.
why correct: The real order moves from the earliest lesson to the most recent rebuilding.
tip: Build a timeline using clues about age and “last year” versus “as a teenager.”

stem: A story about a toy maker opens with a broken toy on his workbench today, then flashes back to show how he built his very first toy as a boy. Why might the author choose to start in the present instead of telling events in order?
options / answer: A) Starting in the present makes the story shorter. | B) Starting in the present confuses readers on purpose with no reason. | C) Starting in the present creates a question that the flashback later answers. | D) Starting in the present removes the need for any ending.
why correct: Opening with the broken toy raises a question about the toy maker’s past, which the flashback then answers.
tip: Ask what question the opening scene raises that the flashback later answers.

stem: A swimmer named Karim holds his old, dented first medal while flashing back to a hard, losing race years ago; the story ends with him holding a shiny new medal. Why does the author include both medals?
options / answer: A) To explain how medals are manufactured. | B) To suggest Karim will stop swimming soon. | C) To prove that medals are not important to Karim. | D) To show how far Karim has come since his first difficult race.
why correct: Comparing the old medal from a loss with the new medal highlights Karim’s growth over time.
tip: When a story shows the same object twice, compare what it meant then and now.

stem: “The marathon runner stretched at the starting line. She remembered her very first race, years ago, when she had quit after only one mile. A whistle blew, and she focused on the road ahead.” Which part of the passage is the flashback?
options / answer: A) The memory of quitting her first race after one mile, years ago. | B) The runner stretching at the starting line. | C) The whistle blowing. | D) The runner focusing on the road ahead.
why correct: The memory of her first race, marked by “years ago,” is the flashback.
tip: Find the sentence or sentences describing an earlier time, then check where the story returns to now.

stem: A flashback can be as short as a single sentence or as long as several paragraphs.
options / answer: True | False
why correct: Flashbacks vary in length; some are brief memories, while others unfold in detail over several paragraphs.
tip: Length is not the test for a flashback — the shift in time is.

stem: “The old carpenter sanded the chair leg. In his mind, he was suddenly back in his father’s workshop forty years earlier, learning to hold a chisel for the first time. The radio crackled, and he was back in his own shop.” Which words signal the shift into the past?
options / answer: A) he was back in his own shop | B) In his mind, he was suddenly back in | C) The radio crackled | D) The old carpenter sanded the chair leg.
why correct: “In his mind, he was suddenly back in” is the exact phrase that opens the memory of the workshop.
tip: Phrases about the mind or being “back in” a place often open a flashback.

stem: A ship’s navigator studies a torn, old map today, then flashes back to the storm years ago when the map was torn while saving the crew. Why does the author include that memory?
options / answer: A) To describe how maps are printed. | B) To show that the navigator dislikes sailing. | C) To explain why the navigator still keeps and values the torn, old map. | D) To introduce the navigator’s childhood friend.
why correct: The memory of the storm explains the personal history and value behind the torn map.
tip: A flashback about an object’s history often explains why a character keeps it.

stem: A passage about two rival inventors jumps in time. Put these events in the order they really happened.
options / answer: The two inventors were childhood friends who built toys together. → The inventors had a disagreement over a shared design and became rivals. → Each inventor built a competing machine on their own. → The inventors finally combined their designs into one working machine.
why correct: The timeline moves from early friendship, through the disagreement, to separate work, and finally to reconciliation.
tip: List the relationship stages in order: friendship, conflict, separation, and reunion.

stem: Which best describes the difference between a flashback and foreshadowing?
options / answer: A) A flashback only happens in poems; foreshadowing only happens in stories. | B) A flashback hints at the future; foreshadowing shows the past. | C) They are two different names for the exact same technique. | D) A flashback shows a past event; foreshadowing hints at a future event.
why correct: A flashback moves backward in time to show a past event, while foreshadowing hints at something yet to come.
tip: Flashback = back in time; foreshadowing = forward hint.

stem: Several flashbacks placed throughout a story can build up a fuller picture of a character’s history.
options / answer: True | False
why correct: Each flashback can reveal a different piece of a character’s past, which together build a fuller history.
tip: Think of multiple flashbacks as puzzle pieces of a character’s past.

stem: Match each signal phrase to its function in a story.
options / answer: That reminded her of = starts a flashback | The ringing phone pulled him back to now = ends a flashback | Long before this voyage, = starts a flashback | In the present moment, = ends a flashback
why correct: Certain phrases consistently open a memory, while others return the story to the present.
tip: Build a list of common phrases for starting and ending a flashback.

stem: A night nurse pauses by a patient’s bed, then flashes back to the night years earlier when she herself was a frightened patient in that same hospital. If this flashback were removed, how would the passage change?
options / answer: A) Readers would not understand why the nurse treats her patients with such gentle patience. | B) The hospital setting would change to a school. | C) The nurse’s patient would recover instantly. | D) The passage would gain new characters.
why correct: The flashback connects the nurse’s own past fear to her gentle care now, giving her behavior a deeper meaning.
tip: Ask what the flashback explains about a character’s present behavior.

stem: A passage about a night nurse moves between past and present. Put these events in the order they really happened.
options / answer: The nurse was a frightened young patient in this same hospital. → The nurse decided then that she wanted to help scared patients someday. → The nurse studied nursing for several years after finishing school. → The nurse now works the night shift, comforting frightened patients.
why correct: The real order runs from her own frightening stay, through her decision and training, to her current work.
tip: Look for clues about her age and role to place each event in time.

stem: “The wildlife photographer lowered her camera. Ten years earlier, as a nervous intern, she had missed the shot of a lifetime because her hands shook. Now her hands were perfectly steady.” Which sentence is the flashback?
options / answer: A) Now her hands were perfectly steady. | B) Ten years earlier, as a nervous intern, she had missed the shot of a lifetime because her hands shook. | C) The wildlife photographer lowered her camera. | D) All three sentences describe the same moment in time.
why correct: The sentence marked “ten years earlier” describes the past, making it the flashback.
tip: A time-marker phrase like “ten years earlier” signals the flashback sentence.

stem: A flashback must always be introduced by the exact word “flashback.”
options / answer: True | False
why correct: Flashbacks are usually introduced through context clues and time-signal phrases, not the literal word “flashback.”
tip: Readers infer a flashback from clues like “years before” or “she remembered,” not a label.

stem: A retired teacher watches her former students graduate, then flashes back to her own difficult first year of teaching, struggling to control a noisy classroom. How does this flashback connect to the theme of the passage?
options / answer: A) It proves that her first year of teaching was her best year. | B) It shows that teaching never gets easier with experience. | C) It shows that patience and growth over time lead to the pride she feels at the graduation. | D) It explains why the graduation was canceled.
why correct: The flashback’s struggle contrasts with the present pride, reinforcing a theme of growth through experience.
tip: Connect a flashback’s content to the feeling or lesson shown in the present scene.

stem: A passage about a young coder jumps between past attempts and the present. Put these events in the order they really happened.
options / answer: The coder’s first program crashed the computer during a school demonstration. → The coder spent an entire summer studying how programs are built. → The coder built a simple working app the following year. → The coder now leads a small team building a much larger app.
why correct: The order moves from the early failure, through a summer of study, to small success, and finally to leadership.
tip: Look for clues about school years and seasons to rebuild the timeline.

stem: A mapmaker’s story saves a flashback about a fatal mistake on an early map for the very end, just before revealing why a modern explorer nearly got lost using an old copy. What effect does placing the flashback near the end create?
options / answer: A) It confirms the explorer’s route was always safe. | B) It removes any need for a conclusion. | C) It makes the ending less important than the middle of the story. | D) It delivers a twist that reframes everything readers thought they understood about the mapmaker.
why correct: Revealing the mapmaker’s old mistake late in the story creates a surprising twist that changes readers’ understanding.
tip: A late-placed flashback often works as a twist that recontextualizes earlier events.

stem: A lighthouse keeper’s daughter keeps her father’s old, cracked lantern on her shelf, flashing back to the storm when he used it to guide a ship to safety; the story ends with her lighting her own new lantern during a storm. Why might the author include both lanterns?
options / answer: A) To show that the daughter is carrying on her father’s legacy of guiding others safely. | B) To prove that lanterns are no longer useful. | C) To suggest the daughter plans to leave the lighthouse. | D) To explain how electricity was invented.
why correct: The old and new lanterns mirror each other, showing the daughter continuing her father’s role.
tip: When an object reappears across a flashback and the present, compare what it represents each time.

stem: A village storyteller is first shown as grumpy and unwelcoming, but a flashback reveals that he lost his own family in a flood years ago and has been alone since. How does this flashback likely change a reader’s judgment of the storyteller?
options / answer: A) It shows that the flood was the storyteller’s own fault. | B) It makes readers feel more sympathy for him by explaining the pain behind his behavior. | C) It makes readers trust him less because he lied about his past. | D) It proves that the storyteller was always a cheerful person.
why correct: Learning about the storyteller’s painful loss helps readers understand his grumpy behavior with more sympathy.
tip: A flashback revealing past pain often shifts readers’ judgment of a character.

stem: In a flashback, a young pilot notices a strange rattling sound in an old plane just before a minor crash landing; years later, as an experienced pilot, she hears the same sound and immediately lands safely. Which flashback detail connects to the safe ending?
options / answer: A) The color of the old plane she flew as a young pilot. | B) The number of passengers on her very first flight. | C) The strange rattling sound she first heard and ignored as a young pilot. | D) The name of the airport where she first trained.
why correct: The rattling sound links the two moments: ignoring it caused trouble once, and recognizing it later prevents trouble.
tip: Look for a specific sensory detail that repeats between the flashback and the present.

stem: A flashback must always appear at the very beginning of a story.
options / answer: True | False
why correct: A flashback can appear anywhere in a story — at the start, in the middle, or near the end — wherever the author needs it.
tip: Don’t assume a flashback only opens a story; check the whole passage for one.

skill: Adjectives, Articles and Order of Adjectives
stem: “A tiny lizard hid under the warm rock.” Which word describes HOW BIG the lizard is?
options / answer: A) rock | B) lizard | C) hid | D) tiny
why correct: “Tiny” tells the size of the lizard.
tip: Size adjectives answer the question “how big or small?”

skill: Adjectives, Articles and Order of Adjectives
stem: Choose the correctly ordered adjectives: “We adopted a ____ puppy.”
options / answer: A) puppy small | B) small brown | C) brown little | D) brown small
why correct: English adjective order usually places size before color: a small brown puppy.
tip: Remember a rough order: opinion, size, age, shape, color, origin, material, purpose.

skill: Adjectives, Articles and Order of Adjectives
stem: “Those mountains look snowy today.” Which word is a demonstrative adjective?
options / answer: A) Those | B) snowy | C) look | D) mountains
why correct: “Those” points out which mountains, so it is a demonstrative adjective.
tip: Demonstrative adjectives: this, that, these, those.

skill: Adjectives, Articles and Order of Adjectives
stem: “After the long hike, the campers felt exhausted.” Which word is the predicate adjective describing the campers?
options / answer: A) long | B) exhausted | C) campers | D) hike
why correct: “Exhausted” follows the linking verb “felt” and describes the campers.
tip: Predicate adjectives follow linking verbs like feel, seem, look, taste.

skill: Adjectives, Articles and Order of Adjectives
stem: Tap the part of the sentence that has an error.
options / answer: The chef served a |  well seasoned |  dish |  to every guest.
why correct: A compound adjective made of two words before a noun usually needs a hyphen: well-seasoned.
tip: Hyphenate two-word adjectives that work together before a noun.

skill: Adjectives, Articles and Order of Adjectives
stem: “Egyptian cotton is famous worldwide.” Which word is a proper adjective?
options / answer: A) cotton | B) famous | C) Egyptian | D) worldwide
why correct: “Egyptian” comes from the proper noun Egypt and is capitalized, making it a proper adjective.
tip: Proper adjectives come from proper nouns and are always capitalized.

skill: Adjectives, Articles and Order of Adjectives
stem: There are ____ clouds in the sky today than yesterday.
options / answer: A) little | B) less | C) fewer | D) much
why correct: “Clouds” can be counted, so the correct comparing word is “fewer.”
tip: Use fewer for countable nouns and less for uncountable nouns.

skill: Adjectives, Articles and Order of Adjectives
stem: Which sentence uses the irregular comparative correctly?
options / answer: A) The new bridge is bestest than the old wooden one. | B) The new bridge is gooder than the old wooden one. | C) The new bridge is more better than the old wooden one. | D) The new bridge is better than the old wooden one.
why correct: “Good” changes irregularly: good → better → best.
tip: Memorize irregular comparatives like good/better/best and bad/worse/worst.

skill: Adjectives, Articles and Order of Adjectives
stem: Tap the part of the sentence that has an error.
options / answer: I am very |  interesting |  in that mystery |  novel.
why correct: A person who feels curiosity about something is “interested,” while “interesting” describes the thing that causes the feeling.
tip: -ed adjectives describe feelings; -ing adjectives describe what causes the feeling.

skill: Adjectives, Articles and Order of Adjectives
stem: Which sentence uses the adjective correctly after a linking verb?
options / answer: A) The blanket feels soft against her cheek. | B) The blanket feels softly against her cheek. | C) The blanket feel soft against her cheek. | D) The blanket feels soft against her cheekly.
why correct: “Feels” is a linking verb here, so it should be followed by the adjective “soft,” not an adverb.
tip: After linking verbs (is, seems, tastes, feels, smells), use adjectives.

skill: Adjectives, Articles and Order of Adjectives
stem: Which sentence uses “looks” correctly, keeping in mind that “looks” can act as a linking verb or an action verb?
options / answer: A) The old barn looks shakily in the strong wind. | B) The old barn looks shaky in the strong wind. | C) The old barn look shaky in the strong wind. | D) The old barn looks shaky in the strongly wind.
why correct: “Looks” links “barn” to a quality, so the adjective “shaky” is correct.
tip: If a verb describes a quality rather than an action, follow it with an adjective.

skill: Adjectives, Articles and Order of Adjectives
stem: “The curious explorer studied the ancient, crumbling wall.” Which two words are coordinate adjectives (adjectives of equal importance, separated by a comma, both describing “wall”)?
options / answer: A) the, ancient | B) studied, wall | C) ancient, crumbling | D) curious, explorer
why correct: “Ancient” and “crumbling” are both adjectives of equal weight describing the wall, so they are separated by a comma.
tip: Coordinate adjectives can usually be swapped or joined with “and” and still make sense.

skill: Adjectives, Articles and Order of Adjectives
stem: Tap the part of the sentence that has an error.
options / answer: The hikers found a |  narrow, rocky, steep |  path |  up the cliff.
why correct: Three or more coordinate adjectives in a series usually need “and” before the last one, plus commas between the others.
tip: In a list of three or more adjectives, use commas and “and” before the final item.

skill: Adjectives, Articles and Order of Adjectives
stem: Which sentence correctly avoids comparing an absolute adjective (one that cannot logically have degrees, like “perfect” or “round”)?
options / answer: A) Her solution to the puzzle was the most perfect. | B) Her solution to the puzzle was perfecter. | C) Her solution to the puzzle was more perfect. | D) Her solution to the puzzle was perfect.
why correct: “Perfect” describes a complete, flawless state, so it should not be compared with “more” or “-er.”
tip: Absolute adjectives like perfect, round, and complete usually cannot be compared.

skill: Adjectives, Articles and Order of Adjectives
stem: Choose the article: “She is ____ honest witness in this case.”
options / answer: A) a | B) the | C) some | D) an
why correct: “Honest” starts with a vowel sound because the h is silent, so it takes “an.”
tip: Choose a/an based on the SOUND of the next word, not just its first letter.

skill: Adjectives, Articles and Order of Adjectives
stem: Which sentence lists the adjectives in the correct order?
options / answer: A) The chef used two small ripe green mangoes. | B) The chef used green small two ripe mangoes. | C) The chef used ripe small two green mangoes. | D) The chef used small two ripe green mangoes.
why correct: The usual order is quantity, size, condition, then color: two, small, ripe, green.
tip: Build a mental checklist: quantity, size, age/condition, shape, color, origin, material.

skill: Adjectives, Articles and Order of Adjectives
stem: A predicate adjective always comes directly before the noun it describes.
options / answer: True | False
why correct: A predicate adjective comes AFTER a linking verb and describes the subject, not directly before a noun.
tip: Predicate adjectives follow linking verbs: The sky is clear.

skill: Adjectives, Articles and Order of Adjectives
stem: Tap the part of the sentence that has an error.
options / answer: This recipe needs |  less |  eggs |  than the last one.
why correct: “Eggs” is a countable noun, so the correct comparing word is “fewer,” not “less.”
tip: Fewer for things you can count; less for things you cannot count.

skill: Adjectives, Articles and Order of Adjectives
stem: Which sentence correctly uses a possessive adjective?
options / answer: A) There tent blew away in the sudden wind. | B) Their tent blew away in the sudden wind. | C) Them tent blew away in the sudden wind. | D) They’re tent blew away in the sudden wind.
why correct: “Their” is the possessive adjective that correctly shows ownership of the tent.
tip: Possessive adjectives (my, your, his, her, its, our, their) come directly before a noun.

skill: Adjectives, Articles and Order of Adjectives
stem: Which sentence uses “smells” correctly, keeping in mind it can act as a linking verb?
options / answer: A) The bakery smells wonderful this morningly. | B) The bakery smells wonderfully this morning. | C) The bakery smells wonderful this morning. | D) The bakery smell wonderful this morning.
why correct: “Smells” describes a quality of the bakery here, so the adjective “wonderful” follows it correctly.
tip: When a sense verb describes a quality, follow it with an adjective, not an adverb.

skill: Adjectives, Articles and Order of Adjectives
stem: Which sentence correctly compares three or more items?
options / answer: A) Of the three trails, this one is the more difficult. | B) Of the three trails, this one is more difficult. | C) Of the three trails, this one is difficulter. | D) Of the three trails, this one is the most difficult.
why correct: “Of the three” signals a comparison among three or more items, which requires the superlative “most difficult.”
tip: Two items: comparative (more/-er). Three or more: superlative (most/-est).

skill: Adjectives, Articles and Order of Adjectives
stem: Which sentence correctly uses a hyphenated compound adjective before a noun?
options / answer: A) The team built a ten-minute presentation for the contest. | B) The team built a ten-minutes presentation for the contest. | C) The team built a ten minute’s presentation for the contest. | D) The team built a ten minute presentation for the contest.
why correct: “Ten-minute” is a compound adjective describing the presentation and is hyphenated before the noun.
tip: Hyphenate a number-plus-unit adjective before a noun, and keep the unit singular.

skill: Adjectives, Articles and Order of Adjectives
stem: Which sentence correctly uses an absolute adjective without comparing it illogically?
options / answer: A) The circle drawn by the compass was the roundest. | B) The circle drawn by the compass was round. | C) The circle drawn by the compass was very most round. | D) The circle drawn by the compass was more round.
why correct: “Round” describes a complete state and is generally not compared using more/most or -er/-est.
tip: Absolute adjectives (round, perfect, complete) resist comparison because they describe an all-or-nothing quality.

skill: Adjectives, Articles and Order of Adjectives
stem: Tap the part of the sentence that has an error.
options / answer: The committee reviewed a |  detailed, well researched, |  and |  persuasive proposal.
why correct: The two-word compound adjective “well researched” needs a hyphen when it comes directly before the noun it describes: well-researched.
tip: Hyphenate a compound adjective made of an adverb and participle only when it sits right before the noun.

skill: Adjectives, Articles and Order of Adjectives
stem: Which sentence lists the adjectives in the correct conventional order?
options / answer: A) We admired a wooden stunning antique chest. | B) We admired an antique wooden stunning chest. | C) We admired a stunning antique wooden chest. | D) We admired an antique stunning wooden chest.
why correct: The conventional order is opinion, then age, then material: stunning, antique, wooden.
tip: Memorize the general order: opinion, size/shape, age, color, origin, material, purpose.

skill: Adjectives, Articles and Order of Adjectives
stem: The committee needs ____ information before approving the project.
options / answer: A) more | B) less information’s | C) much more many | D) fewer
why correct: “Information” is uncountable, and the comparing word “more” fits uncountable nouns correctly.
tip: Use more/less for uncountable nouns like information, and more/fewer for countable nouns.

skill: Adjectives, Articles and Order of Adjectives
stem: Which sentence correctly uses a participial adjective to describe a feeling rather than a cause?
options / answer: A) The audience was fascinate by the magician’s final trick. | B) The audience were fascinated by the magician’s final trick, fascinatingly. | C) The audience was fascinating by the magician’s final trick. | D) The audience was fascinated by the magician’s final trick.
why correct: “Fascinated” correctly describes the audience’s feeling, caused by the trick.
tip: -ed participial adjectives describe how someone feels; -ing ones describe what causes the feeling.

skill: Adjectives, Articles and Order of Adjectives
stem: Which sentence correctly places a long string of coordinate adjectives with commas?
options / answer: A) The museum displayed a rare, delicate, hand-painted vase. | B) The museum displayed, a rare, delicate, hand-painted, vase. | C) The museum displayed a rare, delicate hand painted, vase. | D) The museum displayed a rare delicate hand-painted vase.
why correct: Each coordinate adjective in the series is separated by a comma, and the final one sits right before the noun.
tip: Commas separate coordinate adjectives, but none comes right before the noun itself.

skill: Adjectives, Articles and Order of Adjectives
stem: Which sentence correctly compares using “farther” versus “further” (farther for physical distance, further for extent or degree)?
options / answer: A) The hikers walked far than the map had suggested. | B) The hikers walked farther than the map had suggested. | C) The hikers walked farer than the map had suggested. | D) The hikers walked further than the map had suggested, in distance.
why correct: “Farther” is the traditional choice for physical distance, which fits the hikers walking a longer distance.
tip: Farther usually describes physical distance; further usually describes degree or extent.

skill: Adjectives, Articles and Order of Adjectives
stem: Tap the part of the sentence that has an error.
options / answer: The two scientists |  proposed a |  more unique |  solution to the problem.
why correct: “Unique” is generally treated as an absolute adjective meaning one of a kind, so it is not usually compared with “more.”
tip: Treat unique like an absolute adjective; avoid “more unique” or “most unique.”

skill: Adjectives, Articles and Order of Adjectives
stem: Which sentence correctly uses a predicate adjective after a linking verb, rather than an adverb?
options / answer: A) The committee’s decision seem fair to everyone involved. | B) The committee’s decision seemed fair to everyone involving. | C) The committee’s decision seemed fair to everyone involved. | D) The committee’s decision seemed fairly to everyone involved.
why correct: “Seemed” links “decision” to a quality, so the predicate adjective “fair” is correct.
tip: After linking verbs like seem, appear, and become, choose an adjective, not an adverb.

skill: Adjectives, Articles and Order of Adjectives
stem: Which sentence correctly orders a long string of adjectives across several categories (opinion, age, origin, material)?
options / answer: A) She inherited an old, beautiful, Japanese, porcelain tea set. | B) She inherited a Japanese, old, beautiful, porcelain tea set. | C) She inherited a porcelain, beautiful, old, Japanese tea set. | D) She inherited a beautiful, old, Japanese, porcelain tea set.
why correct: The conventional order places opinion first, then age, then origin, then material: beautiful, old, Japanese, porcelain.
tip: When several categories appear together, work through the order one category at a time.

skill: Poetry: Structure, Rhyme, Meter and Form
stem:
Read this poem.

“The desert wakes at break of day,
Soft golden light begins to play.

The camels rise with gentle sound,
Their shadows stretch across the ground.”

How many stanzas does this poem have?
options / answer: A) two | B) four | C) three | D) one
why correct: A blank line separates the poem into two groups of two lines each, so there are two stanzas.
tip: Count the groups of lines separated by blank lines.

skill: Poetry: Structure, Rhyme, Meter and Form
stem: Read these lines: “The river flows so calm and wide, / Fish dart and dive and glide and hide.” Which pair of words rhymes?
options / answer: A) flows, calm | B) wide, hide | C) river, fish | D) dart, dive
why correct: “Wide” and “hide” end with the same sound.
tip: Rhyming words usually share the same ending sound.

skill: Poetry: Structure, Rhyme, Meter and Form
stem:
Read: “The kitten naps,
The kitten plays,
The kitten purrs
Through sleepy days.”
Which word is repeated at the start of several lines?
options / answer: A) sleepy | B) plays | C) The kitten | D) naps
why correct: “The kitten” begins three of the four lines, which is a repeated phrase.
tip: Repetition often appears at the start or end of several lines.

skill: Poetry: Structure, Rhyme, Meter and Form
stem:
Read: “The wind blows free,
Across the sea,
No set beat to its song,
It wanders right along.”
What is this poem’s rhyme pattern for the first two lines?
options / answer: A) Every line in the poem rhymes with every other line. | B) The lines rhyme in the middle, not at the end. | C) They do not rhyme with any other line. | D) They rhyme with each other (free, sea).
why correct: “Free” and “sea” share the same ending sound, forming a rhyming pair.
tip: Check the very last sound of each line to find rhyming pairs.

skill: Poetry: Structure, Rhyme, Meter and Form
stem: Tap the part of the sentence that has an error.
options / answer: The poem has |  three stanza |  with four lines |  in each one.
why correct: “Stanza” needs the plural form “stanzas” to match the number “three.”
tip: Match singular and plural forms: one stanza, three stanzas.

skill: Poetry: Structure, Rhyme, Meter and Form
stem: Read: “Stars appear one by one tonight, / Tiny sparks of silver light.” Which word best describes the overall mood created by these lines?
options / answer: A) peaceful | B) frightening | C) angry | D) chaotic
why correct: The quiet image of stars gently appearing creates a calm, peaceful mood.
tip: Picture the scene the words describe, then name the feeling it gives you.

skill: Poetry: Structure, Rhyme, Meter and Form
stem: A poem with lines that do not rhyme and have no regular rhythm, like a short descriptive paragraph broken into lines, is called what?
options / answer: A) a limerick | B) free verse | C) a rhyming couplet | D) a haiku
why correct: Free verse poetry has no required rhyme or regular rhythm pattern.
tip: Free verse = free from strict rhyme and rhythm rules.

skill: Poetry: Structure, Rhyme, Meter and Form
stem:
Read: “The market hums with morning trade,
Fruit stacked high in sun and shade.

Voices call and coins exchange,
Colors bright and smells so strange.”
How do the two stanzas work together?
options / answer: A) The stanzas have no connection to each other. | B) The two stanzas describe two completely different markets. | C) The first stanza sets the scene, and the second adds sounds and smells to it. | D) The second stanza contradicts everything in the first.
why correct: The first stanza introduces the market, and the second stanza builds on it with more sensory details.
tip: Ask how each new stanza adds to or builds on the one before it.

skill: Poetry: Structure, Rhyme, Meter and Form
stem: Read: “Tap, tap, tap, the rain falls down, / Drip, drip, drip, upon the town.” Which poetic element is created by repeating “tap” and “drip” three times each?
options / answer: A) the color of the rain | B) the size of the town | C) a rhyme with the word “down” | D) the sound of the falling rain
why correct: Repeating “tap” and “drip” imitates the actual sound of rain falling.
tip: Repeated sound words often imitate the noise they describe.

skill: Poetry: Structure, Rhyme, Meter and Form
stem: A poem has three lines: the first and third rhyme, and the middle line does not rhyme with either. What is this rhyme pattern usually written as?
options / answer: A) ABA | B) AAA | C) ABC | D) AAB
why correct: The first and third lines share the same letter (A) because they rhyme, while the middle line gets a different letter (B).
tip: Label each line’s rhyme sound with a letter, starting from A.

skill: Poetry: Structure, Rhyme, Meter and Form
stem:
Read this poem.

“The harbor wakes before the sun,
Boats creak and sway, their long day begun.

Gulls circle low with hungry cries,
And nets are cast beneath gray skies.

By noon the catch is sorted fast,
And morning's rush has slipped into the past.”

How many stanzas does this poem have?
options / answer: A) two | B) three | C) one | D) six
why correct: Two blank lines divide the poem into three stanzas of two lines each.
tip: Count blank lines, then add one to find the number of stanzas.

skill: Poetry: Structure, Rhyme, Meter and Form
stem: Read: “The city hums with endless sound, / Lights and voices all around.” Which pair of words rhymes?
options / answer: A) lights, voices | B) endless, all | C) sound, around | D) city, hums
why correct: “Sound” and “around” share the same ending sound.
tip: Focus only on the final sound of each line when checking for rhyme.

skill: Poetry: Structure, Rhyme, Meter and Form
stem:
Read: “The orchard waits in silver frost,
Its summer fruit all long since lost.

Yet roots still hold their steady ground,
And spring will come, as spring is bound.”
How does the second stanza relate to the first?
options / answer: A) The first stanza is hopeful, and the second stanza is hopeless. | B) The second stanza describes a completely unrelated season. | C) The stanzas repeat the exact same idea twice. | D) The first stanza shows loss, and the second stanza offers hope for renewal.
why correct: The first stanza focuses on what is lost, while the second stanza turns toward hope for spring’s return.
tip: Track how the poem’s feeling or focus shifts from one stanza to the next.

skill: Poetry: Structure, Rhyme, Meter and Form
stem: Tap the part of the sentence that has an error.
options / answer: This poem has |  a rhyme pattern of |  ABAB |  in every stanza except the last.
why correct: This is already written correctly; a rhyme pattern like ABAB uses capital letters with no spaces or punctuation between them.
tip: Rhyme-scheme labels are written as capital letters side by side, like ABAB or AABB.

skill: Poetry: Structure, Rhyme, Meter and Form
stem: A poem has four lines where the first rhymes with the second, and the third rhymes with the fourth. What is this rhyme pattern called?
options / answer: A) AABB | B) ABAB | C) ABBA | D) AAAA
why correct: The first two lines share one rhyme (AA), and the last two lines share a different rhyme (BB).
tip: Label each line with a letter in order, repeating a letter only when the rhyme matches.

skill: Poetry: Structure, Rhyme, Meter and Form
stem: Which poetic form is traditionally written in three unrhymed lines with a 5-7-5 syllable pattern, often about nature?
options / answer: A) limerick | B) haiku | C) sonnet | D) free verse
why correct: A haiku follows a strict three-line, 5-7-5 syllable structure, often focused on nature.
tip: Haiku: 3 lines, 5-7-5 syllables, usually about nature.

skill: Poetry: Structure, Rhyme, Meter and Form
stem: Read: “The train pulls slowly from the station, / Carrying hopes to each far-off destination.” What is the overall effect of the repeated long “o” and “a” vowel sounds across these lines?
options / answer: A) It has no effect on the poem's rhythm at all. | B) It changes the meaning of the word “train” entirely. | C) It creates a slow, drawn-out rhythm that matches the train’s gradual movement. | D) It makes the lines sound fast and choppy.
why correct: The repeated long vowel sounds slow the reading pace, mirroring the train’s slow departure.
tip: Notice how vowel sounds can speed up or slow down how a line feels when read aloud.

skill: Poetry: Structure, Rhyme, Meter and Form
stem: Read: “The lantern swings from the old ship's bow, / Guiding sailors home, as it always does, somehow.” When a sentence or idea continues from one line into the next without a pause, this is called what?
options / answer: A) a refrain | B) a stanza break | C) a rhyme scheme | D) enjambment
why correct: When the sentence flows past the end of the line without stopping, it is called enjambment.
tip: Enjambment: a thought that runs on past the line break without a pause.

skill: Poetry: Structure, Rhyme, Meter and Form
stem: A short phrase or line that repeats at set points throughout a song or poem, such as after every stanza, is called what?
options / answer: A) a refrain | B) an acrostic | C) an ode | D) an elegy
why correct: A refrain is a phrase or line that repeats at regular points in a poem or song.
tip: Refrain = a line that returns again and again, like a chorus.

skill: Poetry: Structure, Rhyme, Meter and Form
stem: In a poem about rebuilding after a storm, the final stanza suddenly shifts to describing a brand-new morning, using only short, simple sentences. What effect does this structural shift likely create?
options / answer: A) It proves the poem has no connection between its stanzas. | B) It mirrors the fresh start the community feels after the storm has passed. | C) It shows that the storm has returned even stronger. | D) It means the poet made an error in the final stanza.
why correct: Shifting to short, simple sentences about a new morning reflects the community’s fresh, hopeful start.
tip: A sudden shift in sentence structure near the end often signals a shift in feeling or meaning.

skill: Poetry: Structure, Rhyme, Meter and Form
stem:
Read this poem.

“The quarry sleeps beneath the dust,
Its ancient stone begins to rust.

Yet workers come with steady hands,
To shape new life from these old lands.”

How many stanzas does this poem have, and how many lines are in each?
options / answer: A) two stanzas, with three lines each | B) four stanzas, with one line each | C) two stanzas, with two lines each | D) one stanza, with four lines
why correct: The blank line divides the poem into two stanzas, each containing two lines.
tip: Count the blank lines first, then count the lines within each resulting group.

skill: Poetry: Structure, Rhyme, Meter and Form
stem: Tap the part of the sentence that has an error.
options / answer: This poem follows |  a strict |  rhythm pattern |  call meter.
why correct: The verb needed here is “called,” the past participle form, not “call.”
tip: Check that participles like “called” or “named” are spelled correctly after a noun phrase.

skill: Poetry: Structure, Rhyme, Meter and Form
stem: The regular pattern of stressed and unstressed syllables in a line of poetry is called what?
options / answer: A) rhyme scheme | B) stanza | C) enjambment | D) meter
why correct: Meter refers to the regular rhythm created by stressed and unstressed syllables.
tip: Meter is the “heartbeat” rhythm of a poem's syllables.

skill: Poetry: Structure, Rhyme, Meter and Form
stem: A poem written in two rhyming lines that form a complete thought, often used to end a longer poem, is called what?
options / answer: A) a couplet | B) a stanza break | C) a quatrain | D) a refrain
why correct: A couplet is exactly two lines that rhyme and usually express one complete thought.
tip: Couplet = a pair (“couple”) of rhyming lines.

skill: Poetry: Structure, Rhyme, Meter and Form
stem: Read: “The factory hums both day and night; / Its tired workers long for light.” Which word choice most strongly contributes to the poem's weary, exhausted tone?
options / answer: A) hums | B) tired | C) factory | D) night
why correct: “Tired” directly names the workers' exhaustion, strongly shaping the poem's weary tone.
tip: Look for words that directly name an emotion or physical state to find what shapes a poem's tone.

skill: Poetry: Structure, Rhyme, Meter and Form
stem: A songwriter groups her verses into blocks of exactly four lines each. What is each of those blocks called?
options / answer: A) a sestet | B) a tercet | C) a quatrain | D) a couplet
why correct: A poetry block made of exactly four lines has its own special name: a quatrain.
tip: Memorize the family of length names together so you can tell them apart quickly.

skill: Poetry: Structure, Rhyme, Meter and Form
stem: Read: “The old clock ticks, its gears worn thin, / Marking time that none can win.” How does the structure of comparing a clock to an unwinnable race contribute to the poem's meaning?
options / answer: A) It proves the poem has no central theme. | B) It shows that the poem is only about repairing clocks. | C) It suggests the clock will stop working very soon. | D) It reinforces the idea that time moves forward no matter what anyone does.
why correct: Comparing time to a race no one can win emphasizes that time's passage is unstoppable, which supports the poem's theme.
tip: When a poem compares an object to an abstract idea, ask what larger meaning that comparison supports.

skill: Poetry: Structure, Rhyme, Meter and Form
stem: A poem shifts from long, flowing sentences in its first half to short, clipped sentences in its second half, right as the subject changes from a calm morning to a sudden storm. What is the most likely purpose of this structural shift?
options / answer: A) To make the pace of the lines match the sudden change in the weather. | B) To prove that the storm was not actually dangerous. | C) To show that the poet ran out of ideas partway through. | D) To separate the poem into two unrelated topics.
why correct: Shortening the sentences as the storm begins mirrors the sudden, sharp change in the weather.
tip: A shift in sentence length or rhythm often mirrors a shift in the action or mood being described.

skill: Poetry: Structure, Rhyme, Meter and Form
stem: In a poem about an abandoned lighthouse, the final stanza repeats the exact first line of the poem, unchanged. What effect does this repetition most likely create?
options / answer: A) It proves the lighthouse was recently rebuilt. | B) It gives the poem a circular structure, suggesting the lighthouse's story continues unchanged. | C) It means the second half of the poem should be ignored. | D) It shows that the poet forgot what was already written.
why correct: Returning to the exact opening line creates a circular, unchanging structure that reflects the lighthouse's unchanging state.
tip: A poem that ends by repeating its opening line often suggests something has come full circle.

skill: Poetry: Structure, Rhyme, Meter and Form
stem: A six-line stanza is more specifically called what?
options / answer: A) a quatrain | B) a couplet | C) a sestet | D) a tercet
why correct: A stanza made up of exactly six lines is called a sestet.
tip: Learn the stanza-length names: couplet (2), tercet (3), quatrain (4), sestet (6).

stem: Choose the correct word: “Please put the letter over ____.”
options / answer: A) their | B) there | C) thare | D) they're
why correct: “There” points to a location, which fits “over ____.”
tip: There = place, their = ownership, they're = they are.

stem: Choose the correct word: “Is ____ time to leave yet?”
options / answer: A) it is' | B) its | C) it's | D) its'
why correct: “It’s” is the contraction for “it is,” which fits this question.
tip: It's = it is; its = belonging to it.

stem: Which pair of words are homophones (same sound, different spelling and meaning)?
options / answer: A) run, running | B) quick, fast | C) happy, sad | D) flower, flour
why correct: “Flower” and “flour” sound exactly the same but have completely different meanings and spellings.
tip: Homophones sound the same but are spelled differently and mean different things.

stem: In which sentence does “bow” mean to bend forward out of respect?
options / answer: A) The dancers took a graceful bow at the end of the show. | B) The ship's bow cut through the waves. | C) She tied a red bow on the gift box. | D) The archer carried his bow across the field.
why correct: In this sentence, “bow” describes the dancers bending forward to show respect to the audience.
tip: Homographs are spelled the same but can be pronounced and mean differently — use context to decide.

stem: Read: “The wind was too strong, so we had to wind the kite string back in.” How are the two words pronounced?
options / answer: A) The sentence contains a spelling mistake. | B) They are pronounced differently, even though they are spelled the same. | C) Only the second “wind” is a real word. | D) They are pronounced exactly the same way.
why correct: “Wind” (moving air) and “wind” (to coil something) are spelled the same but pronounced differently.
tip: Some homographs change pronunciation depending on their meaning.

stem: Tap the part of the sentence that has an error.
options / answer: The puppy ran |  threw the muddy garden |  and left paw prints |  all over the porch.
why correct: “Through” means to move from one side of something to the other, while “threw” is the past tense of the verb “throw.”
tip: Through = passing across a space; threw = past tense of throw.

stem: Choose the correct word: “My ____ is on the desk.”
options / answer: A) stationary | B) stationarry | C) stationeri | D) stationery
why correct: “Stationery” refers to paper and writing supplies, which fits an item on a desk.
tip: Stationery (with an e) = paper supplies; stationary (with an a) = not moving.

stem: Which sentence uses “desert” to mean a dry, sandy region, not to abandon something?
options / answer: A) The soldiers were ordered not to desert their post. | B) He feared the team would desert him before the game. | C) The camel crossed the vast, sandy desert. | D) She would never desert her best friend.
why correct: In this sentence, “desert” refers to the dry, sandy land the camel crosses.
tip: Note the stress: DES-ert (the place) vs. de-SERT (to abandon).

stem: Which pair of words are homographs (same spelling, different meaning)?
options / answer: A) sun, son | B) cat, hat | C) run, ran | D) bat (the animal), bat (used in baseball)
why correct: “Bat” is spelled the same in both cases but has two completely different meanings.
tip: Homographs look identical on the page but can mean very different things.

stem: Choose the correct word: “It took almost an ____ for the bus to finally arrive.”
options / answer: A) hour | B) our | C) are | D) hour's
why correct: “Hour” is the unit of time that fits after “an” in this sentence about waiting.
tip: Hour = unit of time; our = belonging to us.

stem: In which sentence does “lead” rhyme with “bed” (meaning the heavy metal)?
options / answer: A) The old pipes were made of lead. | B) She will lead the team to victory. | C) The coach will lead the warm-up exercises. | D) Who will lead the discussion tomorrow?
why correct: In this sentence, “lead” refers to the metal and is pronounced to rhyme with “bed.”
tip: Lead (the metal) rhymes with bed; lead (to guide) rhymes with bead.

stem: Choose the correct word: “The teacher gave us good ____ on the project.”
options / answer: A) advise | B) advice | C) advisement | D) advize
why correct: “Advice” is the noun form meaning guidance or suggestions, which fits after “good.”
tip: Advice is the noun (a piece of advice); advise is the verb (to advise someone).

stem: Which sentence uses “object” to mean a physical thing, not to disagree?
options / answer: A) Did anyone object to the new schedule? | B) A strange object appeared on the shore after the storm. | C) The lawyer stood up to object to the question. | D) Several citizens plan to object at the town meeting.
why correct: In this sentence, “object” is a noun meaning a physical thing found on the shore.
tip: Notice the stress: OB-ject (the thing) vs. ob-JECT (to disagree).

stem: Tap the part of the sentence that has an error.
options / answer: The new principle |  insisted that |  every student |  wear a nametag during the tour.
why correct: “Principal” refers to the head of a school, while “principle” means a basic rule or belief, so it cannot give instructions.
tip: Principal = a person (or main thing); principle = a rule.

stem: “The orchard hired extra workers to record record harvest numbers.” How do the two uses of “record” differ?
options / answer: A) Both words mean exactly the same thing and are pronounced the same way. | B) The first “record” describes the harvest, and the second is the verb. | C) The first “record” is a verb meaning to write down, and the second is an adjective describing the largest-ever harvest; they are stressed differently. | D) The sentence has a typo and should use two different words.
why correct: “Record” shifts both meaning and stress depending on whether it is used as a verb or as a noun/adjective.
tip: Check the word's job in the sentence (verb, or noun/adjective) to find its correct pronunciation.

stem: Choose the correct word: “The patient waited with great ____ in the hospital.”
options / answer: A) patients | B) patients' | C) patience | D) patiences
why correct: “Patience” means the ability to wait calmly, which fits this sentence.
tip: Patience = calm waiting; patients = people being treated by a doctor.

stem: Which sentence uses “content” to mean satisfied, not the information inside something?
options / answer: A) The teacher checked the content of each essay carefully. | B) The website's content was updated last week. | C) Please review the content of the report before the meeting. | D) After the long hike, the campers felt completely content.
why correct: In this sentence, “content” describes the campers' feeling of satisfaction.
tip: Notice the stress: con-TENT (satisfied) vs. CON-tent (what's inside).

stem: Which pair best shows a true set of homophones?
options / answer: A) peace, piece | B) quiet, calm | C) large, larger | D) bright, light
why correct: “Peace” and “piece” sound exactly alike but have completely different spellings and meanings.
tip: True homophones must sound identical, even though their spelling and meaning differ.

stem: Choose: “The new policy will ____ every department in the company.”
options / answer: A) affects' | B) a-fect | C) effect | D) affect
why correct: “Affect” is the verb meaning to influence something, which fits this sentence about the policy's influence.
tip: Affect is usually the verb (to influence); effect is usually the noun (a result).

stem: In which sentence does “tear” rhyme with “bear,” meaning to rip?
options / answer: A) Her eyes filled with a single tear of joy. | B) Be careful not to tear the delicate fabric. | C) A single tear rolled down her cheek. | D) He wiped away a tear before anyone noticed.
why correct: In this sentence, “tear” means to rip and is pronounced to rhyme with “bear.”
tip: Tear (rip) rhymes with bear; tear (crying) rhymes with ear.

stem: “Only a minute fraction of the seeds sprouted after the frost.” How is “minute” pronounced and what does it mean here?
options / answer: A) It is pronounced MIN-it and means sixty seconds. | B) It is pronounced my-NOOT and means sixty seconds. | C) It is pronounced my-NOOT and means extremely tiny. | D) It is pronounced MIN-it and means extremely tiny.
why correct: When “minute” means extremely tiny, it is pronounced my-NOOT, matching its use here describing how few seeds sprouted.
tip: Minute (MIN-it) = 60 seconds; minute (my-NOOT) = extremely tiny.

stem: Tap the part of the sentence that has an error.
options / answer: The mayor's new budget |  will |  effect |  every public school in the district.
why correct: “Affect” is the verb meaning to influence something, which fits here better than the noun “effect.”
tip: If something is being influenced, use affect as the verb; effect is usually the noun for the result.

stem: In which sentence does “object” mean “to disagree” rather than a physical thing?
options / answer: A) The museum displayed an ancient object from the dig. | B) A heavy object blocked the narrow hallway. | C) Scientists studied the strange object found near the coast. | D) The mayor expects several residents to object at tonight's hearing.
why correct: In this sentence, “object” is a verb meaning to voice disagreement at the hearing.
tip: Stress on the second syllable (ob-JECT) usually signals the verb meaning “to disagree.”

stem: Which sentence uses “refuse” to mean garbage, not to decline?
options / answer: A) The city collects refuse from every street twice a week. | B) The committee may refuse to approve the new budget. | C) She chose to refuse the invitation politely. | D) Workers can refuse unsafe assignments under this policy.
why correct: In this sentence, “refuse” is a noun meaning trash or garbage collected by the city.
tip: REF-use (noun, garbage) is stressed differently from re-FUSE (verb, to decline).

stem: Tap the part of the sentence that has an error.
options / answer: The contractor gave |  a rough |  estimate |  of the project's cost, witch seemed reasonable.
why correct: “Which” introduces extra information about the estimate, while “witch” refers to a person in folklore and does not fit here.
tip: Which = a question or relative word; witch = a person in folklore. Check the meaning needed.

stem: Which pair of words best shows true homophones in formal, academic writing?
options / answer: A) city, state | B) capital, capitol | C) large, huge | D) govern, government
why correct: “Capital” (a main city or wealth) and “capitol” (a government building) sound alike but differ in spelling and meaning.
tip: Capital = main city or money; capitol = the government building.

stem: Which line uses alliteration (repeated sounds at the START of words)?
options / answer: A) Big brown bears bathed by the barn. | B) The sun set behind the hill. | C) A dog barked twice last night.
why correct: “Big, brown, bears, bathed, barn” all start with the b sound.
tip: Alliteration repeats the first consonant sound in nearby words.

stem: Which line uses alliteration?
options / answer: A) The moon rose slowly tonight. | B) Tiny turtles trotted toward the tide. | C) Birds flew over the lake.
why correct: “Tiny, turtles, trotted, toward, tide” repeat the t sound at the start.
tip: Read the line aloud and listen for a sound that keeps coming back.

stem: Which line uses assonance (a repeated VOWEL sound inside the words)?
options / answer: A) Birds sang sweetly in the trees. | B) The cat sat on the bench. | C) The light, bright kite flies high tonight.
why correct: “Light, bright, kite, high, tonight” all share the long i sound.
tip: Assonance repeats a vowel sound; it does not have to be at the start of the word.

stem: Which line uses consonance (a repeated sound inside or at the end of words, not at the start)?
options / answer: A) The black trucks stacked rocks at dusk. | B) The cat sat on the mat. | C) Birds chirped in the garden.
why correct: The ck sound repeats inside “black, trucks, stacked, rocks.”
tip: Consonance can repeat a consonant sound anywhere in the word, not just the start.

stem: Which line uses alliteration?
options / answer: A) The sun was hot and bright. | B) Dusty desert camels crossed the cracked canyon. | C) The camel walked slowly across the sand.
why correct: “Dusty, desert, camels, crossed, cracked, canyon” share the hard c/k sound at the start.
tip: Alliteration can repeat a sound spelled with different letters, like c and k.

stem: Which line uses assonance?
options / answer: A) The train stopped at the station. | B) The driver waved at the crowd. | C) The train's pale gray paint faded away.
why correct: “Pale, gray, paint, faded, away” all share the long a sound.
tip: Say the line slowly and listen for one vowel sound echoing through it.

stem: The repeated f sound in “Five fat frogs flopped into the pond” is called ____.
options / answer: A) alliteration | B) rhyme | C) assonance
why correct: The repeated beginning consonant sound is alliteration.
tip: Beginning sound repeated = alliteration.

stem: Which line uses alliteration?
options / answer: A) Six sly sailors sailed past the silver ship. | B) The waves crashed onto the shore. | C) The ship sailed across the ocean.
why correct: “Sly, sailors, sailed, silver, ship” repeat the s sound at the start.
tip: Underline the first letter of each word to spot the repeating sound.

stem: Which line uses assonance?
options / answer: A) A moth landed on the lamp. | B) The bright firefly flies high in the sky. | C) The firefly glowed in the dark yard.
why correct: “Bright, firefly, flies, high, sky” all share the long i sound.
tip: Assonance is easiest to hear if you say the line slowly, stretching the vowels.

stem: Which line uses consonance?
options / answer: A) The ball rolled into the goal. | B) The kids played soccer after school. | C) The kids kicked quick, slick shots at the net.
why correct: The ck/k sound repeats inside “kicked, quick, slick, shots.”
tip: Listen for a consonant sound echoing in the middle or end of several words.

stem: Which line uses alliteration?
options / answer: A) Six sweet scones sat on the shelf. | B) The shelf held fresh bread. | C) The baker opened the shop early.
why correct: “Six, sweet, scones, sat, shelf” repeat the s sound at the start.
tip: Alliteration often appears in groups of three or more words in a row.

stem: Which line uses assonance?
options / answer: A) The bees buzzed around the hive. | B) The green bees sleep deep in the leaves. | C) The garden was full of flowers.
why correct: “Green, bees, sleep, deep, leaves” all share the long e sound.
tip: Look for the same vowel spelled in different ways, like ee and ea.

stem: In the line “The slimy snake slithered silently,” the repeated s sound at the start of each word is an example of alliteration.
options / answer: True | False
why correct: “Slimy, snake, slithered, silently” all begin with the s sound, which is alliteration.
tip: A repeated sound at the START of nearby words is alliteration.

stem: Which line uses consonance?
options / answer: A) The water was cold and clear. | B) The river flowed past the village. | C) The river rocks clicked and clacked below.
why correct: The ck sound repeats inside “rocks, clicked, clacked.”
tip: Consonance can repeat a sound in the middle of a word, not only at the end.

stem: Which line uses alliteration?
options / answer: A) Hungry hikers hauled heavy packs uphill. | B) The hikers reached the top at noon. | C) The trail was steep and rocky.
why correct: “Hungry, hikers, hauled, heavy” repeat the h sound at the start.
tip: Four or more words sharing a beginning sound is a strong clue to alliteration.

stem: Match each sound device with the line that shows it.
options / answer: Alliteration = Wild winds whipped the willow tree. | Assonance = The deep green stream gleamed in the light. | Consonance = The black truck backed into the dock. | Onomatopoeia = The balloon went pop!
why correct: Alliteration repeats a beginning sound, assonance repeats a vowel sound inside words, consonance repeats a consonant sound inside or at the end of words, and onomatopoeia is a word that imitates a sound.
tip: Ask: where in the words is the sound repeated — start, middle, or is it a sound-word itself?

stem: Which line uses BOTH alliteration and assonance?
options / answer: A) Sly snakes crawled through the grass. | B) Sly snakes slide through slippery, shiny slime. | C) The grass was wet and green.
why correct: The s sound repeats at the start (alliteration) and the long i sound repeats inside the words (assonance).
tip: Check the start of the words first, then check the vowel sounds inside them.

stem: Which line uses assonance?
options / answer: A) The water sparkled in the morning sun. | B) The stream flowed quietly through the valley. | C) The deep stream seemed to gleam at dawn.
why correct: “Deep, stream, seemed, gleam” all share the long e sound.
tip: Try reading only the vowels aloud to notice which sound keeps repeating.

stem: Which line uses consonance?
options / answer: A) The bright lights flashed, flickered, and cracked. | B) The crowd cheered loudly below. | C) The fireworks lit up the night sky.
why correct: The ck sound repeats inside “flashed, flickered, cracked.”
tip: Consonance is often easiest to hear near the ends of words.

stem: Which line uses alliteration?
options / answer: A) The library was calm and still. | B) Quiet, quick questions filled the library. | C) Students studied at the long tables.
why correct: “Quiet, quick, questions” repeat the qu sound at the start.
tip: Alliteration can repeat a sound spelled the same way, like qu.

stem: Which line uses assonance?
options / answer: A) The ocean was calm that morning. | B) The whale swam near the boat. | C) The pale whale sailed away at daybreak.
why correct: “Pale, whale, sailed, away, daybreak” all share the long a sound.
tip: Stretch out the vowels as you read the line to notice the repeated sound.

stem: Which line uses consonance?
options / answer: A) Trucks rolled past, horns blared and flared. | B) Trucks rolled slowly down the street. | C) The traffic light turned green.
why correct: The r sound repeats inside “trucks, rolled, horns, blared, flared.”
tip: Consonance can repeat a sound in several different positions within words.

stem: A poet writes “Wild winds whipped and wailed through the night.” Why would a poet choose this alliteration?
options / answer: A) To make the line easier to spell | B) To make the line's rhythm sound like the howling of the wind | C) To shorten the poem
why correct: Repeating the w sound mimics the rushing, blowing sound of wind, matching the line's meaning.
tip: Ask what feeling or sound the repeated letter imitates.

stem: Which line uses assonance?
options / answer: A) The sky was dark and starless. | B) The moon rose slowly over the hills. | C) The moon loomed low through the cool gloom.
why correct: “Moon, loomed, cool, gloom” all share the long oo sound.
tip: Long vowel sounds are often the easiest ones to spot repeating.

stem: In the line “Crash! Boom! Bang! went the thunder,” which sound device is used?
options / answer: A) Onomatopoeia, because the words imitate the actual sounds of thunder | B) Assonance, because the words share a vowel sound | C) Alliteration, because the words start with the same letter
why correct: Onomatopoeia uses words that sound like the noise they describe, such as crash, boom, and bang.
tip: If a word sounds like the noise it names, it is onomatopoeia, not alliteration.

stem: The repeated ck sound inside “The black truck backed into the dock” is an example of ____.
options / answer: A) alliteration | B) consonance | C) assonance
why correct: A consonant sound repeated inside or at the end of words is consonance.
tip: Consonance can hide in the middle of a word, not just the start or end.

stem: A poet writes “Fast, flashy cars flew by in a flash.” What effect does this alliteration create?
options / answer: A) It makes the sentence feel slow and calm | B) It makes the sentence feel quick and exciting, matching the speed of the cars | C) It makes the sentence confusing to read
why correct: The quick, repeated f sound mirrors the fast motion of the cars described.
tip: Match the sound of a line to the action or mood it is describing.

stem: Which line uses assonance?
options / answer: A) The whale dove beneath the waves. | B) A ship passed near the shore. | C) The pale whale sailed away across the bay.
why correct: “Pale, whale, sailed, away, bay” all share the long a sound.
tip: Assonance often links words that look different but sound alike inside.

stem: A poet writes “Pitter, patter, pitter, patter” to describe rain. What effect does this repeated consonance create?
options / answer: A) It mimics the steady, tapping sound of raindrops | B) It mimics the sound of thunder | C) It shows the rain is about to stop
why correct: The repeated t sound echoes the light, steady tapping of rain on a surface.
tip: Sound devices often copy the rhythm of the thing they describe.

stem: Which line uses alliteration?
options / answer: A) Water dripped from the ceiling. | B) Dark, damp, dripping decay filled the old cave. | C) The cave was cold and silent.
why correct: “Dark, damp, dripping, decay” repeat the d sound at the start.
tip: A gloomy scene often uses heavier sounds like d or b to set the mood.

stem: Which line uses assonance?
options / answer: A) The sky turned orange and pink. | B) The sun rose over the mountains. | C) The cold, slow glow of dawn broke over the hills.
why correct: “Cold, slow, glow” all share the long o sound.
tip: Read only the stressed vowels aloud to find the repeated sound.

stem: The word “buzz” in the sentence “The bee's buzz grew louder” is an example of onomatopoeia.
options / answer: True | False
why correct: “Buzz” imitates the actual sound a bee makes, which makes it onomatopoeia.
tip: Onomatopoeia words usually sound exactly like the noise they name.

stem: Which line uses consonance?
options / answer: A) The metal gears clattered, clanked, and cracked. | B) The factory was loud and busy. | C) The machine stopped working suddenly.
why correct: The k/ck sound repeats inside “clattered, clanked, cracked.”
tip: Harsh consonant sounds like k and ck often suggest loud, mechanical noise.

stem: A poet writes “Silent snow settled slowly on the sleeping town.” How does the alliteration affect the poem's mood?
options / answer: A) It creates a fast-paced, urgent mood | B) It creates a calm, quiet, gentle mood that matches the falling snow | C) It creates a loud, chaotic mood
why correct: The soft, repeated s sound mirrors the hush of snow falling gently.
tip: Soft consonant sounds like s or wh often create a calm, quiet feeling.

stem: Match each sound device with the line that shows it.
options / answer: Alliteration = Mighty machines marched across the field. | Assonance = The low, slow glow faded into night. | Consonance = The thin wind spun and spent itself at dusk. | Onomatopoeia = The old gate creaked open.
why correct: Alliteration repeats a beginning sound, assonance repeats a vowel sound inside words, consonance repeats a consonant sound inside or at the end of words, and onomatopoeia is a word that imitates a sound.
tip: Identify where the repeated sound falls in the words — start, middle, or the sound itself being imitated.

stem: Which line uses consonance but NOT alliteration?
options / answer: A) The bright, light kite flew high. | B) Grumpy goats grazed on the grassy green hill. | C) The restless engine growled, groaned, and grumbled through the night.
why correct: The gr sound repeats inside the words “growled, groaned, grumbled,” but the words do not all start the sentence's subject with the same sound pattern as a whole alliterative run.
tip: Consonance without alliteration repeats an inside sound while the surrounding words still vary.

stem: A poet writes “Deep, sleepy, creeping tide” to describe the ocean at night. What mood does the assonance create?
options / answer: A) A slow, calm, drowsy mood that matches the quiet tide | B) A frightening, dangerous mood | C) An excited, energetic mood
why correct: The repeated long e sound in “deep, sleepy, creeping” stretches the line and mirrors the slow, quiet tide.
tip: A drawn-out vowel sound often matches a slow, calm action.

stem: Which line uses alliteration to build suspense?
options / answer: A) Someone was walking nearby. | B) Footsteps followed, fading and fast, through the fog. | C) Footsteps echoed down the empty hall.
why correct: The repeated f sound and short phrasing speed up the rhythm, building tension as the footsteps approach.
tip: Fast, clipped alliteration can speed up a line's rhythm to build suspense.

stem: Read this sentence: “The old wooden bridge creaked and swayed over the churning brown river.” What should you picture?
options / answer: A) A bridge with no river underneath it | B) A new bridge standing still over calm water | C) A shaky bridge moving above fast, muddy water
why correct: The details “creaked,” “swayed,” and “churning brown” create a picture of an old, unsteady bridge over rough water.
tip: Picture each descriptive word one at a time, then put them together.

stem: Which sentence helps you picture the scene MOST clearly?
options / answer: A) The orange sun sank slowly behind the jagged purple mountains. | B) It was sunset. | C) The sun went down in the evening.
why correct: Specific colors (“orange,” “purple”) and shapes (“jagged”) let you form a clear mental picture.
tip: Vivid writing uses specific colors, shapes, and sizes.

stem: Read: “Thick gray smoke curled upward from the chimney and vanished into the cold sky.” What picture forms in your mind?
options / answer: A) A chimney with no smoke coming out | B) Smoke rising in curls from a chimney and disappearing into a cold sky | C) A warm, sunny sky with no smoke
why correct: The verbs “curled” and “vanished” and the detail “cold sky” build a clear image of rising, fading smoke.
tip: Pay attention to verbs that describe exactly how something moves.

stem: Which words help you picture the dog MOST clearly? “The shaggy, mud-splattered dog limped slowly toward the porch.”
options / answer: A) slowly, the, toward | B) dog, porch, toward | C) shaggy, mud-splattered, limped
why correct: “Shaggy,” “mud-splattered,” and “limped” describe exactly how the dog looks and moves.
tip: Look for adjectives and specific verbs, not just nouns.

stem: Read: “Tiny silver fish darted in every direction as the heron's shadow passed over the shallow pool.” What should you picture?
options / answer: A) Many small fish scattering quickly as a bird's shadow crosses the water | B) Fish resting calmly at the bottom of the pool | C) A heron swimming slowly in deep water
why correct: “Darted,” “shadow,” and “shallow pool” together create a picture of startled fish scattering under a passing bird.
tip: Combine the action verbs with the setting details to build one full picture.

stem: Which sentence gives you the clearest picture of how the kitchen smelled and sounded?
options / answer: A) The kitchen was being used. | B) Sizzling onions popped in the pan while the warm smell of garlic filled the kitchen. | C) Someone was cooking dinner.
why correct: “Sizzling,” “popped,” and “the warm smell of garlic” let you imagine the sound and smell of the kitchen.
tip: Strong imagery often appeals to more than one sense at a time.

stem: The sentence “The crowd was noisy” helps you picture the scene more clearly than “Thousands of fans roared and stomped their feet in the stands.”
options / answer: True | False
why correct: The second sentence gives specific, vivid details, while the first is vague and general.
tip: Specific details almost always create a clearer picture than a general statement.

stem: Read: “Jagged icicles hung from the roof like glittering daggers in the pale winter light.” What picture does the word “daggers” help you form?
options / answer: A) Icicles that are soft and round | B) A roof with no icicles at all | C) Icicles that look sharp and pointed, like blades
why correct: Comparing the icicles to daggers helps you picture their sharp, pointed shape.
tip: When writers compare one thing to another, picture the second thing to understand the first.

stem: Which detail helps you picture how tired the hikers were?
options / answer: A) Their legs trembled with every step as they dragged themselves up the final hill. | B) They had been hiking since morning. | C) The trail was five miles long.
why correct: “Trembled” and “dragged themselves” show physical signs of exhaustion you can picture.
tip: Look for details that show a feeling through the body, not just facts.

stem: Read: “The marketplace buzzed with vendors shouting prices, carts rattling over cobblestones, and the sharp smell of spices drifting through the air.” What should you picture and sense?
options / answer: A) A quiet, empty market at night | B) A busy, noisy marketplace full of sound, movement, and strong smells | C) A market with only one vendor
why correct: The sounds (“shouting,” “rattling”) and smell (“sharp smell of spices”) combine to show a busy, lively scene.
tip: When several senses are described together, picture the whole scene at once.

stem: Which revision adds the MOST vivid visual detail to “The storm was bad”?
options / answer: A) The storm lasted a long time. | B) The storm was very bad. | C) Lightning cracked the sky as hailstones the size of marbles hammered the rooftops.
why correct: Specific images like “lightning cracked” and “hailstones the size of marbles” let a reader clearly picture the storm.
tip: Add a size, shape, color, or comparison to make a vague sentence vivid.

stem: Which word choice helps you picture the water's movement MOST clearly? “The stream ____ over the smooth stones.”
options / answer: A) was | B) went | C) tumbled
why correct: “Tumbled” shows a specific, tumbling motion over the stones.
tip: Specific verbs almost always paint a clearer picture than general ones.

stem: Read: “The abandoned house leaned to one side, its broken shutters banging in the wind, paint peeling like old skin.” What mood does this imagery create?
options / answer: A) An eerie, neglected feeling, because every detail shows decay and disrepair | B) A busy, crowded feeling | C) A cheerful, welcoming feeling
why correct: Details like “leaned,” “broken,” “banging,” and “peeling” all build a picture of neglect, creating an eerie mood.
tip: Notice how several small visual details can add up to one overall feeling.

stem: Which sentence lets you picture the runner's exact movement, not just that she ran?
options / answer: A) She finished the race. | B) She pumped her arms and sprinted the last stretch, her ponytail whipping behind her. | C) She ran as fast as she could.
why correct: “Pumped her arms,” “sprinted,” and “ponytail whipping” show exactly how her body moved.
tip: Specific body details create a sharper picture than a general statement about speed.

stem: Read: “Dew clung to each blade of grass, catching the early light like scattered diamonds.” What picture does the comparison to diamonds create?
options / answer: A) A field covered in real diamonds | B) Grass that is completely dry | C) Drops of dew sparkling brightly in the morning sunlight
why correct: Comparing the dew to scattered diamonds helps you picture how brightly it sparkles in the light.
tip: A comparison in a description is a tool to picture the real thing more vividly, not a literal statement.

stem: Read: “The climber's fingers, raw and trembling, gripped the last crumbling ledge as pebbles skittered into the void below.” Which detail BEST helps you feel the danger of the moment?
options / answer: A) pebbles skittered into the void below | B) the climber kept going | C) the ledge was near the top
why correct: Picturing pebbles falling into empty space below shows just how high and dangerous the ledge is.
tip: The most vivid detail is often the one that shows consequence or risk, not just action.

stem: Which pair of sentences creates the clearest contrast in imagery between a calm and a chaotic scene?
options / answer: A) The pond was calm. Then it was not calm anymore. | B) The pond lay still and silver under the moon. Minutes later, sirens screamed and red lights flashed across the water. | C) The night was quiet. The night became loud.
why correct: The first pair uses specific visual details (“still and silver,” “sirens screamed,” “red lights flashed”) to show a sharp contrast.
tip: A strong contrast needs two sets of vivid, specific details, not just opposite labels.

stem: Which sentence helps you picture the campfire MOST clearly?
options / answer: A) Someone had started a fire. | B) The campfire was burning well. | C) Orange flames crackled and popped, sending sparks spiraling up into the dark sky.
why correct: “Crackled,” “popped,” and “sparks spiraling” let you both see and hear the campfire.
tip: Look for verbs that show sound as well as sight for the clearest picture.

stem: Read: “The glacier groaned and cracked, a slab of blue-white ice the size of a bus sliding slowly into the churning sea.” Which detail BEST helps you picture the glacier's enormous size?
options / answer: A) a slab of blue-white ice the size of a bus | B) the glacier groaned and cracked | C) the sea was churning
why correct: Comparing the ice slab to the size of a bus gives you a real-world object to measure its enormous size against.
tip: Writers often compare something huge or unfamiliar to an object the reader already knows the size of.

stem: Read: “Fog rolled in thick waves across the harbor, swallowing the masts of the fishing boats one by one.” What picture should form in your mind?
options / answer: A) A clear, sunny day at the harbor | B) Dense fog slowly covering boats in a harbor until they disappear from sight | C) Boats sailing quickly out of the harbor
why correct: “Rolled in thick waves” and “swallowing the masts” build a picture of fog gradually hiding the boats from view.
tip: Visualize description in order, the way the writer builds it, detail by detail.

stem: Which sentence creates the clearest picture of a busy construction site?
options / answer: A) The construction site was loud and busy. | B) Work was happening at the site. | C) Jackhammers pounded the pavement while dust clouded the air and workers shouted over the roar of machines.
why correct: The specific sounds (“pounded,” “roar”) and sight (“dust clouded the air”) let you picture and hear the scene.
tip: A vivid sentence usually combines at least two senses, like sound and sight.

stem: Read: “The abandoned lighthouse stood crooked against the gray sky, its once-white paint now streaked with rust-colored tears.” What does the phrase “rust-colored tears” help you picture?
options / answer: A) Long reddish-brown streaks of rust running down the lighthouse like tears on a face | B) A lighthouse that is freshly painted | C) A lighthouse crying real tears
why correct: Comparing the rust streaks to tears helps you visualize thin, dripping lines of reddish-brown color.
tip: When a description compares an object's marks to something human, like tears, picture the shape and movement, not the literal meaning.

stem: Which revision gives the clearest visual picture of “The kitchen was a mess”?
options / answer: A) Someone had used the kitchen a lot. | B) Flour dusted every counter, and dirty pans were stacked in a wobbling tower by the sink. | C) The kitchen needed to be cleaned.
why correct: Specific images like “flour dusted every counter” and “a wobbling tower” of pans let you picture the mess clearly.
